entries.title: The whole process, from catchment to results: What the app answers
entries.summary: The order to set a catchment up in, what each step needs, and how calibration and what-if runs fit in.
entries.text: A project models one river catchment day by day. Rain becomes natural flow, the flow is shared between the hydrological units, each hydrological unit fills its dam and irrigates, and whatever is left reaches the outlet. Every run answers three questions: how much water is there, can each hydrological unit’s irrigation be met, and does enough stay in the river for the EWR (Environmental Water Requirement)? The setup order follows the workspace’s Build the model section, top to bottom; the results are under Outcomes. Calibrate and run again until the fit is good enough, then use runs and copies of the project for what-ifs.

entries.title: The whole process, from catchment to results: The steps
entries.text: Create the project on the Projects page. See Create a project. Network: add the hydrological units and gauges, say what each drains into, and end at one outflow gauge. Give the hydrological units their areas. See Build the river network. Crops & demand (optional): crops with monthly crop factors, then the hectares each hydrological unit plants. Skip it if nothing is irrigated. See Set up crops and demand. Transfers (optional): pipelines or canals from one hydrological unit’s dam to another. See Add a transfer. Data: upload daily rainfall (required) and observed flow at the outlet (needed to calibrate). See Upload rainfall and flow data. Model settings: A-pan evaporation, how rain gaps are filled, how natural flow is made, the EWR and the simulation period. See Set the EWR. Calibration: the runoff model’s parameters, the calibration record and window, and fitting them to the observed flow. See Fit the runoff model automatically. Run the model on the Runs & results tab, then read the results. See Run the model and read the results. Iterate: improve the calibration, run again, and compare runs on Compare runs. Copy the project to try a what-if without touching the original. See Compare runs and try what-ifs. The Summary tab has a setup checklist that follows these steps. Each line says what is there or what to do next, and links to the tab. It also tells you when the project has changed since the last run. Once there is a run, the Summary opens on the results instead: four cards for the newest run, irrigation first: Irrigation supplied (the share of demand, and how many hydrological units fell below 95 %), the Shortfall (the demand not supplied over the run, in Mm³, and in an average year), Units curtailed (the days a drought restriction cut demand; without any, the Worst-supplied unit and its share) and how full the dams are, each with its change from the run before (the worst-supplied unit has none). The EWR’s results are on the EWR page (a link under the supply list goes there), and the calibration fit on Calibration. Then Needs attention cards (run warnings, new or old data and hydrological units with nothing planted, each a link to where it is fixed), with the Active alerts under them; and Supply by hydrological unit, the eight least supplied first (Show all lists the rest), where a hydrological unit’s name opens its planted areas and More on Hydrological units opens that page. The Dams today card opens the Dams tab. Once the run’s last day is more than a week old, the card says so by its date (Dams on 31 Dec 2024), and “this week” and “last 30 days” elsewhere give way to the date the figures end on in the same way. The published baseline and a link to Project sit under the supply list. Once every setup step is done, the checklist leaves the page: a Setup complete button at the top, beside the rain date, opens the steps over the page.

entries.title: The whole process, from catchment to results: Getting around a project
entries.text: A project’s tabs are grouped in three sections. Review holds the Project page, Applications and the History of changes. Build the model is what the model is made of, in setup order: Network, the Map (the geography: boundary, parcels, dams, gauges and rivers; the Network’s header links to it too), Crops & demand, Transfers, Data, Warnings (every warning and problem in the project with its fix, its count of open items beside it), Model settings and Calibration (fitting the runoff parameters and judging the fit, together). Outcomes is what the model says: the Summary (where a project opens), EWR, Hydrological units, Runs & results (Compare runs opens from there, and from Scenarios, and shows under it while open), Dams, Scenarios and Allocations. Project, under *Review*, is what the project is and who can open it, in one column: Project details (name, description, time zone and WUA name, saved with Save changes at the foot of the page, as model edits are) and the Import record of an imported project; then the Team, Members, Farmers and, for owners, Share links; then Recent notes and the model’s headline facts (hydrological units, catchment area, dam capacity, irrigated area, transfers, time series, runs and the outflow gauge, each a link to where it is edited) and Scheduled reports. Owners also find API keys under Share links, and the page holds the licensing panels. Download in its header takes a copy of the project. The Summary links there under Model facts, details, team and sharing. Dams has a card for each hydrological unit’s dam: how full it was at the end of the latest run, its change over the last 30 days and its last year as a small line (% full, with its first and last day and its lowest level marked; point at it to read a day). The emptiest dams come first, every card shown. Pick a card to chart that dam’s storage (as % full or m³, over 30 days, a year or the whole run); the link can be shared. Under the chart is the assurance of supply of the hydrological unit the dam serves (a dam has none of its own): how often and how fully its demand was met, and its stress by month, with a link to the unit on Hydrological units. Under that, Proposed from the register and the map is one line of what the register of dams (for reference only) and the dam’s polygon on the map propose for that dam; open it, or follow a card’s Proposals, for the values and their sources. Its Dam of picks another dam (the chart follows) or a hydrological unit with no dam yet. Between the chart and the assurance of supply, Seen from space is one line of how the run’s dam surface area compares with what Digital Earth Africa’s satellites saw of the dam’s outline on the map: how many clear views (at least 90% of the dam seen) were compared and how many disagree. Open it for the chart of the run’s area beside the views, the days seen full (likely spilling), seen empty, or where the model and the satellite disagree, and every view in a table. A dam needs its outline drawn on the Map to be seen; an outline that DE Africa Waterbodies merged with a neighbouring water body is compared on views of its own outline only (WOfS and Sentinel). When more than one satellite saw the dam clearly on a day, the most trusted view is compared: Sentinel-2, then WOfS, then Waterbodies, then Sentinel-1 radar. Radar sees through cloud but is never called full or empty on its own; its views are rings on the chart, with a double-line strip under their days. Wind can make radar read a dam lower than it is, so when radar views are among those compared the summary also gives the average difference without them. A card’s figures are the latest run’s; its capacity is the model’s now, and a dam whose own settings (or how its hydrological unit draws on it) were edited since the run says Dam settings changed since the run and what changed, until the model is run again (the Network’s map marks it the same way); edits upstream of it aren’t checked, so re-run after those too. A dam with a minimum operating level also shows how many days of its last year it sat at that minimum. Each card also opens the dam’s hydrological unit on the Network (On the Network) and the hydrological unit’s Planted areas. Before the first run the cards show each dam’s capacity only. On a wide screen the sections are in the sidebar down the left, under the catchment’s name and your role (owner, editor or viewer); Projects, Teams and Help are at the top of it, and your account at the foot. A number beside Data counts the rainfall and evaporation series that are more than a week behind. On a phone, the Menu button in the bar at the top opens Projects, Teams and Help, and the catchment’s name and your role take the bar’s title, and the project’s sections sit behind a Sections button under it that names the tab you are on. The arrow keys move from one tab to the next. Each section opens with one header: its name, a line saying what it shows (the run on the Summary and on EWR, the hydrological units and dams on the Network, where the runoff parameters came from on Calibration, how many series are behind on Data), and its actions on the right. Rain up to says how current the rainfall is (click it for every series). Editors also get Add data, which uploads a file, on the pages that ask for data (Summary, Crops & demand, Data, Model settings and Calibration), and Run model on every page, which opens a small form for an optional Run label, Run forecast when there is forecast rain, and Run model; the run opens in Runs & results when it finishes. On Runs & results that form sits in the header itself. On a phone the page’s own actions are in one ⋯ list (More actions) beside Rain up to, How this page works is the ? beside the name, and Add data (where the page has it) and Run model (on Runs & results the run form) end the header on one row; while new data waits, the button there reads Re-run model. Each page adds its own actions to the header. The Network has Map (the geographic map: boundary, parcels, dams and gauges), Tables, + Add hydrological unit and, once there is an outlet, + Add other user; the Map Upload GeoJSON, Start from the map while the model is empty (the boundary, then the dams, abstraction points and gauges, and the units, their areas and their order are proposed, each value ticked to take it), Divide the model once it has hydrological units (with an elevation model: each point on the map stands for its hydrological unit, and its own area and order are proposed beside its values now, each ticked to take it; each proposed piece carries its number on the map and on its card), and a Getting started pill while the boundary or the rain feed reading it is still to do. The Map’s tools sit on the map’s left edge: Measure, Draw, Point (place a point), Delineate (when the server has an elevation model: the elevation model’s own channels are drawn as solid terrain channels, named in the bar and the Key beside the river network’s dashed lines, which are for reference only; click a terrain channel and the catchment above it, following the terrain, is proposed over the dimmed channels, to accept or reject, or pick Sub-catchments, one per click and each click gets the land that drains to it before any other click, to save as areas; each point goes on the nearest terrain channel, and one beside a much larger channel is offered that channel first, since a click can land on a hillside stream beside the river meant) and Trace (a dam, when the server has water occurrence data: click inside a dam and its outline is proposed as a drawing to adjust and save); a strip over the map names the tool that’s on, and Escape leaves it. Layers turns on the optional layers (quaternary catchments, the river network, the hydrological units, the MAP, CHIRPS and DEM grids, and the relief) and sets the Area fill, and the search box over the map’s top edge finds a gauge, a registered dam, a quaternary or a place (Map search); Key says what the colours mean and what the areas are coloured by. Beside the map, one panel at a time: Details of the picked feature, Features (with Download GeoJSON and Every feature, the table), Checks, Layers and Key; the map’s own Layers button (under the zoom buttons) and Key button (bottom left, beside Show everything) open those tabs, or on a phone a panel over the map. While drawing, Snap to features puts a corner on a neighbour’s corner or edge (hold Alt to place one exactly), and a polygon’s card has Split along a line; Crops & demand Tables, Load crop factors…, Import plantings… and + Add crop; Transfers Show on the Network and + Add transfer; Data Preview all data; Calibration Fit the parameters, which jumps to that panel. EWR and Hydrological units have a menu to pick the run and a link to it in Runs & results, and Dams the same link; Scenarios has + New scenario; Allocations Download CSV, Import and + Add volume; Project Download; Applications Decide the longest waiting. Notices sit in one line under the header: that you can only view the project, what an upload added, or that new data has arrived since the last run, with Re-run model for editors. Model settings is one long form. On a wide screen a column down its left lists every panel under its task (EWR the results are judged by first, then Data & rain, Demand & supply, Runoff, EWR & Reserve, Reading results, Automatic runs), marks the one you are reading and stays in view as you scroll; in a narrower window it is the row of links over the page. Find a setting (at the top of the column, or Find at the start of the row) lists the panels and the settings whose names match what you type: pick one to go straight to it, or press Enter for the first. A setting that lives on another page now is listed with that page’s name and goes there: Data feeds is on Data, and API keys and Scheduled reports are on Project. The panels that set up a fit (Flow calibration, Calibration record, Fit the parameters, WR2012 check) are on Calibration, with the same save bar: edits on both pages save together. Each panel says what it is set to now under its heading. The explanation under each field is hidden until you tick Explain each setting under its field, at the top of the form (your browser remembers it); every field keeps its ⓘ. A panel with something to fix before saving has a red dot in the menu, and the save bar links to it. Nothing you edit takes you off the page. Tables opens a full table over the page: the Network’s has the Hydrological unit table, Crop factors, Planted areas, Transfers and Demands, Crops & demand’s the crop factors and planted areas. + Add hydrological unit, or Edit on its row under All hydrological units (or a double-click on it in the drawing), opens its form in a sheet over the page, its sections folded to a line of their values: the menu over the form, or a section’s heading, opens one, Show every field opens them all, and Explain each setting under its field shows the help under each field; + Add crop, or Edit on a crop’s row, opens the crop’s. Each grid and sheet has its own Save changes, Discard model changes and Done, which brings you back where you were. The Hydrological unit table, Crop factors, Planted areas, Transfers’ monthly rates and the Irrigation systems also take a block copied from a spreadsheet, or a CSV file: paste it into any cell, or use Paste from a spreadsheet… above the grid. With the names in the first column and a heading row (as Download the table as CSV gives them), rows and columns can come in any order; a bare block of numbers fills from the cell you pasted into. In Crop factors a crop name the project doesn’t have adds that crop, so a list of crop types comes in at once; in Irrigation systems a new name adds a system. A preview lists every value it would change before Apply, and nothing is kept until you save. The monthly A-pan (Model settings → Demand) and the pan coefficients (Calibration → Flow calibration) take a paste the same way. Each of these says its layout under Expected format in the paste dialog: the headings, the units, how decimals are read, and an example file to download and fill in. Help → File formats gathers every upload and paste box’s Expected format in one page, each with its example file. To change one hydrological unit’s planted areas without leaving the page you are on, open its Planted areas: select the hydrological unit on the Network and follow Irrigated on its card beside the map, pick the hydrological unit’s name in the Summary’s Supply by hydrological unit, its name beside its bar on Crops & demand, or Planted areas on its card on Hydrological units or Dams. It opens beside the page and saves with the rest of the model. Notes keep what lives in people’s heads (“dam raised in 2019 per owner”) against what it is about. The speech-bubble button, with a count once there are notes, is on each hydrological unit on the Network (its card beside the map and its row in the Hydrological unit table), on a run’s record in Runs & results, beside each panel’s heading on Model settings and Calibration and on Recent notes on the Project page. It opens the notes in a panel down the right: write a new one at the top, and the notes, newest first, scroll under it. Everyone on the project can add one; you edit your own. On a hydrological unit, Also show to this hydrological unit’s farmers lets its farmers read it too; every other note stays with the project team.

entries.title: The whole process, from catchment to results: What “good enough” means
entries.text: A run is only as trustworthy as its calibration. Judge the parameters by the validation scores (days the fit never saw), not by the in-sample fit, and check the simulated natural flow against WR2012 where you can. The guides under “How it works” explain why.

entries.title: Create a project: A new project
entries.summary: Start a new catchment, put it in a team, and copy an existing one to try a what-if.
entries.text: Open Projects in the sidebar (on a phone, under Menu) and press New project. Give it a name, usually the catchment or river. Under Belongs to, pick a team if others will work on it, and press Create project. The project opens on its Summary tab. Work through the setup checklist from the top. One project holds one catchment: its network, crops, settings, input series and runs. A Water Balance Tool workbook becomes one project: anyone can bring one in with Import workbook on the Projects page (and a project downloaded from the app with Import project file (.json)).

entries.title: Create a project: Start from an example
entries.text: To look round a finished model before building your own, press Start from an example on the Projects page while you have no projects. It makes an invented winter-rainfall catchment your own project (four hydrological units, fruit farms with dams, two transfers, a calibrated runoff model and 15 years of made-up rainfall), runs it and opens that run on Runs & results. Every name and number in it is made up. Change it as you like, and delete it from its row’s ⋯ menu when you’re done.

entries.title: Create a project: Reading the Projects page
entries.text: Each row says how its catchment is doing, from its published run (or its latest run when none is published): irrigation supplied over the run in words (the share of demand, green from 95 %, amber from 80 %), the hydrological units short this week, the lowest dam, how far the rain data goes (Rain to 31 Dec 2024 (20 months ago)), when the project was last edited and when it last ran. Once a catchment’s figures are more than a week old, “this week” and “last 30 days” become the dates they end on (“short in the week to 31 Dec 2024”). Needs attention at the top lists the catchments to look at first (red or amber irrigation supply, hydrological units short, alerts firing, failing feeds, newer rain than the figures, figures over a week old), each with its reasons. The chips filter by owner, and Sort or a column heading orders the list; both stay in the page’s address.

entries.title: Create a project: A copy for a what-if
entries.text: On the Projects page, open the ⋯ menu on the project’s row, choose Copy… and name the copy. The model and the data are copied; runs are not. Name it after the change you plan, for example “Raise dam 3 by 20 %”. Make the change in the copy and run it. The original and its runs are untouched. Compare the copy’s run with the original’s. See Compare runs and try what-ifs.

entries.title: Create a project: Who can do what
entries.text: Editors change the model, upload data and run it. Viewers see everything, can fit the runoff model to explore, and can download results, but can’t save or run. A viewer’s workspace says “View only”. In a team, each person has the same role on every team project as in the team; owners can also delete, share and move the project (sharing and moving are on its Project page).

entries.title: Build the river network: The shape of a network
entries.summary: Add hydrological units and gauges, connect each one to the element it drains into, and end at one outflow gauge.
entries.text: The network is a tree. Each element drains into exactly one element downstream, and exactly one element, the Outflow gauge, drains nowhere. An element can have several upstream neighbours. The model works out the calculation order itself, upstream first. A small network. Hydrological units are circles, hydrological units with a dam are filled squares, gauges are triangles, and the outflow gauge is filled. The dashed arrow is a transfer between two dams.

entries.title: Build the river network: Steps
entries.text: Start with Add outflow gauge: the gauge at the catchment outlet. Press + Add hydrological unit for each hydrological unit (its form opens in a sheet over the map), set its Kind, and set Drains into to the element directly below it on the river. To enter many at once, use the hydrological unit table (Tables › Hydrological unit table). Add gauges where you want to read flow in the middle of the catchment, for example at a weir with a record. Give every hydrological unit its area (km²). For a hydrological unit with a dam, set the Dam capacity, the initial storage, its minimum level, and how much of the upstream inflow and of its own runoff enter the dam. A hydrological unit’s full form (Edit on its row under All hydrological units, or double-click it in the drawing) also has the dam’s area when full and its seepage. Set the share of the water supplied that returns to the river as return flow (10 % for a new unit) and any diversion back to the dam. The hydrological unit’s irrigation efficiency comes from its crops’ irrigation systems (Crops & demand). Under Supply, set where its irrigation comes from (the supply rule); Split the crops’ water between sources gives it a crop supply table: fixed shares from its own dam, the river at the unit and another unit’s dam. Where the crops or a demand take from the river at a pump of their own (Water source of a demand), give the pump’s capacity and, if it draws from a pool, the Pool at the pump (m³): it starts full, the pump draws it once the river’s share is used, and it refills from what the river has left. Only with evidence (a gauge below that the model keeps over- or under-simulating at low flows), set the unit’s Base-flow loss and gain (m³/day): water its own runoff loses to groundwater, out of the catchment, or gains from a spring or aquifer beyond the divide, before it reaches the river or the dam (Base-flow loss and gain). A river losing water between two units is a bed loss instead (Bed losses in the reach below). Press Save changes on the save bar (or in the hydrological unit’s sheet). In the schematic you can drag a hydrological unit onto another to change what it drains into. A drop that would make a loop, or move the outlet, is refused with the reason. In the hydrological unit table (Tables › Hydrological unit table), Sort by flow path orders the rows from each headwater down. Once the model has been run, the map shades each hydrological unit by the share of its irrigation demand that run supplied (95% or more, 70–95%, under 70%; Colour hydrological units by › Supply, latest run, on by default); a hydrological unit added since the run is hatched. The same menu colours the hydrological units by their dam level at the end of the latest run. A name longer than 17 characters is shortened on the map, keeping the ending when two names would otherwise look alike (hover a hydrological unit, or read the list beside the map, for its full name); a transfer that can’t curve clear of the names is drawn round them.

entries.title: Build the river network: Dams and natural areas
entries.text: A hydrological unit also covers two other cases, set by its parameters: Stand-alone dam: no crop areas (so no irrigation), 100 % of its runoff (and of upstream inflow, if it sits on the main stem) into the dam, and no diversion. Natural area: no crops, no dam capture and no diversion. It simply passes its runoff on. A river that splits in two (a bifurcation) can’t be drawn. Use a transfer for the side channel, or merge the hydrological units.

entries.title: Set up crops and irrigation demand: How demand is worked out
entries.summary: Crops with monthly crop factors, the hectares on each hydrological unit, A-pan evaporation and effective rain.
entries.text: gross demand (m³/day) = Σ crops [ area × A-pan (mm/month) × crop factor ] ÷ days in the month effective rain Pe = cropped area × the day’s rain (0 at or below the threshold) × effective-rain fraction; crop requirement = gross − min(soil store + Pe, gross) irrigation demand (abstraction) = crop requirement ÷ irrigation efficiency Gross demand is the same every day of a month. Rain above the Rain threshold covers the day’s demand first; what the crop can’t use that day stays in the Soil-water store (25 mm by default) and covers the following days, so wet spells need less irrigation after the rain too. The hydrological unit then abstracts more than the crop needs, to cover its application losses (Irrigation efficiency). Crop factors multiply A-pan evaporation, not FAO reference ET₀. A published FAO-56 Kc overstates demand by about 18–67 % (a third at a pan coefficient of 0.75) unless you first multiply it by the pan coefficient (usually 0.60–0.85).

entries.title: Set up crops and irrigation demand: Steps
entries.text: On Crops & demand, press + Add crop: its sheet opens over the page. Name it and enter its 12 monthly crop factors (Oct … Sep). Each crop then has a row in the Crops list, largest planted area first, with its colour, area, the month it needs most water and a small chart of its factors (Oct to Sep, the highest marked with its value; point at it to read a month); Edit on the row opens the sheet again. A warning icon on a row means a factor above 1.0 (hover or focus it; it opens the sheet). With more than nine crops, the smallest share one grey colour as Other, named in their own row. Under Planted area by hydrological unit, press Edit areas and enter the hectares of each crop on each hydrological unit in the grid. Leave a crop blank on hydrological units that don’t grow it. Each hydrological unit then gets a bar split by crop in the list’s colours, largest hydrological unit first (hover a segment for its crop and hectares); a note under the bars names any hydrological unit with nothing planted, whose demand is zero. Check Irrigation demand by month: what the catchment abstracts for its crops per month (the gross demand ÷ each hydrological unit’s irrigation efficiency, so an efficiency below 100 % raises it), stacked by crop, with the year’s total under it. Show table gives m³/day per month, the mean, and Mm³ per year per hydrological unit and for the catchment. It comes before effective rain, which a run takes off day by day. It uses the monthly A-pan means: with a daily A-pan series on the Data tab, runs use that on the days it has a value, so their demand differs, and a line under the heading says so. On Model settings → Demand, enter the 12 monthly A-pan evaporation values (or, when an A-pan grid is loaded on the server, take them from Calibration → Flow calibration → Evaporation from the map, whose Use saves them at once), the effective-rain fraction, the soil-water store and the Rain threshold. To bring in a list kept in a spreadsheet (a scheme’s register, a farm survey; hundreds of rows at once), press Import plantings… and load a CSV file or paste the rows: a heading row, then one row per farm and crop with its area in hectares (Farm, Crop, Area (ha), and optionally Irrigation system; Download the template under Expected format has the layout). Farms and crops are matched by name, whatever the capitals and spacing. A crop the project doesn’t have is added with crop factors of 0 and marked needs crop factors until you fill them in; a farm it doesn’t have is listed, and with Add them as new hydrological units ticked it becomes a new unit draining into the outlet, marked Needs placing on the Network until you set its area and where it drains. The preview counts what changes and lists every row it can’t read by its line; nothing changes until Apply, and then you save as after any edit. Give each crop its irrigation system in its sheet (a unit can override it per crop in Edit areas); the systems and their efficiencies are under Tables › Irrigation systems. Each hydrological unit’s irrigation efficiency is its crops’ systems combined. Press Save changes on the save bar. The full tables are under Tables in the section header (Crop factors, Planted areas): they open over the page, and Done brings you back. The Crop factors grid also has Load crop factors…, to overwrite them from the reference library, a Water Balance Tool workbook or a node-based workbook (Load crop factors). To change just one hydrological unit, click its name beside its bar, or select it on the Network and follow Irrigated on its card: its crops and hectares open beside the page, with its demand, and save with the rest of the model. With its parcels linked on the Map, that panel also shows From land cover: the area a land-cover map shows as cropland in them. Pick the area and the crop it is planted to (the land cover doesn’t say which), and Use saves it with its source. Under it, Actual ET from satellite says how the newest run’s crop water use compares with FAO WaPOR’s actual ET over the parcels, dekad by dekad; open it for each half water year, the dekads and a CSV. A difference points at the crops, areas, crop factors or A-pan to check; nothing changes by itself. It is off unless switched on for the site. With A-pan at 0 in every month the crops need no water, and every hydrological unit looks fully supplied. The Summary’s checklist warns about this.

entries.title: Upload rainfall and flow data: What the model needs
entries.summary: CSV format, updating a series with new days, and the checks to read before you trust a record.
entries.text: Catchment rainfall (mm/day): required. It drives natural flow and effective rain. CHIRPS rainfall (mm/day): optional. It fills the days catchment rain is blank. Forecast rainfall (mm/day): optional. It extends the record a few days ahead. Observed flow at the outlet (m³/s), from a gauge, a logger or both: needed to calibrate.

entries.title: Upload rainfall and flow data: Steps
entries.text: Prepare a CSV with two columns, date,value, one row per day. A header row is optional. Leave a missing day blank rather than writing 0. Commas, semicolons or tabs, and decimal points or decimal commas, are worked out from the file. A daily table exported from the DWS hydrology site loads as it is: days its quality code marks as missing, and negative placeholders such as -999, become gaps. Press Add data in the section header, or drop the file on the page. Both are on Summary, Crops & demand, Data, Model settings and Calibration; another page says where to drop it. Check the series the form guessed from the file name and header, and the preview chart. For an existing series keep Append / update: new days are added and overlapping days corrected. The preview counts new, changed and unchanged days. Use Replace only to overwrite the whole series. Upload. If the file would change days already stored, the form asks first: it says how many days and between which dates, and Show the changes lists each one. Press Overwrite to go ahead, or Back. The values it replaces are kept: in the History tab, pick that change and press Restore the earlier values. Cancel, the close button or Esc asks before throwing away a file you have picked but not uploaded. Press Re-run model in the notice under the header when you are ready. A missing rain day written as 0 looks like a dry day, and it stops CHIRPS filling the gap. The Data checks panel flags long runs of zero rain in the wet season and years that read far below CHIRPS. By default a run treats a flagged run’s days as missing where CHIRPS reads more than 2 mm, so CHIRPS fills them, and keeps the 0 on drier days; Model settings → Rain gaps (zero-rain runs) sets that threshold and keeps a confirmed dry spell dry.

entries.title: Upload rainfall and flow data: Checks to read on the Data tab
entries.text: The table lists the series that are behind first: rainfall or evaporation a run reads whose data is more than a week old, the same ones the number beside Data counts, each marked Behind. Then the last date of each series, its coverage per year and % missing. With many series the first six show and Show all lists the rest. Click a row (or its View) to chart it: the chart, below the table, comes into view; the link can be shared, and Back returns to the series before. Series details, under the chart, holds the charted series’ Name, Product (a CHIRPS series’ product and version), Measured at (where a flow record was measured: the outlet, or a gauge inside the network, which makes that gauge a calibration location, Calibration → Calibration record), its Source and the Upload unit it was converted from. Editors change the name, product, where measured and source there, each saved as it changes; a new name that changes which series runs read (they read the first of each kind by name) asks first, and a series a data feed or an API key writes by its name keeps it (nor can a series take a name one of them writes to). A row placed at a gauge says *At gauge* and its name. Data checks: negative values, outliers, flat stretches, suspect zero rain and breaks in catchment rain’s ratio to CHIRPS, which the double-mass chart shows by water year. The chart of the catchment rain a run reads shades the days a run treats as missing or spreads a multi-day accumulation over. With both a gauge and a logger, the gauge vs logger table flags water years where they disagree. Choose the record you trust as the calibration flow series (Calibration → Calibration record). A Reference gauge (other catchment) on a neighbouring river is kept for ranking wet and dry years only. The model never reads it. Preview all data (in the header, beside Add data) or a row’s own Preview opens every series’ daily values side by side, searchable by date or value, plus how the model used each day: rain used and its source after gap-fill, the CHIRPS bias factor and corrected value, flow in m³/day, and any calibration exclusion. Its View picks the columns: All, one unit with land (its station raw and adjusted to the unit’s MAP, its CHIRPS raw and bias-corrected with the twelve monthly factors above the table, its rain used and where each day came from), the rainfall stations, the average catchment rainfall or the flow records.

entries.title: Load rainfall and flow automatically with data feeds: What a feed does
entries.summary: Attach a CHIRPS, CHIRPS-GEFS or DWS feed, set one up from the catchment boundary, and read whether each is keeping up.
entries.text: A data feed fetches one source once a day and merges its new days into one series: CHIRPS daily rainfall, the CHIRPS-GEFS 16-day forecast, or a DWS gauge’s verified daily flow. A day the source has no value for never erases what is there. Runs read the series as they read an uploaded one.

entries.title: Load rainfall and flow automatically with data feeds: Rain over the catchment boundary
entries.text: Put the catchment boundary on the Map (delineate, draw or upload it). Open Data → Data feeds, press Attach a feed (an editor: Rain from the map) and choose the Area *The catchment boundary, from the map* (the Map’s own link opens it too). Read the proposal: the CHIRPS cells the boundary covers, the share of each inside it and its weight. A boundary over about 2 500 km² needs feeds for its parts. An owner presses Apply. Where runs already read a CHIRPS record (Runs read), the owner chooses: Keep it, the default, and the feed goes into a new series named to sort after it, so runs keep reading the record, read from its first day (rnl when that is before 1998); or Replace it, and the feed reads the whole record again from its first day and takes its place once complete (the old values stay in the History). The daily product and start date can be changed before Apply. See rain from the catchment boundary for how the cells are weighted.

entries.title: Load rainfall and flow automatically with data feeds: Rain for each unit
entries.text: Give each hydrological unit its parcel on the Map (delineate, draw or upload it, and link it to the unit). Open Data → Data feeds, press Attach a feed and choose the Area *Each unit’s parcel*: one CHIRPS feed per unit, over the cells its parcel covers. An owner picks the daily product (*rnl* from 1981 by default) and presses Create the feed (Create 4 feeds for four units; Update where a unit has one already). Units without a parcel are listed, with a link to the map. Give each unit its MAP and source on its form, then, under Model settings → Flow generation, give each unit its rainfall station, and refit. See runoff from each unit’s own rain for which rain each unit runs on.

entries.title: Load rainfall and flow automatically with data feeds: Attach a feed by hand
entries.text: Press Attach a feed (owners) and choose the Source, then Into series: the kind of series it writes. CHIRPS goes into the CHIRPS series, so it fills the days catchment rain is blank; into catchment rain it becomes the catchment rain itself, used raw. For CHIRPS, choose the Daily product: *sat* from 1998, with preliminary days, or *rnl* from 1981, final days only (see CHIRPS product and version). Without a start date the feed reads the last 60 days, then keeps up. For CHIRPS and the forecast, give the Area: grid cells (latitude, longitude, an optional weight, one a line) or a bounding box (south, west, north, east). A box on the coast can leave out sea cells. CHIRPS’s Area also offers the catchment boundary and each unit’s parcel, from the map (above). For DWS flow, pick from Nearest gauging stations (river gauges within 50 km of the outlet, with the years their record covers) or type the station code, such as A2H012. If the series already has data, the form asks: use a separate series, or fill only its empty days. Then press Attach feed, and Run now to fetch at once rather than wait for the daily run. Verified DWS flow lags by months and is revised in arrears: it suits calibration, not day-to-day operation.

entries.title: Load rainfall and flow automatically with data feeds: Is it keeping up?
entries.text: Each card says its state in words: OK, Stale (no new day for longer than the source usually takes), Failing (with the reason), Waiting or Off, and when its last data and last check were. A warning above the list counts the feeds that need attention, and the Projects page lists failing feeds under Needs attention. A Sample data badge means this server reads invented sample files, not the real sources (Synthetic test data). The Data tab marks a rain series Behind once its last day is more than a week old (Data up to, and Behind).

entries.title: Start a catchment from the map: Before you start
entries.summary: Delineate or draw the boundary, place the dams and gauges, and let the map propose the units, their areas and their order.
entries.text: This works on a model with no hydrological units yet, and the units follow your own boundaries: have each unit’s boundary ready to draw or upload (or save sub-catchments from clicks). With an elevation model on the server, the units’ order comes from the terrain and each area is checked against it; without one, you set the order on the Network. Nothing reaches the model until you tick it.

entries.title: Start a catchment from the map: Steps
entries.text: On the Map, press Start from the map (or the link on the empty map). Step one is the boundary. Delineate from the outlet: the terrain channels appear; click the one at the catchment’s outlet. The outlet goes on the nearest terrain channel (Outlet placement on the channel), and the catchment above it is proposed. Check it against the relief and the mapped rivers, then Accept as the catchment boundary. Or draw the boundary, or upload it as GeoJSON. Put each unit’s boundary on the map (draw it, upload it, or save sub-catchments from clicks), and place the dams, the abstraction points and the gauges with Place a point or by drawing a dam’s outline. In the sheet, say what each feature is (a unit’s boundary, part of its unit’s composite dam, its unit’s river pump, another water user, a gauge in the network, or not in the model) and which gauge is the outlet, then propose. A dam or an abstraction point is never a unit of its own. Read the proposal. Each unit is tinted and numbered on the map, and its card gives its boundary’s area, what it drains into, and the dams and pumps inside it. Read the warnings: a boundary whose area is far off what the terrain drains to its outflow, boundaries that add up past the catchment, dropped features and their reasons. Tick the values to take (Tick every value takes them all), name the units, and apply. One model revision writes them, each unit’s area its boundary, and links each unit’s dams and pump to it. Follow the data step’s links in order: rain from the boundary, the nearest gauging stations, each unit’s composite dam (its volume and the area draining to it are yours to enter; the register of dams is a reference only), cultivated area from land cover, then run the model. The areas come from a 30 m global elevation model, not a survey. In flat land a divide can be hundreds of metres out; check each piece against the map before you tick it.

entries.title: Start a catchment from the map: A model that already has units
entries.text: Use Divide the model instead (Divide the model from the map): say which unit each boundary stands for, and each unit’s area and order are proposed beside its values now. Or click the rivers with Sub-catchments, one per click (Sub-catchments, one per click), save the pieces as areas, link each to its unit and Use its area.

entries.title: Add a transfer: Steps
entries.summary: Move water from one hydrological unit’s dam to another in chosen months, up to a pipe or canal capacity.
entries.text: On Transfers, press + Add transfer in the section header. Each rule is a card: along its top, pick its source (From) and destination (To) hydrological units. Under Max rate by month, enter its maximum rate in m³/s for each month it runs in, Oct … Sep; leave a month blank to keep it off. … in every month copies the largest rate to all twelve. Under Limits, enter a daily cap in m³ if there is one. Under Source, keep Takes from on the source’s dam and set the minimum storage it keeps, or pick the river for an off-take and fill in its fields. With several transfers, set each one’s priority under Limits: lower moves first. The On switch at the top right of the card leaves a rule in the model but stops it running (the card turns grey and says off); Remove deletes it, asking first once it has a rate. Save, then run.

entries.title: Add a transfer: What moves each day
entries.text: A transfer pipeline on piers, crossing the river between two dams. The pipeline: Its capacity is the transfer’s maximum rate in each month; a blank month is off. transfer = min( source’s water above its minimum, room at the destination, the month’s rate × 86 400, daily cap ), 0 in a month that is off The source’s water is yesterday’s storage above the higher of the transfer’s minimum and the dam’s own minimum level, less what earlier transfers took. The room at the destination is the free space in its dam plus that day’s irrigation demand, so water is never pumped into a full dam only to spill. Transfers move before any hydrological unit irrigates. Between two hydrological units, what leaves the source enters the destination: a dam transfer creates and loses no water, and a river off-take loses only its Losses on the way. A rule whose To is Outside the catchment (Transfer out of the catchment) is different: its water leaves the model, and counts as the source unit’s use. Transfers with the same priority share a source dam, or a destination’s room, in proportion to their own limits, so the order of the list never changes a result.

entries.title: Set the EWR and the reporting window: Steps
entries.summary: Enter the monthly pragmatic EWR, then choose the period the curtailment report averages over.
entries.text: Take the monthly Reserve flows for the river’s Ecological category, usually from the Desktop Reserve Model tables without high flows. Pick one value per month (often a percentile) and convert it to m³/day. On Model settings → EWR, the first choice is Daily EWR from: keep *The pragmatic EWR* and enter the 12 values in the Pragmatic EWR row under it, Oct … Sep. The l/s equivalent and the annual volume help catch a unit slip. Or take the daily EWR straight from the Desktop Reserve Model: set Daily EWR from to *The DRM TAB file* or *The DRM percentile tables* (the daily EWR at the outlet), load the DRM’s .tab or .rul file or paste the values (Fill from: beside Daily EWR from; a .tab’s flows are shown in m³/s before you use them, a paste’s values in a preview before Apply), and choose how the tables are scaled to the catchment, by MAR or by area, with the table’s MAR or area. Under the percentile tables a .rul fills three tables, and The EWR is the Reserve table picks which Reserve table is the EWR: the total Reserve flow (with high flows, the default) or the Reserve flow without high flows. Every run then says which EWR it was judged by and the scale factor. Optionally, on Model settings → Reporting (under *Demand & supply*, above the EWR), set the Curtailment reporting window (reporting window) to a drought or dry season. The curtailment table then averages over that period only. To assess the EWR above the outlet too, add a gauge on the Network tab at each EWR site of the Reserve determination (a gauge is an EWR site until unticked; untick one that only records flow). Save and run. With a Reserve rule table too (Model settings → Reserve rule tables, after the EWR), choose which one the results are judged by in EWR the results are judged by, the first panel on Model settings: automatic (the outlet’s rule table, else the first site’s, else the pragmatic EWR), the pragmatic EWR, or one site’s rule table. It changes no result, so no re-run is needed; EWR says at the top which one is in use.

entries.title: Set the EWR and the reporting window: Where the EWR is checked
entries.text: A reach of the river. The EWR is the flow that must stay in it, every day, for the ecosystem to hold its target condition. The river channel: Checked every day at the outlet against the Pragmatic EWR, and at every gauge ticked as an EWR site against the EWR of everything upstream of it. The EWR is assessed at EWR sites: the outflow gauge, against the full Pragmatic EWR, and every gauge ticked as an EWR site (each gauge is, until unticked on its form), against the EWR shares of everything upstream of it. On a day a site falls short, the shortfall is charged to the hydrological units upstream of it in proportion to what each took that day, never more than it took; the rest is natural. That EWR charge says which hydrological unit causes a shortfall. The results report Days EWR not met, an EWR grid by month and, with an observed record, whether the model fails on the days the real river did (EWR test against observed flow).

entries.title: Calibrate by hand: Before you start
entries.summary: Change a runoff parameter, run, and read the hydrograph and statistics until the fit is right.
entries.text: On Calibration → Calibration record, choose the calibration flow series (gauge or logger) and the Calibration window: a period with a record you trust. Add Calibration exclusions for periods you can’t trust, each with its reason. Enter each record’s gauged range (its highest and lowest field gauging) under Quality flags (the line under the exclusions: Change opens it), so days read off the extrapolated rating curve are flagged. The Runoff model is GR4J: its parameters are under Flow calibration. (The workbook’s legacy model was removed in engine 1.0.0.)

entries.title: Calibrate by hand: The loop
entries.text: Change one parameter at a time. For GR4J start with X1 (soil store: less flow when larger), then X4 (timing of the peaks), then X3 (how slowly flow recedes). To see what the change does first, press Preview on the save bar: the last run against the same run with your unsaved change, worked out in your browser (KGE, NSE, PBIAS and supply). Nothing is saved and no run is made. Save and run. A run started on Calibration opens there, under How the shown run fits. Read the Hydrograph (observed flow against simulated outflow) and Calibration against observed flow: KGE, NSE, PBIAS, log-NSE (low-flow fit) and the annual water balance. Fix volume first (PBIAS near 0), then the shape of the peaks, then the recessions and low flows. Compare the run with the previous one to see what the change did. Hand calibration is scored only on days the parameters were tuned on (in-sample). Before relying on the parameters, run Fit automatically with validation to see how they score on days they never saw.

entries.title: Fit the runoff model automatically: Steps
entries.summary: Let the optimiser search the parameters, read the validation scores, then apply and save the fit.
entries.text: On Calibration → Calibration record, set the calibration flow series, window and exclusions first. The fit uses the form as it stands. Under Calibration → Fit the parameters → Fit automatically, choose the Objective by what the fit will feed (see *Choosing an objective* below), before you see any score. Keep Validate (split-sample and dry → wet) ticked. With both a gauge and a logger, you can also score the fit against the record it doesn’t use (Also validate against). The Search line above the button shows the bounds, model runs, starts and seed; Change opens them. Choose Bounds Typical (Perrin et al.’s published range) when a short record can’t pin the parameters down, and leave Model runs per fit (1 500) and Starts (5) at their defaults unless you have a reason. Each start is a separate search from its own seed and the best is kept; the notes say when starts reach nearly the same score with scattered parameters. Press Fit automatically. A progress bar shows the stage and the best score so far; Cancel stops it. You can open other tabs while it runs: the fit carries on, and its result waits on this page. Read the result: the notes, current vs fitted parameters, and the scores table. The shaded validation columns are the honest measure. Press Apply to form, then Save changes on the save bar. Nothing is stored until you save. Run the model with the new parameters. A run started from Calibration opens there, under How the shown run fits, so you read the new fit on the same page. Expect validation to score below the fit. When it is much lower, or the notes say wet-year behaviour is weakly constrained, the record can’t pin the parameters down. Report that; don’t hide it.

entries.title: Fit the runoff model automatically: Choosing an objective
entries.text: Each objective weighs the record differently, so choose it by what the fit will feed, and before you see any score: KGE′ (default): the overall water balance, peaks and events. Year-balanced KGE′: a record where a few wet years would otherwise dominate. Mean of KGE′(Q) and KGE′(1/Q): EWR, low-flow and assurance-of-supply decisions, when the gauge’s low flows are well rated. Non-parametric KGE: the same decisions when the rating at the extremes is uncertain. It reads the rank order and the shape of the flow-duration curve, so it is less sensitive to rating error. NSE on √Q or log Q: mainly to compare with older studies that used them. Don’t fit several objectives and keep the one whose score looks best. Scores of different objectives don’t compare, and choosing after seeing them is the overfitting the Calibration rules (automated calibration) exist to stop. To try several, list them in the rules: every fit is then judged on one selection score on a held-out test, chosen in advance. Check a low-flow fit for volume too: the WR2012 fit statistics and KGE′ are reported beside every fit.

entries.title: Fit the runoff model automatically: Afterwards
entries.text: The saved parameters carry a Fit record: objective, seed, window, exclusions, engine version and every score. Each run keeps the record it was made with. Editing a fitted parameter by hand marks the record “parameters edited since fit”. The same inputs, engine version and seed reproduce the fit exactly.

entries.title: Check natural flow against WR2012: Steps
entries.summary: Enter the quaternary’s published naturalised flow, and every run compares its natural flow with it.
entries.text: Find the Quaternary catchment the catchment lies in, and its WR2012 naturalised MAR and 12 monthly mean flows. The app doesn’t ship WR2012 data. On Calibration → WR2012 check, tick Compare runs with WR2012 naturalised flow. Enter the quaternary code, its area, MAP (optional), MAR in Mm³/a, the period and the source. Enter the monthly means in Mm³ per month. Their sum should match the MAR within 5 %; the m³/s row shows a unit slip. Under How the check judges, choose the scaling (area, or area and rainfall) and save. Every run from now on has a WR2012 check panel.

entries.title: Check natural flow against WR2012: Reading the check
entries.text: The run compares simulated natural flow (never the outflow) with the scaled reference: the MAR ratio, the 12 monthly ratios with dry-season months marked, and the correlation of the monthly pattern. A MAR off by 10 % is noted, by 25 % (or 15 % too wet) queried, and by 50 % makes the run unusable for EWR findings until explained. The thresholds are editable. The optional MAR penalty, switched on in Fit the parameters → Fit automatically, makes the fit pull the natural MAR towards WR2012, and shows the fit with and without it.

entries.title: Run the model and read the results: Run
entries.summary: What each results section shows, in order, and what to look at first.
entries.text: With unsaved changes, Run model asks first and offers Save and run. Press Run model in the header of any section and optionally type a Run label (on Runs & results the field is in the header itself), then Run model. It needs a network and a rainfall series; until then the form says what is missing. The runs are listed on the left, newest first, beside the run shown; pick one to show it (with a single run, the list is one row above it). Its header links to EWR and Hydrological units for that run. A run tagged Can’t be re-run was made before runs stored their inputs. The new run opens when it finishes. A run keeps a snapshot of the inputs it used, so later edits never change it.

entries.title: Run the model and read the results: Read, top to bottom
entries.text: Summary: first what to check before relying on the run, then (folded away) notes on how the input data were handled, and a line of model checks (arithmetic checks, calibration, plausibility, the WR2012 flag), each linking to its panel. Then a sentence or two in plain words (which hydrological units fell short, then how often the river’s requirement was met), and the headline figures, the calibration NSE and PBIAS among them when there is observed flow. The table per hydrological unit is on Hydrological units (see below). Water balance by water year: summed over the hydrological units (rain with the runoff coefficient under it, storage at the start and end, each gain and loss, in Mm³, and the residual with the runoff model’s under it, each of which should be 0), with a link to EWR’s water account, the catchment’s own. How the run fits observed flow (the hydrograph, flow duration, calibration, the runoff model, the WR2012 check, EWR vs observed and the plausibility checks) is on Calibration, for the same run: the Summary’s model checks link there. Record: the run’s notes, whether it is the project’s evidence run (see below), how to reproduce it, its validation statement and its publication. The model’s working: Arithmetic checks (the engine’s own checks on the run: whether each hydrological unit’s daily balance closes and the reports add up, the list behind Show the N checks when every check passed; whether the water balance closes in every water year, with a link to the table; and Trace a day; see the arithmetic checks; a failed one is a bug in the model, not your data) and Chart any daily series: any stored daily series of the catchment, a hydrological unit or a gauge. The row of links under the header, On this page, jumps to each of these sections and marks the one you are reading; it stays in view as you scroll. In a narrower window the last few are under More at its end. On a wide screen it is a column down the right of the results instead, each link named as its panel’s heading, with the main panels of EWR and Hydrological units listed under their pages at its foot. EWR, Hydrological units, Data, Model settings, Calibration and Compare runs have the same menu, a column down the left of the page on a wide screen, and a hydrological unit’s form on the Network has it as a row of links over the form. EWR, under *Outcomes* in the sections, is the page for the EWR’s results, one run at a time (the newest, or pick another from its Run menu; the link under the Summary’s supply list opens it too). A line at the top says which EWR the results are judged by, with Change to choose another in Model settings → EWR the results are judged by. Two tiles: the headline, EWR not met (the share of days at the outflow gauge, the days, and how many in an average year) or, when a Reserve rule table judges the results, Reserve rules met (the share of whole months, at which site, with the pragmatic EWR’s days under it); and the mean simulated outflow and its share of natural flow, each with its change from the run before (the worst month is the EWR by month grid’s All years row). Beside them (under them on a narrow screen), Days below the reserve in each of the run’s last twelve months (with a Reserve rule table judging, it is headed Days below the pragmatic EWR, the daily test it counts). Then EWR against outflow with a 30 days / 1 year / All switch and the days below the pragmatic EWR shaded, beside the days below the reserve each water year. When a Reserve rule table judges the results (by whole months), those bars are headed Days below the pragmatic EWR, each water year, the daily test they count, and the chart is headed Flow vs pragmatic EWR (or Flow vs daily EWR when the daily EWR comes from the DRM tables) when the table is at another site than the outlet, since it then draws only that EWR (with the outlet’s table it draws the rule requirement too). Below them, the findings: Reserve rules met, by month (without a rule table, one line saying it needs one, with a link to Model settings → Reserve rule tables), Days below the EWR, by month with the EWR required and met at each site each water year, and the water account (the catchment’s, from natural flow, in m³, with a link to the run’s water balance on Runs & results). Then, under How sure, and what if, the tools you run yourself: the uncertainty bands on those findings (with the sensitivity runs), the outcome matrix and the seasonal outlook, each one row with Run… until it has run. On the EWR by month heat map (as % of days) and the reserve strip at the top, green means the EWR was not met on fewer than 5 % of the days, amber fewer than 20 %, and red 20 % or more; these are provisional defaults until the hydrologist confirms them (a team can set its own for its portfolio). Hydrological units, also under *Outcomes*, is the hydrological units’ page for one run (the newest, or pick another from the run menu in its header; the Summary’s Supply by hydrological unit links there). Three tiles: irrigation supplied, with the hydrological units below 95 % and its change from the run before under it; the hydrological units short on any of the run’s last 7 days (Short this week, which opens the curtailment over those days) and the total shortfall. Then a card per hydrological unit, the three least supplied first (Show all lists the rest in place), in the Summary’s and the Network’s colours: its % supplied, its shortfall, its days short in the reporting window and in the last 7 days, and any cut the curtailment asks of it, with links to its hydrological unit on the Network and its planted areas. Pick a card, or a unit from the menu at the top of the chart (‹ and › step through them, least supplied first), to chart that hydrological unit’s supply against its demand (the days it was short shaded), over 30 days / 1 year / All, with a link to its dam’s storage on the Dams page; the link can be shared, and on a wide screen the chart stays beside the cards as you scroll. Under the chart is that unit’s assurance of supply: how often and how fully its demand was met, and a strip of its stress by month, with a link to every year’s grid. Below them: the Hydrological unit results table (hydrological units under 95 % flagged, with a small bar beside each %), the Curtailment targets with their Reporting window (each hydrological unit’s supply against a fairness benchmark, its EWR charge and the supply cut that meets it, and the EWR sites; see Curtailment targets) and Assurance of supply. The Download menu on a run gives the daily series and the summary as CSV, for your own checks or a report. The two tables with a column per hydrological unit, Fragmented flow and Fragmented EWR, have a Preview beside them that shows the file’s table first, searchable by date, with Download CSV to save it. Report, beside it, opens a printable catchment report of the run: the network, the inputs it used, calibration, curtailment, EWR compliance for the outlet and every hydrological unit, the hydrological unit table, warnings, self-checks and the run’s notes. Press Download PDF once it has finished preparing and choose Save as PDF in the print dialog; it prints on A4 in the light theme, without the app’s sidebar or menu bar. Generate PDF and Email me the PDF make the same PDF on the server instead; the emailed link opens a page that names the catchment and run, says whether the PDF is queued, being made, ready or failed, and offers Download the PDF for an hour. Viewers can open it too.

entries.title: Run the model and read the results: Notes and the evidence run
entries.text: Under Run notes, write why the run’s results stand, for example why a WR2012 query stands, and press Save notes. Everyone who can see the project reads them, in run comparison and in the summary CSV too. The Notes button at the right of that heading is something else: the team’s discussion of the run, where anyone on the project can add a comment. Under Evidence, give the reason and press Nominate as evidence to mark the run the project’s results rely on (Evidence run (nomination)). A nomination can’t be edited or removed; nominating another run replaces it, and both stay in the Nomination history. A run of the legacy runoff model, made before engine 1.0.0 removed it (badged Workbook comparison), a scenario run and a forecast run can’t be nominated: their Evidence panel says why and links to the evidence run. A run made by an engine with a known bug (or with parameters from a calibration that had one) is tagged May be affected in the run list, and its header shows May be affected by a known bug. Each bug changes results only under its own conditions: press the badge to open the run’s Validation statement, whose errata table says when, then re-run on the current engine and compare. The project’s owners are emailed once when a new bug is confirmed. A project keeps its newest runs (20 by default) and deletes the oldest when a new run goes over that. Evidence runs, current or former, are never deleted, and a project that has nominated one can’t be deleted either.

entries.title: Compare runs and try what-ifs: Steps
entries.summary: Set up to two what-ifs against a baseline: which inputs changed, what that did to the results, and every figure in full.
entries.text: Run a baseline. Change one thing (raise a dam, add crops, add a transfer, refit the parameters) in the same project or in a copy, and run again. That run is a what-if. A scenario’s run, made and run on Scenarios, is a what-if too. Open Compare runs from the link at the top of the runs list on Runs & results (or Compare with published, or a scenario’s comparison); while it is open the sidebar shows it under Runs & results. It starts on the latest run (What-if 1) against the published run (Baseline), or against the run before it when nothing is published. Each run card has its own project and run picker, so any run from any project you can see can take any place. To weigh two changes against each other, press + Add a second what-if. It picks the newest run that isn’t already on the page; Remove takes it off again. Read the cards (each what-if’s main change), then What the change does: each outcome for the baseline and every what-if, with the change from the baseline under each what-if’s value (dam storage at the end of the run too, as a share of each run’s own dam capacity), and the takeaways in plain words under it. Days below the reserve, each year shows the same test year by year (October to September); when a compared run has a rule table it is headed by the daily EWR the bars count (Days below the pragmatic EWR, each year, or the DRM table the daily EWR comes from), since the rule table judges whole months instead. Each run’s bars count its own daily EWR: when the runs’ sources differ, the chart says each run’s daily EWR and names each run’s beside it. Below that, Full comparison has every detail for the baseline against one what-if (pick which): Inputs that differ (every input difference), Headline results, fit and validation, uncertainty, the reserve by month, hydrological units and the daily series. There the baseline is run A and the what-if run B. To hand the result round, press Export impact report (with two what-ifs, pick which). It opens that what-if’s printable report with Impact against the baseline first: the same outcomes, takeaways and input changes. Download PDF saves it. Results are daily averages over each run’s own period. When runs cover different periods the page warns you, and so do the takeaways: part of the change then comes from the dates, not from your edit. A takeaway appears only for a material change (a day a year below the reserve, a point of the demand supplied, a hydrological unit crossing 95 %); the table shows everything. Each run shows its run notes in the full comparison, and the page says when either run is, or was, the project’s evidence run. The page’s address holds every run on it, so a comparison can be bookmarked or shared with anyone who can see the projects.

entries.title: Model a what-if with a scenario: Before you start
entries.summary: Describe a change as a scenario on a saved run, keep the proposal apart from the assumptions, run it and read what it does.
entries.text: A Scenario is a list of changes on a Base run: the inputs that run stored, never the live model. Start from the run the change should be judged against, usually the published run. Each change is labelled a Proposal or a Baseline assumption (Proposal or baseline assumption): to see a proposal’s effect alone, settle the baseline assumptions (a corrected setting, new rain data) in the project first and run it again, then start the scenario on that run.

entries.title: Model a what-if with a scenario: Steps
entries.text: On Scenarios, press + New scenario, name it after the change (“Upper dam +20 %”) and pick its Base run. Open Proposer under Application details and tick The proposer’s hydrological units: the units whose owner is proposing the change. Changes to them, and anything the scenario adds, are the proposal. Add each change under Add a change: pick the kind, the target and the new value. It reads in words against the value it replaces. For many edits at once, Edit in the model tables and Record them (Edit in the model tables (override mode)). Check the list: a red Baseline assumptions changed callout means some change alters what the river is taken to be today; a change marked Doesn’t apply must be fixed or removed before the scenario can run. Press Run scenario. Scenario against its base shows the headline results, each hydrological unit, Assurance of supply and the daily series against the base run, every change as scenario − base. For a dam, read Yield under this scenario (Historical firm yield). For how sure the change is, open the full comparison and compute the paired band (read the uncertainty). To test a demand restriction, use Scale demand (one change for the whole catchment, or for chosen units and months) rather than editing crop areas: it scales what each unit would take and leaves the crops as they are. Its From and To dates (both included) limit it to a stretch of the record, so a dry-year stress is one change per drought year, with the other years as the base. To test a wetter or drier climate, scale every rain series the project has, one change each. A change applies to the base run’s stored inputs. When the model or the data move on, Rebase… on the “Based on” line of Application details carries the changes to a newer run and lists any that no longer apply.

entries.title: Read how sure a result is: Three questions, three tools
entries.summary: Uncertainty bands, sensitivity runs and the paired band: what each answers about EWR compliance, and how to run and read it.
entries.text: How far could this result be off, given what the flow record can’t rule out? The Uncertainty bands (behavioural ensemble): many parameter sets that all fit the record acceptably, run through the whole model, with the 5–95 % range of what they give. Which uncertain input moves it most? The Sensitivity runs: rain, the pan coefficient, dam evaporation, abstraction and the dams’ starting storage, each changed alone, with a verdict on whether EWR compliance holds across the range. How sure is the change between two runs? The paired band: the change under each kept parameter set, so the uncertainty both runs share cancels.

entries.title: Read how sure a result is: Steps
entries.text: On EWR, open Uncertainty from the page’s menu. On EWR, press Run… beside Uncertainty bands to open the form. Under Run an ensemble, set the rule before looking at any band (Ensemble rule: sample and acceptance tests): the number of parameter sets, the bounds and the three tests a set must pass. For an evidence report, use the rule the project declared (Declared uncertainty rule (evidence)). Press Run ensemble and keep the tab open while the browser runs the sets. Read Parameter sets kept and the coverage line first. With fewer than 30 kept there is no band; with coverage of the held-out record below 70 % the band is too narrow to trust. Then read each result’s 5 %, median and 95 % beside this run’s own value. Under Sensitivity runs, press Run sensitivity. Read the verdict at each EWR site (Sensitivity verdict and threshold), then the tornado: the factor with the longest bar is the one better data would settle first. To weigh a change, open Compare runs with the run that has the ensemble as the baseline and the what-if beside it, and press Compute the paired band under Uncertainty. Each tool leaves something out. The bands vary the runoff parameters, the pan coefficient, the rain source and the record judged against, never the abstraction or the dams’ starting storage; the sensitivity runs vary those one at a time and never together. A result that holds under both is well supported; one that is “not determinable with current data” says what to measure next.

entries.title: Weigh a season’s demand level: What the two panels answer
entries.summary: Run the outcome matrix and the seasonal outlook at a few demand levels, read how past years went at each, and publish the level the WUA sets.
entries.text: Both run the catchment at a few demand levels (100, 85 and 70 % of today’s demand by default) and count how past years went. The Outcome matrix looks at the whole record, split into dry, normal and wet years: how the river fares at each level in each kind of year. The Seasonal outlook starts from the catchment as it stands on the decision date (dams, soil, the runoff model’s stores) and runs the coming season with the weather of each past year (Analogue years). Neither forecasts the weather, and neither recommends a level: the WUA decides.

entries.title: Weigh a season’s demand level: Steps
entries.text: Run the model on the latest data. Both panels need an ordinary run, not a scenario or forecast run. In Model settings, check Outcome matrix (how years are classed and the risk cut-offs) and Seasonal outlook (the season, the planning share and the review date). On EWR, press Run… beside Outcome matrix, type the levels and press Run demand sweep. Read across a row for one level in every kind of year, and down a column for every level in one kind of year. Press Run… beside Seasonal outlook, type the levels (and a monthly plan, if the WUA is considering one) and press Run seasonal outlook. Read each level’s season-end storage, demand met and days below the EWR as the median with its 10–90 % range, and the Planning figure and planning share. For a mid-season check, read the Review triggers: the level each band of total dam storage on the review date supported in past years. Once the WUA has decided, pick Level the WUA has set under Farmers and press Publish to farmers (Publishing an outlook level to farmers). A lower demand level doesn’t always mean fewer days below the EWR: part of the water irrigated from a dam drains back to the river on dry days. With fewer than 10 analogue years the outlook gives no ranges and no planning figure.

entries.title: Set up a team and share a project: Make the team
entries.summary: Make a team for your colleagues, give each a role, move a catchment into it, and share single projects with people outside it.
entries.text: Open Teams in the sidebar and press New team. Name it after the consultancy, department or WUA; you are its owner. On the team’s page, under Members, type a colleague’s email and pick a Role, then press Add. Each person gets an Invitation and joins once they accept it. Repeat for each colleague. The pending invitations are listed under the form, with Resend and Revoke; an invitation works for 7 days. A Team role holds on every team project: a viewer reads them, an editor edits and runs them, and an owner owns them and manages the team. Change a member’s role from the list at any time.

entries.title: Set up a team and share a project: Put a catchment in the team
entries.text: For a new catchment, pick the team under Belongs to in the New project dialog. For an existing one, open it, go to its Project page and, under Team, choose the team in Move to and press Move. Only the project’s owners can move it. Everyone in the team now has the project with their team role. People listed under Shared directly with keep their own access too. An owner only through the team can’t make the project personal again: add yourself under Members as an owner first.

entries.title: Set up a team and share a project: Share one project with someone outside the team
entries.text: A colleague or client who works on the model: add them under Members on the Project page with a role. Anyone with a role is a member of that project only. A farmer: press Invite farmers under Farmers and tick their hydrological units. They read only those units, from the published run (Farmer and their linked units). Someone who only needs to look (a forum, an NGO): make a Share link under Share links. It opens the published baseline without signing in, for as long as you choose. Every addition, role change and link is recorded on the History page with who made it.

entries.title: Push logger data with an API key: Make a key
entries.summary: Let a logger gateway or a script add daily readings to a project’s series without signing in, and keep an eye on it.
entries.text: Make sure the series exists: upload its record once on the Data tab, with the name the gateway will send. A key creates a series only when the project has none of that kind. As an owner, open the Project page and go to API keys. Give the key a Name that says where it runs (“Drift logger gateway”), choose how long it Works for, and under What it may write choose Only these series and tick the ones it feeds. Press Make key and copy the key at once: it is shown only this once. Store it in the gateway’s own settings, never in a shared file.

entries.title: Push logger data with an API key: Send the readings
entries.text: The gateway sends each day’s readings to the ingest address with the key, as in the example request shown under the new key: the series’ kind and name, its unit, the first date and one value a day. Only the days sent change, in the series’ own units, and sending the same days again changes nothing, so a gateway can safely resend the last week every day. Each push shows in History as API key “name”. When the project re-runs automatically, a push that changed days queues a run. A push that looks wrong (a negative value, a value far above the record’s usual range, or a series it had to create) is still stored, but holds the automatic runs until a person runs the model.

entries.title: Push logger data with an API key: Keep an eye on it
entries.text: The key’s row shows when it was Last used. Switch on API data behind in the Summary’s alert rules to be emailed when a series the key sends stops getting readings (Alert rules). If a key leaks or the gateway is retired, press Revoke: the key is refused from its next request. Make a new key for a replacement gateway.

entries.title: Ask the assistant about a project: Ask a question
entries.summary: Ask questions about a project’s model and results in plain words, and review the changes it recommends before you save or try any.
entries.text: Open the project and press Assistant on the page title’s line, after How this page works (on a phone, its chat-bubble icon). It shows on every page of the project when your organisation has the assistant switched on. Type a question about this project, such as “Why does the simulated flow at the outlet gauge not respond to rainfall?”, and press Send (or Enter). The answer comes in as it is written. The lines above it say what the assistant read to answer: the network, a series, the run’s summary, a gauge’s fit or the help guides. Ask a follow-up in the same box: the assistant sees the whole conversation. Stop ends an answer early; New conversation starts again.
