Past chats, at the top of the panel, lists your earlier conversations on this project, newest first. Open one to read it or carry on asking; Delete removes one, Clear past chats all of them. A recommended change in a past chat can’t be applied, since the project may have changed since: ask again for a fresh one. Past chats are kept only in this browser, on this device: they never reach our servers, and signing out deletes them, so the next person on a shared computer sees none. In a private window, or with site data blocked, there are no past chats. It reads the run you have open (on Runs & results, EWR and the other run pages), or the project’s latest run. It reads only what your role lets you see, and it never changes anything. Its answers are advice, not model output: check them against the run’s own results before you rely on them, as the line under the box says.

entries.title: Ask the assistant about a project: Review a recommended change
entries.text: Ask it what to change (“Which settings would you change to improve the fit at the outlet?”) and it may answer with a Recommended change: a title naming exactly what it changes, then each change, its value now and the suggested one, with why under it. A change it couldn’t make never appears on the card. It keeps the model of the catchment apart from how its water is managed. The calibrated parameters (GR4J’s X1–X4, the pan coefficients, the CHIRPS bias settings) are fitted to the observed flow, so it changes them only in a Recalibration, to improve the fit, never to make the EWR, a yield or the assurance look better. For those it recommends a Management change: a dam’s runoff capture or release, a hands-off flow, a transfer’s months, rates or caps, the drought restriction or demand. When no management lever would help, it says so. A recalibration or a correction: press Apply to the settings form (editors and owners only). Model settings opens with the change in the form, not yet saved, and the Reason for this change filled in as “Assistant suggestion: …”. Check the values, then press Save changes to keep it, or Discard to drop it. Run the model to see what it does. A management change: press Try it as a scenario (editors and owners only). It becomes a Scenario on the run you have open, named after the card, and Scenarios opens on it. Run it and compare it with the run to judge the change; the project itself is unchanged. Each is checked like any other save or scenario, and the History page keeps a saved change with its reason.

entries.title: Ask the assistant about a project: Limits
entries.text: Each person can send a set number of messages an hour. Past it, the panel says how long to wait. Each project has a monthly budget, shown under the box. Once it is used up the assistant rests until the date shown. Nothing you type is kept on our servers. Your browser keeps your 20 newest chats on each project until you delete them or sign out.

entries.title: Sign in with two steps: What it is
entries.summary: Add a code from an authenticator app or by email to your password, keep your recovery codes, and get back in after losing your phone.
entries.text: Two-step sign-in asks for a 6-digit code after your password, so someone who learns the password still can’t get in. There are two ways to get the code, and you can turn on both: an Authenticator app on your phone (such as Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator or Aegis; the stronger, since only your phone makes the codes) and a Code by email (the easier, each code working for 10 minutes, but only as safe as your inbox).

entries.title: Sign in with two steps: Turn it on
entries.text: Open your Account page (the foot of the sidebar; on a phone, under Menu) and find Two-step sign-in. For the app, press Set up the app, enter your current password, scan the QR code with the app (or type the key it shows), and enter the app’s first code. For email, press Turn on beside Code by email, enter your password and the code we email you. The first way you turn on brings ten recovery codes, shown once: press Download the codes or Copy the codes, keep them away from your phone and your email (a password manager, or on paper), then press I’ve saved them. From then on, each sign-in asks for a code after the password. Email me a code instead or Use a code from the app instead switches between the two, and the recovery-code link takes one of those. Some actions ask for a fresh code even while you are signed in, such as signing or issuing an evidence pack. A browser that signed in before you set it up must sign out and in again before such an action.

entries.title: Sign in with two steps: Recovery codes
entries.text: Each recovery code works once, in place of a code from the app or the email. The Account page says how many are left and warns at two or fewer; Make new recovery codes (with a code) replaces the whole set, and the old ones stop working.

entries.title: Sign in with two steps: A lost phone or inbox
entries.text: With a recovery code: sign in with it, then on the Account page Remove the app (or Turn off the email codes) and set it up again on the new phone. Without one: sign in with your password, and on the code step choose Lost your phone and your recovery codes? (or Can’t get the email and lost your recovery codes?). We email you a link that works for an hour. The link opens Remove two-step sign-in: press Start the 3-day wait. Until it ends your codes keep working, and we email you every day with a link to cancel; signing in with a code cancels it too. When the wait ends, two-step sign-in is removed and every device is signed out. Sign in with your password alone and set two-step sign-in up again on your Account page. If you get a removal email you didn’t ask for, someone knows your password: cancel it with a code and choose a new password.

entries.title: Sign in with two steps: When a project requires it
entries.text: An owner can require it: the Two-step sign-in panel on the Project page (owners only; a team’s admins have the same switch in the team’s settings, which covers every team project) has Require two-step sign-in, off by default. While it is on, the project’s owners give a code before they manage members, invitations, share links, API keys or data feeds, or delete the project, and so does anyone who signs a run. To turn it on you must yourself be signed in with a code, so it can’t lock everyone out. Some actions always need it, whatever the switch says, because they reach farmers, the public or a licence decision: publishing to farmers, deciding applications, endorsing a baseline, and signing or issuing an evidence pack. Your Account page says so when your roles need it.

entries.title: Issue an evidence pack: Before you start
entries.summary: Turn a run’s evidence report into a signed, hashed pack with a short code that anyone can check on the public verify page.
entries.text: The baseline must be the project’s nominated evidence run. For an Licence application, run the application on that baseline. Declare the uncertainty rule under Model settings → Evidence, and run an ensemble to it, so the report has bands to cite. The signer needs two-step sign-in, and, while the project requires it, a current registration check recorded on the Project page.

entries.title: Issue an evidence pack: Steps
entries.text: Open the Evidence report: Evidence report beside Report on Runs & results, or from the head of a scenario’s comparison. Read the checks at the top. Fix every one marked “stops issue” (Checks that stop issue), run the model again and nominate the new run if the baseline changed, then read Expect questions about. For an application with registered volumes, press Run at full authorised use, so page 1 carries the impact against full authorised use. Press Create evidence pack. The pack’s page opens: a draft, with its checklist under Where this pack stands. In Appendix B.2, the applicant’s specialist presses Sign off this evidence pack…, fills in their registration and ticks every confirmation. An assessor may add a second sign-off as a review. Once every line of the checklist is ticked, an editor presses Issue pack and confirms. Signing and issuing ask for a fresh code, from the authenticator app or by email. The server then prints the pack’s PDF, builds its Reproduction bundle and re-runs it; the pack page shows each as it lands. Hand the short code to whoever needs to check the pack, use Send to the authority… for the full pack, and Share link… for the public. Issuing is public and permanent: the verify page shows the signers’ names and registrations, and an issued pack is never edited or deleted. A change of evidence is New version…; a pack that shouldn’t stand is Withdraw…, with a reason anyone holding the code can read.

entries.title: How the model works: The daily chain
entries.summary: The chain from daily rain to hydrological unit supply, dam storage, outflow and the EWR check.
entries.text: One run, every day of the simulation window. The runoff model makes the catchment’s natural flow; the network then routes it through hydrological units and dams to the outflow gauge, where the EWR and the calibration are checked. Rain. Each day takes the first available of catchment rain, bias-corrected CHIRPS and forecast rain. See How rain gaps are filled. Natural flow. The Runoff model (GR4J) turns rain and evaporation into the flow the catchment would produce with no hydrological units. Under flow generation (Per unit) it runs once for each unit with land, each on its own rain: its rainfall station × unit MAP ÷ station MAP when it has one; else the unit’s own gauge; else the catchment gauge × unit MAP ÷ gauge MAP; else the unit’s own CHIRPS, levelled to its MAP; else the catchment rain. The outlet’s natural flow is then their routed sum. Shares. The EWR is split between the hydrological units by each unit’s natural MAR share, from GR4J on its own rain; each unit’s runoff is its own. Demand. Crops, A-pan and effective rain give each hydrological unit’s crop water requirement; divided by the irrigation efficiency it is the abstraction demand, what the hydrological unit takes from its dam and the river. Hydrological unit balance. Upstream first, each hydrological unit fills its dam, irrigates, spills and passes water on. See A day on one hydrological unit. Outlet. The outflow gauge’s flow is the simulated outflow. It is checked against the EWR and scored against observed flow. Every other gauge ticked as an EWR site (the default) is checked too, and a shortfall at any EWR site is charged to the hydrological units upstream of it (EWR charge); a gauge unticked only measures.

entries.title: How the model works: Properties you can rely on
entries.text: Flows and volumes are m³/day inside the model. Nothing is rounded mid-calculation; rounding is for display only. Every hydrological unit’s daily balance closes: inflow + rain on the dam − irrigation use − dam evaporation − change in storage = outflow. Invariant tests check this on random networks, and every run checks it again on its own results (Arithmetic checks on Runs & results). A run is a snapshot: it records its inputs and engine version, so its results can always be explained and reproduced. Where the engine departs from the Water Balance Tool workbook, the engine audit records why.

entries.title: A day on one hydrological unit: One hydrological unit, up close
entries.summary: How a hydrological unit element splits its inflows around the dam, irrigates, spills and passes water downstream.
entries.text: A hydrological unit (here a farm) on a tributary: its dam, the orchard it irrigates and the pipeline to a neighbour’s dam. Follow the numbers in the order the model works through a day. Inflow from upstream: The stream brings the outflow of the elements above. The upstream share of it enters the dam. The hydrological unit’s own runoff: The hydrological unit’s share of the catchment’s natural flow. Its own-runoff share drains into the dam. Dam storage: Yesterday’s storage plus rain on the dam, today’s captured inflow, diversion and transfers, less evaporation, seepage and irrigation, up to the capacity. Spill over the wall: Water above capacity spills and continues downstream the same day. Irrigation draw: The dam supplies the hydrological unit’s irrigation demand, or what it holds above its minimum level if that is less. The crops: The crop gets the supply × the irrigation efficiency. Part of the losses runs back to the river as return flow; the rest leaves the catchment. Transfer to a neighbour: A Transfer can move water out of (or into) this dam in chosen months. Outflow: Spill, water that passed below the dam, seepage and return flow leave as the hydrological unit’s outflow, the next element’s inflow.

entries.title: A day on one hydrological unit: Around the dam
entries.text: Water arriving from upstream and the hydrological unit’s own runoff each split into a part that enters the dam and a part that passes below it. A diversion can take some of the bypass back into the dam. Irrigation draws from the dam; spill, bypass and return flow leave downstream. Upstream inflow × upstream share enters the dam; the rest passes below it. Hydrological unit runoff × own-runoff share enters the dam; the rest passes below it. The River to dam (diversion) takes up to its daily capacity from the water passing below, back into the dam. A Transfer adds to or takes from the dam. Transfers move first, before any hydrological unit irrigates. The dam catches the rain on its surface and loses open-water evaporation and any seepage; the share of the seepage set by Seepage returning (all of it by default) reaches the river below the wall, and the rest leaves the catchment. Irrigation takes the smaller of the demand and what the dam holds above its minimum level (yesterday’s storage plus today’s inflows and the rain on it, less evaporation and seepage). Storage above capacity spills. Return flow is the share of the irrigation water supplied that returns to the river the same day (never more than the losses). Outflow = spill + water passing below the dam not diverted + returning seepage + return flow. It is the next element’s upstream inflow.

entries.title: A day on one hydrological unit: The balance
entries.text: upstream inflow + runoff + transfer + rain on the dam − (irrigation − return flow) − dam evaporation − seepage lost − Δ storage = outflow It closes to the cubic metre every day (the balance check). The seepage that returns is part of the outflow; the seepage lost (what Seepage returning doesn’t return) and the dam’s evaporation leave the catchment.

entries.title: How GR4J turns rain into flow: Under the ground
entries.summary: Two stores and two unit hydrographs, four parameters, and a water balance that always closes.
entries.text: The cut face of the catchment beside the river. GR4J is a conceptual model: its two stores stand roughly for the moist soil and the groundwater, not for measured layers. Rain: Rain first meets evaporation. What is left is net rain. Evaporation: Plants and soil return water to the air, up to the potential evaporation. The soil store (X1): Net rain partly fills the production store. A larger X1 holds more rain back, so less of it becomes flow. The routing store (X3): Water that percolates on is released slowly. A larger X3 means slower, longer recessions between storms. Flow in the river: The routing store’s release plus a quick direct part is the Natural flow; X4 sets how many days a storm takes to arrive.

entries.title: How GR4J turns rain into flow: The structure
entries.text: GR4J (Perrin et al. 2003). Rain first meets evaporation. What is left partly fills the soil (production) store; the rest, with what percolates out of it, is spread in time by two unit hydrographs. 90 % passes through the routing store, 10 % goes directly to the outlet. X1 (mm): capacity of the soil-moisture store. Larger means more rain is held and evaporated, so less flow. Typical 100–1 200. X2 (mm/day): exchange with groundwater outside the catchment. Fixed at 0 by default, so the catchment is closed. X3 (mm): capacity of the routing store. Larger means slower, longer recessions. Typical 20–300. X4 (days): time base of the unit hydrographs, the timing of the peak. Typical 1.1–2.9.

entries.title: How GR4J turns rain into flow: Forcing and warm-up
entries.text: Rain is the gap-filled catchment rain, with no rain threshold. Potential evaporation is the monthly Pan coefficient × A-pan, spread over the days of the month. A warm-up (a year by default) runs over the start of the record first, so the stores begin at a realistic level; warm-up days are never shown or scored. rain − actual evaporation − flow − groundwater exchange = change in storage (every day) The Runoff model panel on a GR4J run shows this balance in mm and as a share of rain. It is the first thing to check when a fit looks too wet or too dry.

entries.title: How calibration works: What is scored
entries.summary: What is scored, how the optimiser searches, and why validation on unseen days matters more than the fit.
entries.text: The catchment outlet. The observed record comes from here; the model’s simulated outflow is its prediction of the same place. The gauging hut: A gauge or logger records the water level, turned into observed flow by a rating curve. High flows beyond the highest measurement are extrapolated, so they are the least certain. The weir: A control that makes level and flow relate reliably. The model’s Outflow gauge stands for this point. The river above it: What arrives here is the whole catchment’s outflow, hydrological units and dams included, which is why the whole model is scored, not the runoff model alone. An observed gauge or logger measures the river as it is, with its hydrological units and dams. So every candidate parameter set runs the whole model (runoff model, then the network) and scores the simulated outflow against the observed record. The fitted parameters describe the natural catchment; the network adds the impacts. Scored days are days with an observation, inside the Calibration window, outside every exclusion, and not left out by the quality flags (by default days below the lowest gauging, suspect and infilled days; days above the highest gauging are censored). At least 30 are needed.

entries.title: How calibration works: The search
entries.text: Fit automatically. DDS starts from the current parameters, perturbs them within their bounds, runs the whole model and keeps a candidate only when it scores better. By default it tries 1 500 candidates per search. The optimiser is DDS (Tolson & Shoemaker 2007). Early on it perturbs every parameter; later it changes fewer, homing in on the best set found. Candidates are always kept within the bounds. The search is deterministic for a seed: the same data, engine version and seed give the same fit. The app runs five searches (starts) from different seeds and keeps the best; when several reach nearly the same score with scattered parameters, the notes say the record can’t pin those parameters down. KGE′ (Kling–Gupta, 2012) (default): correlation, bias and variability in one score, less peak-dominated than NSE. Year-balanced KGE′: each water year counts once, so a few wet years can’t dominate a drought-heavy record. Non-parametric KGE: rank correlation, the flow-duration curve’s shape and the bias, so less sensitive to rating error at the extremes. NSE on √Q (medium flows) and NSE on log Q (low flows). Mean of KGE′(Q) and KGE′(1/Q) (the scores table calls it Low/high-flow KGE′ (Q and 1/Q)): half the score on the flows, half on their inverses, so recessions and low flows count as much as the peaks. Suggested when the fit feeds an EWR (low-flow) decision. Choose the objective by what the fit will feed, before seeing any score, never by which one scores best: scores of different objectives don’t compare.

entries.title: How calibration works: Validation: the honest measure
entries.text: Each test fits on one part of the record and scores another part it never saw. The dry → wet test fits on the driest water years and scores the wettest, which is the hardest test for a catchment used in drought. Split-sample (Klemeš 1986): fit on the first half of the scored days, score the second half. Dry → wet: with at least 4 water years of 180 or more observed days, fit on the driest half and score the wettest half. Independent record (optional): score the fitted parameters against the second instrument, for example the logger when the fit used the gauge. The result adds plain-language notes on its limits: too few years to test wet years, wet years barely wetter than dry ones, or a validation score more than 0.2 below its calibration score. A short record that is mostly drought gets these notes rather than a clean bill of health. A fit that scores well in-sample but poorly in validation usually means the record can’t pin the parameters down, not that the optimiser failed. More model runs won’t help; more varied data, typical bounds or a WR2012 check will.

entries.title: How rain gaps are filled: One value per day
entries.summary: Which rain series a day uses, and how CHIRPS is bias-corrected to the catchment before it fills a gap.
entries.text: Each day takes the first series that has a value. CHIRPS is scaled by its calendar month’s catchment ÷ CHIRPS factor before it is used. A day with no value anywhere is treated as dry, and the run counts those days. A 0 is a reading, so it blocks the fallback. Long wet-season runs of zeros that the Data checks flag are the exception: by default a run treats their days as blank where CHIRPS reads more than 2 mm, so CHIRPS fills those, and a day CHIRPS reads 2 mm or less keeps its 0, since CHIRPS reports too many light-rain days (zero-rain runs). On Model settings → Rain gaps you can change the 2 mm, keep a confirmed dry spell dry, run every flagged run as recorded, or list other bad periods to treat as missing. The uploaded series is never changed. A large reading after 3 to 7 blank days, on a day CHIRPS reads little although it saw rain over those days, looks like several days read at once (a multi-day accumulation). By default a run keeps its recorded total and spreads it over the days it covers in proportion to bias-corrected CHIRPS. Days recorded as 0 are readings, so a large reading after them is real rain and stays on its day. More than 7 blank days in a row is an outage: such a reading straight after one is set aside and CHIRPS fills its day, since it may hold weeks of rain or one day’s. Under Multi-day accumulations on the same panel you can run them as recorded, keep readings you know were one day’s rain, or list accumulations the check misses. The result is the final catchment rainfall, which the runoff model (GR4J) and the effective-rain part of demand use. The daily CSV export puts it beside CHIRPS as uploaded and bias-corrected CHIRPS, so filled days can be checked. Under flow generation (Model settings → Flow generation), each unit with land gets a rain series of its own: its rainfall station × unit MAP ÷ station MAP when it is given one, its gaps filled by its CHIRPS corrected against a station; else, in this order, its own gauge, with the same zero-run and accumulation checks, its gaps and set-aside days taking its CHIRPS levelled to its MAP; else the catchment gauge × unit MAP ÷ gauge MAP, when the gauge’s MAP is set and the unit has one; else its own CHIRPS, levelled by its MAP ÷ the CHIRPS mean over the MAP period; else the catchment rain, with a warning. Demand, rain on the dams and the WR2012 check keep the catchment rain. A seasonal outlook, the uncertainty ensemble’s CHIRPS-only member and a run resumed from a saved state keep each unit’s rule and factors pinned as the base run had them, rather than refitting them on a shorter record; the run’s Rain for each unit panel then says its factors are pinned. Where Settings assigns a rainfall station, the Data page shows what a run reads: a hydrological unit’s row, or Average catchment rainfall, says how its rain is made (the station × area MAP ÷ station MAP, gaps from CHIRPS corrected against a station), and Show rain used charts that rain with the station and CHIRPS lines behind it and a strip for the days that didn’t come from the station. Download (CSV) → Full has every one of those lines by day.

entries.title: How rain gaps are filled: The CHIRPS factors
entries.text: factor(month) = Σ catchment rain ÷ Σ CHIRPS over the days of that calendar month that have both Water years that read far below CHIRPS are left out whole, and so are the days of flagged zero runs (unless kept dry), of periods listed as missing and of multi-day accumulations, because their catchment rain is suspect. A month with fewer than 90 shared days, or under 50 mm of CHIRPS on them, uses the factor pooled over all months. Factors are kept between 0.25 and 4. Each run lists them in its warnings and the summary CSV. Choose Raw CHIRPS only when the series you loaded is already corrected to the catchment; otherwise it is corrected twice.

entries.title: Curtailment targets: The idea
entries.summary: How the app compares each hydrological unit’s supply with a fairness benchmark and works out the cut that meets the EWR.
entries.text: Over the reporting window, add up what every hydrological unit asked for and what it received. Their ratio is the catchment’s equitable share of supply (a fairness benchmark): had the supplied water been shared in proportion to demand, every hydrological unit would have received that fraction. equitable share volume = demand × Σ supplied ÷ Σ demand above (−) / below (+) equitable share = equitable share volume − supplied The differences cancel across the hydrological units, so this only compares; a positive value is not water the hydrological unit can get. Each hydrological unit’s EWR charge (its share of the shortfall at the EWR sites below it) is then split into irrigating less and storing less, and the supply cut for the irrigation part is added: the total change in supply. Negative means reduce. The volume left never goes below 0, nor below the hydrological unit’s basic-needs floor (25 litres a person a day for the people its domestic and municipal demands serve); what the floor keeps of the cut is shown in its row. The equitable share is a fairness benchmark only: it assumes water can move freely between hydrological units, and ignores network position, storage, licences and existing lawful use. Not an allocation or licence condition.

entries.title: Scenarios: try a change without copying the project: What a scenario is
entries.summary: Make a named list of changes on a run (a bigger dam, a new crop, less rain), run it, and read it against the run it started from.
entries.text: A Scenario is a named list of changes on a base run: raise a dam by 20 %, replace a crop, remove a hydrological unit, add a transfer, scale the rain by −10 %. It runs and compares against its base without copying the project, and the model itself never changes: the base run stays as it was, and is kept while the scenario exists. Use one to answer “what if”. Copying the project (create a project) is the other way, for a change too large to describe as a list of edits.

entries.title: Scenarios: try a change without copying the project: Steps
entries.text: Run the model at least once: a scenario needs a run to start from. On Scenarios, press + New scenario, name it and pick its base run (the published run by default, else the latest). Under Add a change, add each change in turn. Each reads in words against the value it meets (“dam capacity 120 000 → 144 000 m³”), so a second change to the same value shows the first one’s result as “was”. Tick Explain each setting under its field (beside Undo; the same switch as in Settings, remembered by your browser) to see how each kind of change works under its fields. Read the label on each change: a Proposal is the change being assessed; a Baseline assumption changes what the river is like today (rain, a setting, a Reserve rule) and puts a red Baseline assumptions changed callout above the list. Press Run scenario. The run joins Runs & results tagged Scenario, and Scenario against its base shows the headline water balance and each hydrological unit against the base run. To bring an older scenario up to date, open Based on … Rebase… under Application details: Check lists any change that no longer applies, then Rebase onto this run. A change that doesn’t apply to its base (a hydrological unit removed since, say) says why, and Run scenario stays off until it is fixed or removed.

entries.title: Scenarios: try a change without copying the project: Scenarios and licence applications
entries.text: A licence Licence application is a scenario too: one an applicant builds on the published baseline. It shows on the Scenarios list with its status, and its changes are frozen once submitted. applications page covers the rest.

entries.title: Applications: licence applications, applied for and assessed: What an application is
entries.summary: How a water-use licence applicant models their change on the published baseline, and how the project’s assessors read and decide it.
entries.text: Someone applying for a water-use licence (to build or raise a dam, to abstract more, to irrigate more land) needs to show what their change does to the river and to the users around them. In this app their proposed change is a licence Licence application: a Scenario on the published baseline, run by the same model as everything else. Two sides use it. The applicant (the developer, the farmer or their consultant) builds and submits it. The assessors are the project’s editors and owners (other than the applicant), who read it. Only an assessor the responsible authority has confirmed as acting for it (Acts for the authority on the Project page) records the authority’s decision; the app records that decision, it never makes one.

entries.title: Applications: licence applications, applied for and assessed: Before anyone can apply
entries.text: Publish a run as the baseline: in Runs & results, Publish this run. Applications start from it; with nothing published an applicant can’t start one. On the Project page, add the applicant as a member with the Applicant role, and link them to their own hydrological units if they already farm in the catchment. An applicant never sees the model. Their view is a page of their own applications, other farms show only by an anonymous name (“Farm 1”), and nothing unpublished reaches them.

entries.title: Applications: licence applications, applied for and assessed: What the applicant does
entries.text: Start a New application (a name; it starts on the published baseline). Add the proposed change with the scenario editor: a new hydrological unit with its dam, a bigger dam, a river pump, more hectares of a crop. Press Run scenario, then read Your results against the baseline: the Ecological Reserve, the catchment’s flow, their own hydrological units, and the farms downstream of them. Fill in the notice’s Address and Closing date for written objections while it is a draft. Press Submit to the assessors. Its changes are frozen; it can still be withdrawn, or reopened as a draft. While it is a draft only the applicant and the people they share it with can see it.

entries.title: Applications: licence applications, applied for and assessed: What the assessors do
entries.text: The Applications tab lists every submitted, withdrawn or decided application (never a draft), with its applicant, status, when it was submitted, its changes, runs and evidence packs. It is hidden from the sidebar until you turn it on in Choose sections, and viewers never see it. Decide the longest waiting opens the application that has waited longest for a decision. Open one to read its changes and runs in Scenarios and answer the applicant’s questions about rules they can’t see. Once the authority has decided, an assessor confirmed as acting for it presses Record the authority’s decision and records it with its reasons; anyone else reads it but has no such button. Assess together runs several applications on one baseline, each on its own and all together, for their combined effect on the river. Draft an evidence pack from a run’s evidence report, then sign and issue it: a frozen, versioned copy anyone can check with its short code.

entries.title: Allocations: registered volumes against modelled use: What the page is for
entries.summary: Import the volumes each user is registered or licensed for, and see where a run’s modelled use is above or below them.
entries.text: Each water user in the catchment is registered (WARMS) or licensed for a volume a year. This page sets those volumes beside what a run modelled each hydrological unit using, per water year, so you can see where modelled use runs above or below the registration. It is under *Outcomes* in the sidebar, shown by default. Modelled use is modelled, not metered: a difference is something to look into, not a finding. A registration is not an entitlement.

entries.title: Allocations: registered volumes against modelled use: Steps
entries.text: Press Import and upload a WARMS extract or a CSV (Download the CSV template shows the columns). A WARMS extract asks how you obtained it; the preview says how many rows matched a hydrological unit. Or press + Add volume for one at a time: a take from the river or a borehole, or a dam’s storage. Match any volume the header counts as “not matched” to its hydrological unit. Pick the run to compare with in the header’s run menu, and read each unit’s modelled use against its registered volume. The baseline only compares. A scenario’s Allocation mode can make its run cap each unit’s use at its registered volume, or take every registered volume in full (licence data never drives the baseline); this page then says what the run did.

entries.title: Allocations: registered volumes against modelled use: Who sees names
entries.text: Owners and editors see every volume. Viewers see only catchment totals per water source held by five or more users, until an owner ticks Viewers see each farm’s registered volumes under What viewers see.

entries.title: Allocations: registered volumes against modelled use: Reading the comparison
entries.text: The list puts first the units to look into: each unit and water source with its status over a mean water year. Pick one to see its water years, the band and its registered volumes. Each water year reads above registered, within band, below registered, or no registered volume (Modelled use vs registered volume). A part year is compared with the volume prorated to its days and isn’t counted with the whole years. The comparison band is set at the foot of the page, in the Comparison band card beside What viewers see: editors change it and press that card’s Save. It changes how the comparison reads, never a run’s water. A dam’s registered storage (a s21(b) row) is set against the dam’s modelled capacity, never against the year’s use (Registered storage vs dam capacity). After a cap run, the picked unit says on how many days the cap held use back, and why (What the cap held back). On the map opens a map of the hydrological units, each unit’s polygon shaded by its band of modelled use against its registered volume, for the water source and the period you pick (the mean of the whole water years, or one); a unit with no polygon on the Map is listed under it with its band, and a click on a unit opens its comparison. Viewers who see only totals don’t get it. Every hydrological unit and water year charts modelled use ÷ the registered volume for each whole water year, one row per unit and source, with the table under it. Under Registered volumes, Imported files lists each import with its rows, who imported it and its SHA-256; an editor can Remove this import, which takes its rows out again.

entries.title: The Map: the catchment’s geography: What the page is for
entries.summary: Draw or upload the boundary, parcels, dams, gauges and rivers, and let the map propose areas and the catchment above a point.
entries.text: The Network is the model’s schematic: what drains into what. The map is the geography: the catchment boundary, each unit’s area, the farm parcels, dams, gauges and rivers. A model builds and runs without it; with it, areas come from the drawing instead of being typed, and results can be read on the map.

entries.title: The Map: the catchment’s geography: Steps
entries.text: Draw the boundary with Draw a shape, or Upload GeoJSON (WGS84). The header counts the features and gives the boundary’s area. Add dams, abstraction points and gauges with Place a point, and parcels with Draw a shape. Snap to features puts a corner on a neighbour’s corner or edge. With an elevation model on the server, Delineate draws the terrain channels (solid lines): click one at the catchment’s outlet and the catchment above it is proposed, following the terrain, to accept or reject. The river network’s dashed lines are for reference only and can sit off the terrain channels. A catchment over about 100 km across is worked out in the background (or tick work it out in the background); the map shows the proposal when it is ready. Where pans drain part of it, Which area lets you take the gross area (the default, as WR2012’s quaternaries are) or the effective one without them. On a dam’s card, say whether it stands On the river or Off-channel (filled by a pump or a furrow): Start and Divide place an off-channel dam’s unit where its own outflow meets the river, and propose its inflow and runoff shares from that. An accepted boundary is on the map only, not in the model yet. Its card, and the message after accepting, offer the next step: Divide the model gives each unit its boundary’s area and order (Start from the map while the model is empty makes a unit of each boundary), each value ticked to take it. While the model is empty, Start from the map proposes the units, their areas and their order from the boundary and the points; each value is ticked to take it. With water occurrence data on the server, Trace a dam proposes a dam’s outline from a click inside it. Measure and Download GeoJSON are there for everyone, viewers too.

entries.title: The Map: the catchment’s geography: Layers and search
entries.text: Layers (the button under the zoom buttons, or the Layers tab beside the map) turns on the optional layers, each kept in the page’s address so Back undoes it and the view can be shared: Quaternary catchments (the outlines around the catchment, their codes listed as buttons), River network (the reaches around the catchment, biggest first: pick one for its facts and source, and an editor can add it to the map as a river), Hydrological units (each unit’s polygon with its name), MAP grid (a loaded mean annual precipitation grid’s points in view, each with its MAP), CHIRPS grid (CHIRPS’s 0.05° cells and their centres, where a unit’s CHIRPS rain comes from), DEM grid (one in a hundred of the elevation model’s cells, each with its height) and Relief (hills shaded from the elevation model). The DEM grid and the relief need an elevation model on the server; a grid with too many points in view asks you to zoom in. Area fill, at the top of the panel, sets how strongly units, dams and results colours are filled (outlines stay): lower it to see the map, relief and grids through them. The search box over the map’s top edge (Find, or Enter) finds the map’s own reference layers first, then places (Map search): gauging stations by code or name, the register of dams by number or name, quaternary catchments by code, then towns, farms, rivers, pans, peaks and areas. Every word you type must start a word of the name, in any order. One match moves the map to it; several are listed, and picking one moves the map. Nothing is drawn or saved. Place names come from a gazetteer the server operator loads: where none is loaded the search says so, and it still finds gauges, dams and quaternaries. Snap to features puts a corner on a neighbour’s corner or edge; with Follow edges on too, two corners in a row on one outline take that outline’s corners between them, so a parcel drawn against its neighbour or the boundary shares their edge with no gap or overlap (Snap to features). Delineate → Sub-catchments, one per click gives each click on a terrain channel the land that drains to it before any other click: click from the outlet up, check the pieces, then save them as areas, link each to its unit and Use its area (Sub-catchments, one per click).

entries.title: Dams: every dam’s level in one run: What the page shows
entries.summary: How full each dam ran, how long it sat at its minimum, and how storage moved over the record.
entries.text: Every hydrological unit with a dam capacity of at least 1 m³, with its storage from the latest run: how full it is as a share of that day’s capacity, a sparkline of the record, and how many days it sat at its minimum level. Pick a dam for its chart. Levels are shares of the capacity on the day, so a dam losing capacity to sediment, or coming into service part way through the record, reads correctly. Open in Runs & results goes to the run the page shows.

entries.title: Dams: every dam’s level in one run: Proposals and assurance
entries.text: Under the picked dam’s chart, Assurance of supply is the supply of the hydrological unit the dam serves, since a dam has none of its own: how often and how fully its demand was met, and its stress by month (Assurance of supply), with a link to the unit on Hydrological units. Under that, in the same panel, Proposed from the register and the map is folded to one line of what is proposed for that dam; open it, or follow a card’s Proposals, for the values (Dam values from the register and the map). It lists the registered dams within 1 km of the dam on the map, each with its capacity for reference only (a unit’s dam stands for all its farm dams, many of them unregistered, so its volume is yours to enter), and the dam’s polygon on the map, which proposes its area as the full-supply area. Each row shows its source and what the model holds now; Use (editors, the area only) asks first, then saves that one value as a change naming its source. Dam of picks another dam, and the chart follows, or a hydrological unit with no dam yet. Before the first run the proposals sit in a panel under the cards.

entries.title: EWR: is enough left in the river?: What the page shows
entries.summary: One run’s river against its Ecological Reserve: the days the EWR was not met, the water account and how this run differs from the one before.
entries.text: Every EWR result for one run, gathered here so the Summary can be about irrigation: the headline tile, the share of days the EWR was not met at the outflow gauge (Days EWR not met) or, when a Reserve rule table judges the results, the share of months its rules were met, with its change from the run before; the days below the reserve in each of the last twelve months; the flow chart against the EWR (Environmental Water Requirement); Reserve compliance at each EWR site; and the Water account of where the catchment’s water went. The page shows the newest run; pick another with the Run menu in the header (Back returns to the one before). Open in Runs & results opens the same run there.

entries.title: EWR: is enough left in the river?: How sure, and what if
entries.text: Under the findings, How sure, and what if holds the tools you run yourself, each one row with Run… until it has run: the Uncertainty bands on the findings, with the Sensitivity runs (Read how sure a result is); the Outcome matrix, how the river fares at a few demand levels in dry, normal and wet years; and the Seasonal outlook, the coming season from the catchment as it stands, with the weather of each past year (Weigh a season’s demand level). They need an ordinary run, not a scenario or forecast run, and change no result.

entries.title: Hydrological units: how much demand each run supplied: What the page shows
entries.summary: Each unit’s irrigation demand against what a run supplied, who is short this week, and the curtailment and assurance of supply panels.
entries.text: One card per hydrological unit with the share of its Irrigation demand (abstraction) the run supplied, beside the picked unit’s chart. Three tiles head the page: Irrigation supplied over the whole record (Irrigation supplied), with the units below 95 % and the change from the run before under it; Short this week, how many units were short on any of the run’s last 7 days, which opens the curtailment over those days; and the Total shortfall, in Mm³ a year and m³/day (Irrigation deficit). Below the cards: the curtailment panel with its reporting window and share-the-pain board (curtailment targets), and Assurance of supply. Pick another run with the run menu in the header, and Open in Runs & results opens it there.

entries.title: Project: members, publishing and sharing: What the page holds
entries.summary: What the project holds, who can open it and with which role, and how a run reaches the people outside the model.
entries.text: One column, read top to bottom in the order the page’s On this page list gives: the project’s details, then who can open it, then its notes, facts and reports. Download in the header: the whole project as one JSON file (model, settings and input series), for every member. Members: who can open the project and with which role. Owners add people and change roles. Farmers: which hydrological units each farmer is linked to; a farmer reads only their own. Share links (owners only): read-only links for people outside the project, to the published baseline; the list also holds every link to an application, so an owner can withdraw any of them from one place. API keys (owners only): keys a logger gateway or a script sends daily readings with (Push logger data with an API key). Two-step sign-in (owners only): Require two-step sign-in for the project’s owners and signers (Sign in with two steps). The model, after who can open it: headline facts (units, gauges, catchment area, dams, irrigated area, transfers, series, runs), each linking to where it is edited. Scheduled reports, last, under the model: the latest run’s report PDF emailed to chosen members every week or month. Editors and owners add, pause and remove schedules; viewers read them. Scheduled reports and API keys save as you change them; the project’s details wait for Save changes at the foot of the page.

entries.title: Project: members, publishing and sharing: Licensing panels
entries.text: Registration checks (editors and owners): someone at your organisation looks a specialist signer up on the public register and records it here (+ Record a check), so the verify page says “checked against the register” for their sign-offs; anyone else’s reads “self-declared”. The app checks nothing itself. An owner’s switch makes issuing an evidence pack wait until each specialist signer has a check from the last year (Registration check). Responsible authority (editors set it): who decides the project’s licence applications, a catchment management agency or the Department of Water and Sanitation, with its office. Recorded decisions and the evidence report name it (Responsible authority and endorsement). Acts for the authority: who may record the authority’s decisions. An owner proposes an editor or owner; a proposal grants nothing until someone already acting for the authority confirms it, and the first is confirmed by the operator on the authority’s letter. Licence record (editors and owners): the outcome of the licence the project’s evidence supports. Issued packs and signed-off runs keep their signers’ names until three years after the licence ends, or after another outcome; until one is recorded an owner confirms every five years that the record is still needed (Licence record (how long names are kept)).

entries.title: Project: members, publishing and sharing: Roles
entries.text: A viewer reads everything; an editor also changes the model, uploads data and runs it; an owner also manages members. A farmer reads only the units linked to them. An applicant builds licence applications on the published baseline and never sees the model (applications page).

entries.title: Project: members, publishing and sharing: Publishing a run
entries.text: Nobody outside the model sees a run until an editor publishes it: in Runs & results, Publish this run, with the catchment’s restriction notice. That run is the Published baseline: farmers read their figures from it, share links show it, and applications start from it.

entries.title: Model settings: what the model runs on: What the page holds
entries.summary: The settings a run reads besides the network and the data: the period, rain gaps, demand, flow generation, the EWR and how results are read.
entries.text: One long form, under Build the model, before Calibration. Flow generation comes first, the lead card and the side index’s first link: how rain becomes each unit’s natural flow (Per unit), not the runoff model’s parameters, which are fitted under Calibration → Flow calibration. EWR the results are judged by follows it; then the panels by task: Data & rain (Simulation period, Rain gaps, Data quality), Demand & supply (Demand, Drought restrictions, Reporting), EWR & Reserve (EWR, Reserve rule tables), Reading results (Outcome matrix, Seasonal outlook, Evidence) and Automatic runs. Each panel says what it is set to under its heading. The panels that set up the runoff model’s fit, Flow calibration, Calibration record, Fit the parameters and WR2012 check, are on Calibration. Both pages edit the same settings: an edit on one and an edit on the other wait together for Save changes on the one save bar, which shows on both, and a problem on either page is listed there with a link to its panel. Going from one page to the other keeps your edits and never asks; leaving the project with edits unsaved asks first. Viewers read every panel with its fields read-only. See Set the EWR and the reporting window for the EWR.

entries.title: Calibration: fit the runoff parameters and judge the fit: What the page is for
entries.summary: Where the fit is set up and where a run’s fit is read: one page for the calibration loop.
entries.text: Calibration is a loop: set the runoff model’s parameters, run the model, compare the modelled flow with the observed record, and adjust. This page brings the two halves of that loop together, so the loop stays on one page. It is under Build the model, after Model settings, and every member sees it. Its header says where the parameters came from (the fit, its score and whether anything changed since), with Fit the parameters to go to that panel. Under the header, one line answers how the shown run fits: its NSE, KGE and volume bias, with All the scores to the panel, or why there are none yet. When the GR4J parameters in the form differ from the ones the shown run used, that line says so and a note over the run’s results lists each change (X1 350 → 321 mm), so the old run’s scores aren’t read as the edit’s: run the model to score them. The side index lists both halves’ panels: the four that set up the fit, then those of the run shown, with Calibration check and Where the parameters came from indented under Calibration against observed flow. Set up the fit holds Flow calibration (the GR4J parameters, the rain GR4J runs on and its potential evaporation, with Evaporation from the map), Calibration record (the observed flow a fit is scored against, its window and what is left out), Fit the parameters (fit automatically, the fit record and the calibration rules) and WR2012 check. They are the same settings as Model settings’: their edits wait for Save changes on the one save bar with the rest, and a problem on either page is listed there with a link to its panel. Viewers read them with every field read-only and no fit controls. How the shown run fits shows the Model quality panels for one run: Hydrograph, Flow-duration curve, Calibration against observed flow and EWR test: model against observed flow, with Runoff model, WR2012 check and Plausibility checks when the run has them. Pick the run under its heading: it starts on the run picked on Runs & results, or the latest (a viewer’s, the published one), and Open in Runs & results goes to that run’s own page. With no observed flow record yet it says to add one on Data; with a record but no run, to run the model with Run model at the top. Viewers see every result, without the fit controls. Flow calibration here is not Flow generation on Model settings: Flow calibration holds the runoff model’s parameters (how rain becomes flow), the model selection how the rain reaches each hydrological unit.

entries.title: Calibration: fit the runoff parameters and judge the fit: The loop: fit, save, run, read
entries.text: Choose what the fit is scored against. In Calibration → Calibration record, pick the observed flow series (a gauge or a logger), the Calibration window and any Calibration exclusions, each with its reason. Do this before you look at a score. Fit. In Calibration → Fit the parameters → Fit automatically, choose the objective by what the results will feed, keep Validate ticked, and press Fit automatically. You can open other pages while it runs; the result waits here. Read the shaded validation columns, then press Apply to form. To set a parameter by hand instead, change it under Flow calibration (Calibrate by hand). Save. The fitted parameters are an unsaved edit until you press Save changes on the save bar. The bar is the same on Model settings, so an edit there and one here save together; a problem on either page is listed on the bar with a link to its panel. Preview on the bar shows what your unsaved change does to the last run first, worked out in your browser. Run. Press Run model in the header. A run started here opens back on this page. Read. Under How the shown run fits, the new run is shown: the Hydrograph, the Flow-duration curve and Calibration against observed flow (its scores, the calibration check of flow against use, and where the parameters came from), then the WR2012 check and the plausibility checks when the run has them. Pick an earlier run under the heading to compare by eye, or use Compare runs for the full comparison. Repeat until the validation scores are as good as the record allows. The header always says where the shown parameters came from and whether anything has changed since the fit. Links to these panels from before they moved here (an old Model settings or Runs & results bookmark, a note, an email) still land on the panel here, for the same run.

entries.title: Warnings: every flagged period and run warning, with its fix: What the page lists
entries.summary: Patch suspicious rain, leave bad flow out of calibration, or keep the values as recorded, one period at a time or many at once.
entries.text: The Data checks list one row per period a data check flagged on a stored series: a flat stretch, outliers, negative values, a zero rain run, an accumulation, a water year far below CHIRPS, or a break in a double-mass curve. Each row names the record, the days, what the check saw and what the next run does with it. It has its own row in the sidebar, after Data, with the number of open items beside it; the Data checks panel on Data and the run warnings on Runs & results and Calibration link here too. Filter by Status (Open, Patched, Excluded, Kept, Handled by default, All), by Check and by Record; each chip says how many rows it would show, and the filters stay in the address, so a link or Back keeps them. Handled by default rows are periods the run already deals with: a flagged zero run set aside and filled, an accumulation spread over its days, a negative flow read as missing.

entries.title: Warnings: every flagged period and run warning, with its fix: Solving a warning
entries.text: Every row says How to fix in plain words, with the action that does it. Some fixes are one setting the page can change for you: Spread accumulations, Set flagged zero runs aside, Remove the broken periods. The row then reads Fixed: rerun to confirm until you press Run now, and the new run’s warnings show here. Others take you to the exact field, opened and outlined (Go to Keep dry, Go to the calibration window), or to the page where it is fixed (Add data, Go to Data feeds). A failing feed has Fetch now; a run a known engine bug may affect has Run the model. Anything you accept as it is, Keep, with a note saying why if you like: it moves under Kept with the note, and Reopen brings it back. The filters at the top (Source, Status, Severity, Area, Record and Find) work on every row and stay in the address; tick rows, or Select all N matching, to keep or reopen many at once.

entries.title: Warnings: every flagged period and run warning, with its fix: Problems elsewhere
entries.text: Problems elsewhere gathers what other pages show as needing attention, each with Go to … where it is fixed: problems in the model (the dot beside Network, Crops & demand or Transfers), unsaved settings that stop Save changes, data feeds that are failing or behind, series whose last day is old, and the newest or published run a known engine bug may affect. These have no tick box: their fix is on their own page. The Source chips at the top show one kind at a time (Data checks, Model, Unsaved settings, Data feeds, Data behind, Runs, Run warnings), each with its count, and the number beside Warnings in the sidebar is the page’s Open count: the open data-check periods, these problems and the run’s open warnings, less those kept.

entries.title: Warnings: every flagged period and run warning, with its fix: Deciding a period
entries.text: Rain: Patch or Keep. Patch treats the days as missing, so the run fills them as it fills any gap in the rain (the catchment gauge’s periods go to Model settings → Rain gaps as rain treated as missing; any other rain record’s to its unreliable periods there). Keep keeps the values as recorded: a zero run as dry days, an accumulation as one day’s reading. Flow: Exclude from calibration or Keep. Exclude reads the days of that one record as missing, so the calibration scores, the fit and the plausibility checks leave them out; the other records keep theirs. The periods are listed under Calibration → Calibration record. Keep scores a flagged outlier or flat stretch as read, Fit automatically included. Many at once. Tick rows, or Select all N matching for every row the filters show (folded rows too), then Patch, Exclude or Keep. Neighbouring and overlapping periods are joined into one; a list that would pass its limit (100 periods a list, 200 unreliable periods a rain record, 300 kept checks) is refused with a message, never cut. Run the model. Each decision saves at once, with a reason in the History (“Warnings: patched 3 flat stretches”), and the usual note says the inputs changed since the latest run. Reopen on a decided row takes it back out of its list. A viewer reads the list and its statuses without the tick boxes and buttons. A flat stretch that grows with new data is a new period, so it comes back as open.

entries.title: Warnings: every flagged period and run warning, with its fix: Run warnings
entries.text: Run warnings lists what the shown run warned about (the latest run, or the one picked on Runs & results), things to check first, then notes on how the data were handled. Each warning the engine gives a code links to the setting that changes it (Go to Rain gaps, Go to Calibration record) or to Data when the fix is to load or rename a series; the rest are listed as they are.

entries.title: History: every change, who made it and when: What the page shows
entries.summary: The model’s change log: read any earlier version, see how it differs from now, and restore it as a new change.
entries.text: Every saved change to the model and settings, every upload, run, publication and membership change, newest first and grouped by day, each with who made it, when, and the reason they gave. Filter by Hydrological unit, Kind of change or Parameter; a field’s own history line links here with those filters set. Pick a saved version to see Differences from now. An editor can restore it; restoring saves it as a new change, so nothing is ever erased. It is hidden from the sidebar until you turn it on in Choose sections.

entries.title: Water balance
entries.summary: A day-by-day account of where the catchment’s water goes: runoff, dams, irrigation, transfers and what reaches the outlet.
entries.text: The model tracks every cubic metre each day. Rain becomes natural flow, natural flow is shared out to the hydrological units, each hydrological unit fills its dam, irrigates, spills and passes water downstream, and the outlet gauge receives what is left. Each hydrological unit’s daily balance closes to the cubic metre: inflow (with rain on the dam and groundwater pumped) minus consumptive use, dam evaporation and seepage lost from the catchment, minus the change in storage, equals outflow. A catchment answers three questions: how much water is there, can each hydrological unit’s irrigation be met, and is enough left in the river for the environment?

entries.title: Project (catchment)
entries.summary: One catchment model: its network, crops, settings, input series and runs. One Water Balance Tool workbook becomes one project.
entries.text: A project holds everything for one river catchment. Copy a project to try a what-if without touching the original; runs inside a project record exactly which inputs they used.

entries.title: Run
entries.summary: One execution of the model on the project as it was at that moment. Results are kept, with a snapshot of the inputs used.
entries.text: Pressing Run model computes every day of the simulation window and stores the daily series and the summary. Later edits to the model don’t change an existing run, so results can always be explained. Each run records the engine version it was computed with.

entries.title: Evidence run (nomination)
entries.summary: The one run a project stands behind, nominated by an editor with a reason. Nominations are never edited or removed.
entries.text: On Runs & results, under Record → Evidence, an editor can nominate the run shown with Nominate as evidence and a required reason. Nominating another run later replaces it; both stay in the nomination history, with who nominated each, when and why. In the runs list the current one carries an Evidence badge and a replaced one Former evidence, and comparing runs says when either side is or was the evidence. A run of the legacy runoff model (removed in engine 1.0.0) can’t be nominated: it is workbook comparison only. When the nominated run is such a legacy run and a later run uses GR4J, the results say so: the nomination still stands until another run is nominated, with a reason.

entries.title: Roles: owner, editor, viewer
entries.summary: Viewers read everything; editors also change the model, upload data and run it; owners also manage members.
entries.text: Each person has a role on each project. A viewer sees every input and result, can fit the runoff model to explore and download results, but can’t save or run; the workspace says “View only”. An editor changes settings and model data, uploads series, runs the model, writes run notes and nominates the evidence run. An owner also adds and removes members, changes roles and deletes the project. A project can belong to a team. Team roles use the same names: a team’s owners own every team project, its editors edit them and its viewers view them, and a team owner also manages the team. Someone who is both a direct member and a team member gets the higher of the two roles. Two roles see far less. A farmer reads only the farms linked to them. An applicant (a licence applicant or their consultant) reads what a farmer with the same links reads, plus their own licence applications on the published baseline; they never see the model.

entries.title: Two-step sign-in
entries.summary: A 6-digit code after your password, from an authenticator app or by email; one-use recovery codes cover a lost phone.
entries.text: After your password, a second step: a 6-digit code, so someone who learns your password still can’t get in. Turn it on under Two-step sign-in on your Account page, one way or both. An authenticator app on your phone (the stronger) makes a new code every 30 seconds; set it up with your password, the QR code and the app’s first code. A code by email (the easier) is sent each time and works for 10 minutes, so it is only as safe as your inbox. The first way you turn on gives ten recovery codes, shown once: download or copy them and keep them away from your phone and your email. Each works once in place of a code; the Account page counts what is left, warns at two or fewer, and Make new recovery codes replaces the set. Lost the phone and the recovery codes too: on the sign-in code step, the lost-phone link emails a link that starts a 3-day wait, after which two-step sign-in is removed and every device signed out. You are emailed every day until then, and a code cancels it. An owner can require it on a project (the Project page’s Two-step sign-in panel) and a team admin on a team. Publishing to farmers, deciding applications, endorsing a baseline and signing or issuing an evidence pack always need it.

entries.title: Something went wrong (error messages)
entries.summary: What the common error messages mean, such as “The server is busy; try again in a moment”, and what to do about each.
entries.text: Most errors say what was wrong in their own words, beside the form or button. When the server gives no reason, the app shows one of these: • The server is busy; try again in a moment. Too many requests reached the server at once and it turned yours away unread. The app has already sent it again three times, about a second apart, before saying so: wait a moment and try again. • Could not reach the server. No connection, or the server is down: check your connection, then try again. • The request was invalid. Something you entered didn’t pass the server’s checks: the message names the field where it can, so correct it and try again. • You are not signed in. Your session ended: sign in again. • You do not have permission to do that. Your role on the project doesn’t allow it (a viewer can’t save or run). • Not found. It was deleted, or you no longer have access to it. • That conflicts with existing data. Someone changed the same thing meanwhile: reload the page and make your change again. • That is too large to send. The file or the paste is too big: split it. • The server had a problem. Something failed on the server: try again, and if it keeps happening tell the operator what you did and when.

entries.title: Team
entries.summary: A group that owns catchments together: each member has the same role on every team project as they hold in the team.
entries.text: A team holds catchments for a consultancy, a department or a WUA. Everyone in it gets every team project with the role they hold in the team: a viewer reads every team project and its runs, an editor edits them (model, data and runs), and an owner owns them (delete, share, move) and manages the team. Someone also shared a project directly gets the higher of the two roles. A project without a team is personal: only the people listed under Members on its Project page can open it. An owner moves a project into a team, or back to personal, from the Team panel on the Project page; an owner only through the team must first add themselves as a direct owner to make it personal. Only teams where you are an editor or owner are offered, for a new project, a move or a copy. The team page lists its projects worst first by their EWR status and holds its members. Team settings hold the name, the EWR traffic-light thresholds, the privacy contact, and leaving or deleting the team; the only owner has to hand over before leaving.

entries.title: Invitation
entries.summary: Adding someone by email sends an invitation: they join, with the role named, only once they accept it. It lapses after 7 days.
entries.text: Adding a person by email, on a project’s Members or Farmers panel or a team’s page, always sends an invitation, whether or not the address has an account. Nobody is made a member unasked, and the person adding never learns whether the address is registered. Someone without an account signs up from the email; someone with one accepts or declines under Your invitations on their account page. Until it is accepted, the invitation is listed as pending with who sent it and when it expires, with Resend (which renews it and makes you its sender) and Revoke. It works for 7 days. An invitation whose sender has since lost the right to add people (no longer an owner) can’t be accepted until someone resends it. A farmer’s invitation names the hydrological units they will be linked to and the language of the email; it is kept apart from the members’ list.

entries.title: Farmer and their linked units
entries.summary: A farmer reads only the hydrological units an owner links to them, from the published run: never another unit, nor the model.
entries.text: A farmer is a member with the farmer role, linked by an owner to one or more hydrological units. They read only those units’ figures, from the published run, on the farm view: their dam, their supply, the WUA’s notice and the notes shown to them. They never see another unit’s name or figures, the model, the runs or the members, and the workspace is closed to them. Owners invite farmers from the Farmers panel on the Project page, one by email or many from a CSV (email, unit, language), and change a farmer’s units or remove them there. A link goes with its unit: deleting the unit in the Network and saving removes the farmer’s access to it (the Network asks first, naming them), and restoring an earlier version doesn’t link them again. An applicant can also hold unit links, for an irrigator applying to raise their own dam; they read what a farmer with the same links reads, plus their own applications.

entries.title: Applying party and specialist
entries.summary: Applicants in one applying party share their licence applications; the party’s specialist signs their evidence packs.
entries.text: An applicant (a licence applicant or their consultant) shares applications only with the members of their own applying party, so put an applicant and their consultant or client in the same one. An owner types the party in the applicant’s row under Members; blank is none. A member with a party can be ticked Specialist for this party: the registered professional the applicant appointed. They sign the evidence packs of the party’s applications; an editor still drafts and issues the pack. Nobody who edits the project may also be in an applying party, so the people who build the model and the people who apply against it stay apart.

entries.title: Registration check
entries.summary: A record that someone looked a specialist signer up on the public professional register. The app itself checks nothing.
entries.text: A specialist who signs an evidence pack declares a professional registration (SACNASP or ECSA). The app can’t confirm it, so someone at your organisation looks it up on the public register and records the check on the Project page: the member, register, category and number, the name on the register, whether they were found, who checked, when, and a note. The register’s address is given beside the form. The verify page then says “checked against the register” for that person’s sign-offs; anyone else’s registration reads “self-declared”. An owner, or an editor acting for the responsible authority, records checks. With the owner’s tick box on (the default), issuing an evidence pack waits until each specialist signer has a check from the last year.

entries.title: Licence record (how long names are kept)
entries.summary: Issued evidence packs and signed-off runs keep their signers’ names until three years after the licence ends or is refused.
entries.text: An issued evidence pack and a signed-off run keep the names of the people who made and signed them, also after their accounts are deleted, because a licence decision may have to be explained later. They are kept until three years after the licence expires, or three years after any other outcome. An owner records the outcome on the Project page in the authority’s words: licence issued (with the date the licence expires), licence refused, application rejected (formal requirements) or not considered (use already authorised), or that the application was withdrawn; the date and why (for example the authority’s letter). Until an outcome is recorded, an owner confirms every five years that the record is still needed. Nothing is deleted automatically: once the record is past its closing date, the panel says to ask the operator.

entries.title: Share link
entries.summary: A read-only link for someone outside the project, opened without signing in, to the published baseline, an application or a pack.
entries.text: A share link opens a read-only page without signing in, for someone outside the project such as a catchment forum or an NGO. An owner makes a link to the published baseline on the Project page: who it’s for, and how long it works (1 week, 30 days, 90 days or 1 year). It shows the catchment’s reserve status and the WUA’s notice, never a hydrological unit’s name or figures, or the modeller’s note, and it opens only once a run is published. The new address is shown once: copy it then, since it isn’t kept and can’t be shown again. Anyone holding it can open the page until it ends or is withdrawn. Assessors and applicants make links to a submitted application, and editors to an issued evidence pack; while such a link is live, members can post comments for public participation. The owner’s list on the Project page holds every public link in the project, with what it opens, when it was made, when it ends and when it was last opened. Withdrawing one stops it at once.

entries.title: Copy of a project
entries.summary: A new, separate project with the model, settings and input series of another. Runs, notes and members are not copied.
entries.text: Copy… in a project’s ⋯ menu on the Projects page makes a new project from the model, settings, description, time zone and input series of another. The model gets fresh ids in the same order, so the copy runs exactly as the original. Runs, evidence nominations, notes, members, farmers and the change history are not copied: the copy’s history starts with “Copied from …”, and you are its owner. It stays in the original’s team when you are an editor or owner there, and is personal otherwise. Anyone who can open a project, viewers included, can copy it. A copy is for a lasting fork: a new baseline, or a project that has to start again without its evidence. To test a change against a run and compare the two, a scenario is lighter: it keeps the change as a list of edits on that run, inside the same project.

entries.title: Project file (JSON)
entries.summary: The whole project in one JSON file: model, settings and input series, without runs. Importing it makes a new project.
entries.text: Download → Download project (JSON) on the Project page saves the project as one file: the model, the settings and the input series, with the time zone. Runs, notes, members, farmers and the history stay behind. Every member can download it, viewers included. Import project file on the Projects page turns such a file (or the workbook importer’s project file, up to 5 MB) into a new project: a preview shows what is in it before anything is sent, and the model can run straight after the import. The import record then keeps what the importer noted.

entries.title: Project time zone
entries.summary: The time zone the project’s downloads, alerts and farm pages count days in. Africa/Johannesburg unless changed.
entries.text: An IANA time zone name, such as Africa/Johannesburg (the default). Every download of the project (CSV, JSON, the workbook, the report PDF) is dated by the calendar day there, so an export made just after local midnight carries today’s date. The same day dates what the server counts for a person: the ages on the project list, the data feeds’ health, the farm page’s freshness and forecast date, and the alerts, with their 06:00 daily summary. It doesn’t shift the series: a day of rain or flow stays the day its source gave it. An editor changes it with Save changes; a copy keeps it.

entries.title: Import record
entries.summary: What the importer noted, and what it couldn’t map, when the project was imported from a file, kept as it was shown then.
entries.text: Only a project made by an import has one. It names the file, when it was imported, who imported it and the importer’s version, then the importer’s notes and, for a Water Balance Tool workbook, the unmapped report: the sheets and cells it found no place for. It is kept as it was shown at the import, so a reviewer or an assessor can check long afterwards what the importer interpreted. Every member reads it, viewers included.

entries.title: Change history and restoring
entries.summary: Every saved change to the model, settings, data, members and publications, with who, when and why. Restoring adds a new change.
entries.text: Each save of the model or the settings is kept as a version: who saved it, when, the reason they typed beside Save changes, and the lines that changed. Uploads, merges and deletions of series, runs, publications, members, farmer links, invitations, share links, API keys and alert rules are recorded too, with who did each (or which API key). The History tab lists them newest first, filtered by hydrological unit, kind of change or parameter; a field’s “Changed 3×” line links there. An editor can restore any earlier version of the model and settings. Restoring saves it as a new change, so nothing is erased and the restore can itself be undone. It needs no unsaved edits, and a restored unit comes back without its farmer links. A run’s Restore these inputs does the same from a run. Series values aren’t part of a version. A person’s replace, merge or delete keeps the values it replaced (the newest 5 versions, for up to 180 days), with Restore the earlier values; a data feed’s or an API key’s merge keeps none. Viewers read the history; farmers and applicants never see it.

entries.title: Notes
entries.summary: Plain-text notes kept on a hydrological unit, a run, a settings group or the project, read by the project team.
entries.text: Notes keep what lives in people’s heads (“dam raised in 2019 per owner”, “logger moved in March”) against what they are about: a hydrological unit in the Network, a run, a settings group, or the project itself. The count on each notes button opens them in a side sheet; the Project page lists the newest across the project. Every member can add one. The author edits their own (marked edited); the author or an editor deletes it, which hides it from everyone but keeps it for the audit trail. Notes are plain text and read by the project team only, except a note on a unit ticked Also show to this unit’s farmers, which its linked farmers read on their farm page. On an application, comments carry their own audience (the assessors, the parties, the team or public participation). A note goes with its target: deleting a unit or a run deletes its notes. A copy of the project doesn’t take them. A run’s own notes, by contrast, are the modeller’s one written explanation of that run.
