entries.title: API key
entries.summary: A secret a logger gateway or a script uses to push daily readings into this project’s series without signing in. It writes series only.
entries.text: Owners make keys on the Project page, under API keys: a name, how long it works (until revoked, 90 days, 1 or 2 years), and what it may write, any series of the project or only the ones ticked. The key (wm_…) is shown once, with a copyable example request; only a hash of it is kept, so a lost key can’t be shown again, only replaced. The list shows each key’s state, what it writes, who made it and when it was last used. The gateway sends daily readings to the ingest endpoint with the key. Only the days sent are merged into the named series, converted to its units, and sending the same days again changes nothing. A key creates a series only when the project has none of that kind; otherwise a person adds the series first. A key can’t read the model, runs, members or anything else, and allows 60 requests a minute. Each merge shows in History as API key “name”, and keeps no copy of the values it replaced. When the project re-runs automatically, a merge that changed days queues a re-run as the key’s creator. A push that looks wrong (a negative value, one above the series’ outlier limit, or a series it created) is still merged, but holds automatic runs until a person runs the model. Revoking a key refuses it from its next request; the row stays. An alert can warn when a series a key sends falls behind.

entries.title: Alert rules
entries.summary: Which alert emails a catchment sends, and at what level. Nothing is sent until an editor switches a kind on.
entries.text: On the Summary, Active alerts lists what is firing now; an editor’s Set up alert emails opens the rules. Each kind has a level: • Dam low (per unit with a dam): the published figures put the dam below a % of its capacity (30 % unless changed). • EWR at risk in the forecast: the newest forecast run has this many days at risk at the outlet (3). • Restriction notice: the published restriction or notice changes. • Data feed behind and API data behind: a feed this many days past its usual delay, or a series an API key sends with no new reading for this many days (2). • Data feed failing (failures in a row), Background jobs failed (in 24 hours) and Hydrological units short (on an automatic publication’s last 7 days). Nothing is sent until a kind is switched on. Each alert is sent once when its figure crosses the level, and again only after it has recovered. Farmers get their own units’ dam alerts and the restriction notices, and viewers may opt in to the model’s alerts; the operational ones go to editors and owners (failing feeds and failed jobs to owners, editors opting in). Each person chooses on their account page whether to get each alert right away, in a daily summary at 06:00 or not at all. What recipients answered to “Was this alert useful?” shows under the rules, without names.

entries.title: EWR status (traffic light)
entries.summary: Green, amber or red by the share of the last 30 days the outlet’s EWR was not met: by default green under 5 %, amber under 20 %.
entries.text: A catchment’s EWR status is judged at the outlet over the 30 days up to the last day of its figures (the published run, or the latest run when none is published). It is green when the EWR was not met on fewer than 5 % of those days, amber fewer than 20 %, and red otherwise. Those are provisional defaults, still to be confirmed by the catchment’s hydrologist. A team’s owners can set the team’s own thresholds in Team settings, and every team project is then judged by them; a personal project uses the defaults. The status orders the teams list and the team page. The project list shows irrigation supplied instead: the share of all units’ demand supplied over the run, green from 95 %, amber from 80 %, red below (provisional too, and not yet a team setting). The EWR page lights each month of a run with the same EWR bands. The EWR status summarises one outlet over one month: read the run’s EWR page for the sites and days behind it.

entries.title: Needs attention
entries.summary: The catchments in view to look at first, most urgent first: red irrigation supply, units short, alerts firing, failing feeds or old figures.
entries.text: At the top of the Projects page, up to four cards name the catchments to look at first and why, most urgent first: red irrigation supply, hydrological units short this week, alerts firing, amber irrigation supply, failing or late data feeds, rain recorded after the latest figures, or figures more than 7 days old. A catchment that hasn’t run is not flagged. Show all, most urgent first sorts the whole list the same way.

entries.title: Privacy contact
entries.summary: Whom people ask about the personal information in a team’s projects. Team owners set it; members and farmers can read it.
entries.text: The person or office people ask about the personal information kept in a team’s projects (a name or office, an email address and an optional postal address), as POPIA asks of a responsible party. Team owners set it in Team settings; members read it there, farmers see it from the farm menu, and invitations name it.

entries.title: Published baseline
entries.summary: The run an editor publishes for the people outside the model: farmers read their figures from it, and licence applications start from it.
entries.text: An editor publishes a run from Runs & results with Publish this run, with the catchment’s restriction notice. It is what people outside the model read: farmers see their own farm’s figures from it, share links show it, and an applicant’s application starts from it. Publishing another run replaces it; the earlier publications stay on record. With nothing published, farmers see no figures and an applicant can’t start an application.

entries.title: Scenario
entries.summary: A named list of changes to a run (a bigger dam, a new crop, less rain) that runs and compares against that run without copying the project.
entries.text: A scenario is a named, ordered list of changes on a base run: raise a dam by 20 %, replace a crop, remove a farm, add a transfer, scale the rain by −10 %. It runs and compares against its base without copying the project, and because it keeps the base’s ids every change lines up in Compare runs. Editors make scenarios on the Scenarios tab to explore; a licence application is a scenario an applicant makes on the published baseline.

entries.title: Base run
entries.summary: The saved run a scenario starts from: its changes apply to that run’s stored inputs, never to the live model.
entries.text: A scenario never reads the project’s model as it stands now. It takes the inputs one saved run stored (the model, the settings and every series), applies its changes to them in order, and runs the result. Editing the model afterwards changes nothing in the scenario, and its comparison is always against the run it started from. A new scenario starts on the published run when there is one, else on the latest; any run that isn’t itself a scenario run can be picked. A licence application always starts on the published baseline. The base run can’t be deleted or trimmed while a scenario uses it. Rebase onto another run moves a team scenario to another run of the model with the same changes. Check lists first any change that no longer applies there (a hydrological unit removed since, say); after the rebase such a change is marked as not applying, and the scenario can’t run until it is removed. A scenario run keeps the base it was made on, so until the scenario is run again its comparison says it still reads the earlier base.

entries.title: Scenario change (override)
entries.summary: One edit in a scenario’s list: set a field, add or remove an element, scale rain or demand. Each applies to what the ones before it left.
entries.text: A scenario is an ordered list of changes, each aimed at one element by its id: change a hydrological unit’s field; add, remove or move a unit, or insert one on a reach; set a unit’s crop area; add, change or remove a crop, a transfer, land cover, a borehole, a demand object or a registered volume; change a setting; scale a rain series or the daily A-pan; scale demand; set or remove an EWR site’s rule table. Each change reads in words against the value it meets (“dam capacity 120 000 → 144 000 m³”), so a second change to the same value shows the first one’s result as the value it replaces. Changes apply in order, each to the model the ones before it left. One that can’t apply (its target is gone, a value is out of range, or it would leave a model the project couldn’t save: a loop, a second outlet, a duplicate name, crops on a gauge) is marked “Doesn’t apply” with the reason and changes nothing, and the scenario can’t run until it is removed or the base changes. Consecutive changes to one hydrological unit, or to one demand object, are checked together as one edit, so fields the model ties together (a supply rule and the dam it needs) can change in either order; a group that still breaks a rule is skipped whole, never half applied. A few edits have no change: a unit’s kind (remove it and add a new unit instead), and observed flow, which the run is scored against rather than driven by.

entries.title: Proposal or baseline assumption
entries.summary: Each change is a Proposal (the change being assessed) or a Baseline assumption (it changes what the river is taken to be today).
entries.text: Every change in a scenario is labelled. A Proposal is the change being put forward: the proposer’s own dam, supply rule or river pump, crops, boreholes, demand objects or registered volume, a transfer between their own units, a new unit or a new structure on a reach. A Baseline assumption changes what the base run takes the catchment to be today: a setting or the calibration, rainfall or evaporation, an EWR site’s rule table or which gauges are EWR sites, the catchment’s split of runoff (land areas), a dam’s survey date or sediment rate, bed losses in a reach, someone else’s hydrological unit, a crop’s factors or efficiency (they apply on every unit that grows the crop), and demand scaled across the whole catchment. Any baseline assumption puts the red “Baseline assumptions changed” callout above the list, here and on the compare page: an assessor will want to know why the baseline moved. What counts as the proposer’s is the ticked list The proposer’s hydrological units on a team scenario, plus anything the scenario itself adds or inserts; on a licence application it is the applicant’s own linked units, set by the server. Ticking a unit says whose a change is; it doesn’t limit where a change applies. The rules are conservative: a change that can’t be placed is a baseline assumption, and so is a new priority water user inserted above other farms, since whether a new use ranks above existing lawful use is the authority’s call. To read a scenario as the impact of a proposal, keep baseline assumptions out of it: settle them in the project, or in a scenario of their own, so the comparison shows the proposal’s effect alone.

entries.title: Edit in the model tables (override mode)
entries.summary: Edit a scenario in the Network, Crops and Transfers tables; Record turns your edits into scenario changes. The live model is untouched.
entries.text: Edit in the model tables opens the workspace’s own Network, Crops and Transfers tables on the scenario’s model: the base run’s inputs with the listed changes applied. Edit them as you would the real model, then Record: the app works out the changes that turn the model it loaded into the one you edited (crops first, then units removed, unit fields, units added or inserted, moves, crop areas, transfers, land cover, boreholes and demand objects), checks each as the form would, and adds them in one go, so one Undo takes them all back. Nothing is recorded unless the whole list applies and gives back exactly the model you edited. A few edits have no change to record. The record panel names them and holds the rest back until they are undone: a unit’s kind, the outlet moved, a new unit that drains nowhere, a field a scenario can’t set on that kind of unit, and the capacity of a dam with a survey curve when the curve is left as it was (paste the enlarged dam’s survey with it, or add the capacity with the form). A dam capacity typed in the table keeps the surface area the table shows; to enlarge a dam along its own area–volume relation, add the capacity with the form instead. Registered volumes and settings aren’t in these tables: add them with the form. Row order is display only and isn’t recorded.

entries.title: Scale demand
entries.summary: A change that multiplies irrigation or other users’ demand (0–200 %) for chosen units and months. Crop areas stay as they are. (% of what they’d take)
entries.text: Scale demand answers “what if everyone takes 85 %?” in one change. It multiplies what each target would take: for a hydrological unit the crop water requirement after effective rain and the soil-water store, so the abstraction scales while the crop areas, the irrigation efficiency and the return-flow share stay as they are; for an other water user its monthly demand. Pick whose demand (hydrological units or other water users), the new demand as a % of what they’d take (0 to 200 %), and optionally the units and the months it applies to (none ticked is all of them). For hydrological units, Part of their demand limits it to the crops, or to the demand objects of one category, on top of any scaling of the whole. Scalings multiply: 90 % twice is 81 %. A cut never takes a domestic or municipal demand object below its basic-needs floor. On a full-allocation run it scales the registered use: 85 % asks for 85 % of each registered volume. It is a proposal only when every unit it names is the proposer’s; with no units ticked it scales the whole catchment and is a baseline assumption. The outcome matrix and the seasonal outlook make their demand levels with the same change.

entries.title: Scale rainfall or daily A-pan
entries.summary: A change that multiplies one rain series or the daily A-pan series by a % change, over the whole record or between two dates. (%)
entries.text: Scales one driving series of the base run: station rain, CHIRPS, forecast rain, an alternative gauge’s rain, reanalysis rain, or the daily A-pan evaporation. Change (%) is the change, −10 for 10 % less; the factor may run from 0 to 10. From and To limit it to those days (inclusive); either left empty reaches that end of the record. Missing days stay missing, so gaps are filled as in the base run. Each change scales one series. The sensitivity runs scale every rain series the project has together, so the CHIRPS bias correction stays as it is and the whole forcing moves; to model a wetter or drier climate, do the same, one change per rain series. The monthly A-pan means and the pan coefficient are settings (Change a setting); on a project with a daily A-pan series they reach only the days the series doesn’t cover, so an evaporation scenario there scales the series too. Observed flow can’t be scaled: the run is scored against it, it doesn’t drive the model. Always a baseline assumption: the climate is not the proposer’s to change.

entries.title: Future climate
entries.summary: A change that multiplies every rain record and the evaporation inputs by one climate model’s monthly change factors for a pathway.
entries.text: A future climate is one climate model’s view of a drier or wetter catchment, put into a scenario as one change. Its factors come from NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, NASA’s downscaled climate projections: for each model, pathway (SSP2-4.5, a middle road, or SSP5-8.5, a high-emissions one) and 30-year window (2036–2065 or 2066–2095), the ratio of the model’s future monthly rain to its own 1985–2014 rain, and the same for evaporation (Hargreaves–Samani, from temperature). Work out the change factors once per catchment: a background job reads them over the catchment boundary on the Map tab, and reads them again when the boundary changes. The change multiplies every rain record (station, CHIRPS and the other products, unit and station rain) by the month’s rain factor, the evaporation inputs (the A-pan row, the daily A-pan, reference ET, a monthly PE row) by the month’s evaporation factor, and every MAP by the year’s. The historical sequence stays: droughts come when they did, no longer and no more often. GR4J keeps its calibrated parameters. One model is one view: to see the spread, make a scenario for several models, or run the Future yield section of an application’s evidence report, which runs them all. Always a baseline assumption: the climate is never the proposer’s to change. A scenario takes one future climate, and no rain or evaporation scaling beside it.

entries.title: Assess together (cumulative impact)
entries.summary: Several applications on one baseline, each alone and all together, so their combined effect on the river and existing users shows.
entries.text: One application at a time can hide what several do together. Assess together takes two or more submitted or decided applications on the same base run and runs the baseline, each application alone and all of them combined, all on the current engine so every column compares. Applications that collide are refused, never merged: two that change the same field of the same element (both raise one dam), or one that removes what another changes or uses. Check they combine lists each conflict with the two changes behind it, and any change that applies alone but not with the others (two new dams given one name); until an applicant changes their application the set can’t be assessed. The result has one row per measure: per EWR site the days the EWR is not met and the mean shortfall; per Reserve rule-table site the months met and the deficit; for the catchment the mean flow at the outlet, the water supplied to existing users and their share of demand met (a unit an application adds is its own proposal and is left out). Each row gives the baseline, each application alone with its change, all together with its change, and the interaction. Owners and editors run it; it adds nothing to the project’s runs. An application’s evidence report reads a completed assessment of it with every other submitted or decided application on its baseline, and says when there is none.

entries.title: Interaction (cumulative impact)
entries.summary: The change with every application together, less the changes each makes alone added up. Zero means their effects simply add.
entries.text: Interaction = (all together − baseline) − the sum over applications of (alone − baseline). When the applications draw on separate water it is close to zero: their effects add. It moves away from zero when they meet. Two abstractions on one stream can do less together than their sum, since the same water can only be taken once; a threshold measure such as days below the EWR can show more together, when each alone stays just above the line and together they cross it. A change shown as worse means together they do more harm than their separate effects suggest. Read it beside the combined change, not on its own: a small interaction on a large combined change is still a large combined change. Days and months are whole counts; volumes are in m³ or m³/day.

entries.title: Licence application
entries.summary: A licence applicant’s proposed change (a new dam, more abstraction), modelled on the published baseline for the assessors to decide.
entries.text: Someone applying for a water-use licence (a developer, an agribusiness or their consultant) is added to the project with the Applicant role. They never see the model itself: they start an application on the published baseline, describe their proposed change as a scenario (a new or raised dam, a new abstraction, more land under irrigation), run it and see their results against the baseline: the Ecological Reserve, the catchment’s flow, their own hydrological units and the farms downstream. Other farms show only by an anonymous name. While it is a draft only the applicant and the people they share it with can see it. Once they submit it, its changes are frozen and it appears on the Applications tab, where the project’s owners and editors (the assessors) open it, read its runs and record a decision with reasons. The applicant can withdraw it, or reopen it as a draft. The assessors issue its evidence packs, and can Assess together several applications for their cumulative effect on the river.

entries.title: Evidence pack
entries.summary: An application’s evidence report frozen as a signed, versioned document with a short code anyone can check against the app.
entries.text: An evidence pack is a run’s evidence report frozen as a hashed, versioned, signed document that stays the same once it is issued. An applicant attaches it to their water-use licence application, and anyone holding it can check it against the app with its short code on the public verify page. An editor drafts one from a run’s evidence report; it is signed, then issued, and can later be superseded by a new version or withdrawn.

entries.title: Evidence report
entries.summary: The licensing report of one run: the nominated baseline alone, or an application against it. A draft until it is issued as a pack.
entries.text: The evidence report is the licensing document of one run, built whole by the server and drawn by the page. It has two modes. A baseline report is the project’s current nominated evidence run on its own. An application report is a scenario run, reported against the base run it was made on, with the change in every figure and the applicant’s statement. Open it with Evidence report beside Report on Runs & results, or from the head of a scenario’s comparison. Viewers and up read it. Some runs can’t be evidence at all, and the page says why instead of drawing the report: a run that isn’t the current nominated run (or an application run on it), a run on the removed legacy runoff model, or a forecast run. Otherwise the report opens with its checks (on screen only): each one passed, failed and stops issue, or failed and is only printed, with what was found and the way out, then Expect questions about, the points an assessor will raise. Until it is issued as an evidence pack every page carries a draft stamp, and Download draft PDF prints it as such. The report always reads the runs as they are now; a pack freezes it.

entries.title: Checks that stop issue
entries.summary: What an evidence report must pass before it can become a pack and be issued. A failing check names its units and the way out.
entries.text: Only a report that may be issued becomes a pack. The checks that stop issue are: the baseline is the project’s current nominated run; the declared uncertainty rule is set and the ensemble it cites exists (and, for an application, the paired band); the application changes no baseline assumption, only the applicant’s own works; every river pump in the runs has a capacity; and, for an application, its own river abstraction leaves the EWR, or a set hands-off flow, in the river in every month it can take. The two river checks read the runs’ stored models, so they judge exactly what the pack cites. At issue the server checks again, in one step: the pack is a draft, its stored manifest still hashes to its recorded hash, the live report may still be issued, a specialist has signed the current pack statement, each such signer’s registration has a current check (while the project requires it), both runs still carry the server’s stamp, and no erratum found since the draft applies to either run’s engine. If any fails, nothing is issued and the refusal names it. Exploring stays free: a model with an uncapped pump or no hands-off flow still saves and runs; only a pack can’t be issued on it. Other checks are printed in the report without stopping issue.

entries.title: Evidence pack lifecycle
entries.summary: Draft, signed, issued, then superseded by a new version or withdrawn with a public reason. An issued pack is never edited or deleted.
entries.text: Draft. An editor makes a pack from a run’s evidence report with Create evidence pack. It freezes the report as it is at that moment; a draft has no public page. Signed. A registered professional signs the draft. Only a draft can be signed, and a sign-off can’t be undone. Issued. An editor issues a signed draft once every line of its checklist is ticked. From then on its verify page answers publicly, with the signers’ names and registrations, and the server prints its PDF and builds its reproduction bundle. Only one pack of an application (or of the baseline evidence) is issued at a time. Superseded. A change of evidence is a new version (New version…), drafted from the same run’s report as it stands now. When it is issued, the old one is marked superseded and its verify page points to the newer version. Nothing is edited. Withdrawn. An editor withdraws a pack, at any stage, with a reason of up to 1 000 characters. The verify page then says it is withdrawn and gives the reason, so write it for the licensing authority, not the team. Withdrawing can’t be undone. Delete is only for an unsigned draft. A signed draft is withdrawn instead, and a pack that was issued is never deleted, nor is its project, so its verify link keeps answering for as long as the licence record is kept. Issuing and withdrawing ask for a fresh code, from your authenticator app or by email. The project’s editors (and the application’s owner) get an email when a pack is issued or withdrawn.

entries.title: Manifest and manifest SHA-256
entries.summary: The pack’s frozen content and its fingerprint: any change to the evidence changes the hash; its status and sign-offs don’t.
entries.text: The manifest is what a pack is: its id and version (and the hash of the version it replaces), the project, the engine version, and the whole evidence report: every setting, the model, the hash of every input series, the results, the flags and checks, the methodology and errata cited, and the locality map. Its SHA-256 is taken over a canonical JSON text (RFC 8785), so the same content always gives the same hash, and any change to the evidence gives another. Not in the hash: the pack’s status, when and by whom it was drafted or issued, a withdrawal reason and its successor, so a pack keeps its hash from draft to withdrawn. The sign-offs aren’t in it either: each signer’s statement names the hash instead. The PDF and the reproduction bundle have hashes of their own; the bundle contains the manifest. Download manifest saves those canonical bytes, so the file checks on the verify page; a copy saved pretty-printed still matches, since the page compares the canonical form too. If the stored manifest ever stops matching its recorded hash, the pack page says so in red and the pack can’t be issued.

entries.title: Short code and verify page
entries.summary: The first 12 digits of the manifest hash. Anyone can enter it on the public verify page to see if the pack still stands.
entries.text: The short code is the first 12 hexadecimal digits of the manifest hash, written xxxx-xxxx-xxxx. It is printed on every page of an issued pack, beside the full hash and the verify address, and it is not a secret. The verify page is public: no account or sign-in. Enter the code (any case, with or without dashes) or the full 64-digit hash, and it shows only what the pack itself prints: whether it is issued and current, superseded (with the newer version’s code) or withdrawn (with the reason), the catchment, version, issue date, engine and report format, the methodology statement, the manifest, PDF and bundle hashes, the errata the pack recorded and any found since, and each signer with their registration (self-declared, or checked against the register by whom and when). A draft, a pack withdrawn before issue, and an unknown code all give the same answer: no issued pack has this code. The page can also check a file: choose a PDF, manifest or reproduction bundle and it is hashed in your browser, never uploaded, and compared with the recorded hashes. Verifying proves that this app issued a pack with that content, who signed it and whether it still stands; whether the results follow from the inputs is the reproduction bundle’s job. A withdrawal shows on the page at once.

entries.title: Evidence pack PDF
entries.summary: The issued pack printed once by the server and stored under its own SHA-256, which the verify page shows.
entries.text: When a pack is issued, the server prints its page in a headless browser, from the frozen manifest, with its stamp, verify line and sign-offs on every page. The PDF is stored under its own SHA-256, in storage that refuses any other bytes under that name and that the app can’t overwrite or delete; the first PDF recorded stands. From then on the verify page shows its hash, and the downloaded file hashes to it (sha256sum pack.pdf). The PDF shows the pack as it was when printed: a later supersede or withdrawal is for the verify page to say. Until the server’s PDF is recorded, Download PDF on the pack page prints the page in your own browser, which is not the recorded PDF. A print that fails is tried again on its own (up to three times); after that an editor can ask again with Try again. The PDF names every hydrological unit with its figures, as the manifest does, so it is the assessors’ document: share links and the applicant’s view don’t offer it.

entries.title: Reproduction bundle
entries.summary: A ZIP of both runs’ inputs, results and the manifest, built at issue, that anyone can re-run offline to get the same results.
entries.text: Issuing a pack builds a ZIP with everything needed to re-run it: an index with the SHA-256 of every file, the manifest, each run’s stored input snapshot and results, every input series as a CSV named by its hash, the application’s changes, and a README saying which engine version to use. It is checked, stored and its hash recorded in the same step as the issue; if that fails, nothing is issued. The verify page publishes its hash. Anyone holding the bundle can re-run both runs with only the bundle and the app’s source at the pack’s engine version, with no database, account or network (pnpm reproduce:pack). Each check is printed: the files match their hashes, the manifest hashes to the pack’s hash, the inputs and changes are the manifest’s, the stored results are the manifest’s, and re-running each run gives the same results digest. A run made with another engine version is expected to differ, and the output says which version to use. The server also re-runs a pack from its stored bundle after issue, and the pack page says what it found: reproduced, not reproduced (with each failed check), another engine, or still running. An editor can ask for it again (after a failure, or on a newer engine; the new outcome is kept beside the old). That is the app’s own claim, never printed and not on the verify page: an assessor repeats it with the bundle. The bundle names every unit with its registered volume, so it goes to the assessors, not through share links or the applicant, and a viewer the project doesn’t let read each farm’s volume can’t download it (nor the manifest) when its runs carry them: an editor or owner can.

entries.title: Errata found since
entries.summary: Known engine bugs recorded after a pack was drafted or issued that apply to its runs. Listed apart; never added to the pack.
entries.text: An erratum is a known bug in a version of the engine, recorded with what goes wrong, when it applies and the version that fixes it. A pack records the errata of its runs’ engines (and of the engines their fits were made with) when it is drafted, and the signer reads them before signing. An erratum added to the list later that applies to either run is shown apart, never added to the pack: on an issued pack it is listed as found since issue, on the pack page, the verify page and the applicant’s view, while the pack, its PDF and its hash stay as they were. On a draft it blocks issue: draft the pack again, which records it, then sign and issue that one. So a pack is only ever issued with every erratum known at the time.

entries.title: Professional sign-off
entries.summary: A registered professional’s permanent statement about one run or pack: ten confirmations, bound by a hash to the exact words shown.
entries.text: A registered professional signs a run (or an evidence pack) as it was made. The dialog asks for their name, registration body (SACNASP or ECSA), category, field and number; candidate and certificated categories can’t sign, since they work under a professional’s supervision and that professional signs, and a field outside catchment hydrology gets a warning to sign only within their competence. They then tick each of ten confirmations on its own (who they are, competence, conflicts of interest, the input data, the calibration, the EWR tables, the network or the proposed works, assurance levels and demand, plausibility, and that they read the methodology, limitations and errata), read the run’s known limitations and the errata of its engine to the end, and say what the sign-off covers. The server keeps a SHA-256 of the exact statement shown, so a signature is bound to those words and versions; a statement that changed since the dialog opened is refused. A sign-off is permanent: it can’t be changed or withdrawn, only followed by another. It covers this run only, makes no finding on whether a water use is lawful, doesn’t cover dam safety, relies on the app’s calculations, and is not a signature on any form the authority requires. The registration details are the signer’s own declaration unless the host has recorded a check against the register. A report whose run is nominated as evidence, or an impact report, says in bold on its cover when it isn’t signed: not for use as evidence in a licence application.

entries.title: Signing an evidence pack
entries.summary: The applicant’s specialist signs the draft (an assessor may add a review); issue then waits for a current registration check.
entries.text: A pack is signed against the pack statement: the run statement’s ten confirmations plus an eleventh naming the pack’s version and manifest hash. Only a draft is signed. There are two kinds. Specialist for the applicant is the professional responsible for the evidence, and issue needs one. Reviewed for the responsible authority is an optional second sign-off by an editor, never enough on its own. The evidence is the applicant’s, so the applicant’s own specialist normally signs: the project owner marks a member of the applying party as its specialist, and that person signs the draft packs of their party’s applications. Editors may sign too. Registration check. The app checks no registration itself. Someone at the host looks the signer up on the public SACNASP or ECSA register, and an owner, or an editor acting for the responsible authority, records what they found under Registration checks on the Project page. A check is current for a year. While the project requires it (on by default), issue waits until each specialist signer has a current check; the verify page then says “checked against the register by …”, and every other registration reads “self-declared”. Signing, issuing and withdrawing ask for a code from the last 10 minutes (from your authenticator app, or by email), and you need two-step sign-in set up before your first sign-off. The signer’s name, registration and date are shown publicly on the verify page, even after a withdrawal, for as long as the licence record is kept. A new known limitation or erratum since the signature means signing again.

entries.title: Report disclaimer
entries.summary: Model estimates, not an authorisation to use water, and the operator accepts no responsibility: printed on every report and export.
entries.text: Every catchment report ends with the disclaimer, all five paragraphs and its version, and its key points are in the Read this first box on the cover and in the footer of every printed page. In short: the results are estimates from a computer model, not measurements or predictions, and can be wrong; the report supports, and doesn’t replace, the specialist hydrology report, and is not an authorisation to use water (only the responsible authority decides that under the National Water Act); modelled shortfalls, curtailment and equitable shares are not official restrictions or allocations; whoever made the run chose its inputs, and a sign-off is that professional’s own statement; and the operator of the software didn’t prepare the report, checks none of it and, as far as the law allows, accepts no responsibility to anyone who relies on it. Have the results checked by a qualified hydrologist before acting on them. Nothing in a report covers the safety of a dam. One line of it heads every CSV of a run’s results, and a Read this first sheet opens the run’s .xlsx workbook. A sign-off records the disclaimer version the signer was shown. Farmers don’t see it: their farm page and alert emails carry their own short lines.

entries.title: Responsible authority and endorsement
entries.summary: Who decides the licence (DWS or a CMA), and whether a member acting for it endorsed the published baseline. The report says both.
entries.text: Under the National Water Act only the responsible authority decides a licence and what evidence it accepts: the Department of Water and Sanitation or a catchment management agency. An editor names it, with its office, on the Project page, and every evidence report says whom it is for in its For row (or that no authority is named). The authority decides who acts for it (Project page, Acts for the authority). An owner may propose an editor or owner of the project, directly or through its team, but a proposal grants nothing until someone already acting for the authority confirms it; with nobody acting for it yet, the authority asks the operator in writing to confirm the first. The owner can withdraw a proposal but not remove a confirmed delegate; anyone acting for the authority can, and every change is in the History. Confirmed delegates record its decisions on applications, and they can endorse a published baseline (Runs & results, Publication: Endorse as the responsible authority, with an optional note). An endorsement is recorded once, with their name, and can’t be changed or withdrawn. An evidence report on a baseline nobody endorsed says “Not endorsed by the responsible authority” and carries a caution on page 1. A pack freezes both when it is drafted: an authority named or an endorsement made later changes the live report, never the pack.

entries.title: Impact against full authorised use
entries.summary: The application judged with every holder taking their full registered volume, beside the impact against today’s modelled use.
entries.text: Page 1 of an application’s evidence report judges it twice. The headline is against full authorised use: the baseline and the application both run again with every holder taking their full registered volume (the full allocation mode). A proposal that passes only because other holders don’t take their whole entitlement would hurt them as soon as they do, and the authority weighs existing lawful use and the effect on other users. Beside it, a table gives that volume by how it is held: only a licence or an existing lawful use verified under s35 is an entitlement; a WARMS registration, a claimed existing lawful use, a general authorisation and Schedule 1 use are not. It shows totals only, never a holder. The second board is against modelled current use: the baseline as it ran, so existing use is what the model found holders use; it answers what changes tomorrow. The pair is two model runs, so an editor starts it from the evidence report with Run at full authorised use. It is kept for that application run and read only while it was made on the baseline’s engine with the project’s outcome settings as they are now; otherwise the report prints a fixed “Not assessed” row saying why, and the button reads Run it again. A pack freezes whichever board page 1 had when it was drafted.

entries.title: Impact by year class
entries.summary: The change in dry, middle and wet years: an annual waterfall at the outlet and the months below the Reserve, baseline vs application.
entries.text: The baseline’s complete water years are ranked by their natural flow at the outlet and split into classes, terciles by default (dry, middle, wet) or quintiles, by the project’s outcome settings. Each column sets the baseline beside the application over the same years. The annual waterfall is the mean a year at the outlet: natural flow, existing use in the baseline, the proposed extra use (application minus baseline), the rest (dams, storage, groundwater, land cover) and the flow left. Below it, the months below the Reserve at the project’s Reserve site, baseline, application and the change (or the days below the pragmatic EWR, when the runs have no rule table). The verdict is written from the months below the requirement, never from the annual totals, and has no colour: it reports what the runs did, it doesn’t recommend. A class with fewer than 3 years reads “Not enough years”. Existing use is the baseline’s as that run modelled it; for existing authorised use, compare against a baseline run at full allocation. In an evidence report the board is built into the report, so a pack freezes it.

entries.title: Share link to an evidence pack
entries.summary: A read-only link for people without an account: the pack’s standing and river figures, never a farm, a name or the full report.
entries.text: An editor shares an issued pack by a read-only link (Share link… on the pack page), so an NGO, a catchment forum or an assessor without an account can read it during a comment period; an applicant can link their own application’s pack the same way. You choose who it is for and how long it lasts, copy it once, and can withdraw it at any time. The link shows what the verify page shows and, while the pack is issued, figures from its frozen manifest: the river’s rows (Reserve months met per site, days below the EWR, no-flow days) with their bands, Reserve compliance at each EWR site, and the change by calendar month. Volume rows appear only when at least 5 farms hold water and the application changed no baseline assumption. It never shows a user’s, farm’s or allocation’s figures or name, the other applications, the settings, model or inputs, the applicant’s statement, or anyone but the signers; nor the PDF, the manifest or the bundle. Readers can post public comments while the pack is issued and a link is live; every edit is kept. If the pack is later superseded or withdrawn, the link keeps working but shows only its standing, the reason or the newer version’s code, and the comments: no figure.

entries.title: Send to the authority
entries.summary: Emails the members acting for the responsible authority a link to the issued pack. The email carries no file and no download link.
entries.text: The pack’s PDF and reproduction bundle name every water user with their figures, so they go to the authority that decides the licence, not through the applicant. On an issued pack, an editor picks Send to the authority… and chooses among the members the authority confirmed as acting for it (all, or some; a proposal not yet confirmed isn’t offered), with an optional note. Each gets an email naming the pack, its version, code and the authority, with the note. It carries no file and no download link: it links the pack’s page, where the member, signed in and still an editor, downloads the PDF and bundle, and the public verify page. So a forwarded email opens nothing. Only an issued pack can be sent. The history records who it went to and whether a note went, never the note itself. Addresses outside the app aren’t offered.

entries.title: Applicant’s printable copy
entries.summary: A PDF of the applicant’s own view of an issued pack, other users’ figures withheld. Not the pack: it has its own hash.
entries.text: An applicant, and the people they share their application with, read its issued packs in a view of their own: their own hydrological units by name, every other farm or water user downstream only by a number (as in their results), and the river’s figures. The assessors’ copy, its PDF and its bundle name everyone; this view doesn’t. Make a printable copy has the server print that view as a PDF, recorded once with its own SHA-256 (asking again changes nothing). Its first page and every footer say “Applicant’s copy: other water users’ figures withheld. Not the pack.” with the verify address, the pack’s code and its manifest hash. File it where the application needs the evidence: what an applicant files reaches the interested and affected parties, so it withholds the others’ figures. It is not hashed as the pack, never replaces it, and the verify page knows nothing of it: the authority checks the pack itself.

entries.title: Restriction notice
entries.summary: The WUA’s own notice (level, cut and words), published with the baseline for farmers. The app never writes restriction wording.
entries.text: When an editor publishes a run as the baseline, the publication carries the water user association’s restriction notice: a level (none, advisory or restricted), an optional cut in %, when the next update is expected, and the WUA’s own words in each language it writes. Farmers read the notice first on their farm page, in their language (or another one written, when theirs is empty). The app never writes restriction wording itself. An editor changes the notice with Edit notice without publishing again. The notice is the WUA’s. The model’s curtailment targets and equitable shares are not restrictions or allocations: only a notice from a body with the legal power to make one is. The drought restriction rule under Settings is separate: a model input that cuts demand in a run, which can be started from the published notice.

entries.title: Registered volume (allocation)
entries.summary: One volume a year from one water source under one authorisation, for a hydrological unit or other water user. Not an entitlement. (m³ a year)
entries.text: An allocation is one volume a year, from one water source (surface or groundwater), held under one authorisation, for a hydrological unit or other water user, with its purpose and the dates it is valid (inclusive; either end may be open). The registration or licence number and the property are kept to match it to a unit; the registered user’s name, a reference and the file it was imported from (name and SHA-256) are kept beside it. A unit may have several, such as a registration and a later licence, or surface and groundwater: the comparison adds up every one in force on each day. Every run’s input carries the volumes in force (never the names). So a stored run replays with the volumes it ran on, changing a volume makes the latest run out of date, and comparing two runs lists the volumes that changed. A scenario can set or remove a volume for one run. A registered volume is what an authorisation says, not an entitlement, and the app never decides whether a use is lawful.

entries.title: Registered irrigated area
entries.summary: The area a take is registered or licensed to irrigate, from WARMS or typed in. Kept beside the volume; the model never reads it. (ha)
entries.text: A WARMS registration of irrigation states the area irrigated beside the volume taken, and a licence often does too. The app keeps it on the take (a 21(a) row) in hectares: imported from a WARMS extract’s irrigated-area column (“Irrigated Area (ha)”, “Area under irrigation” …; a bare “Area (ha)” isn’t read, as it may be the property’s extent) or the template’s `irrigated_area_ha`, or typed into + Add volume. A dam’s storage row (21(b)) has none: an area there would be counted twice beside the property’s take, so the import refuses it. It is a record of what the authorisation says. The model never reads it: the area a unit irrigates in a run is its planted crop areas, and changing a registered area leaves the latest run current.

entries.title: Authorisation
entries.summary: How a volume is held: a WARMS registration, a licence, a general authorisation, Schedule 1, or existing lawful use, claimed or verified.
entries.text: How a volume is held, in the National Water Act’s terms: Registration (WARMS): registered with DWS (GN R1352 of 1999). A registration is not an entitlement and doesn’t confirm that a use is lawful. Licence: a water-use licence (s40). General authorisation: use within a published general authorisation (s39, such as GN 538). Schedule 1 (permissible use): small uses allowed without a licence (s22(1)(a)(i)). They aren’t registered with DWS, so a farmer’s registered totals leave them out. Existing lawful use, claimed: claimed or registered under s32, not verified. Existing lawful use, verified under s35: only this verification confirms an existing lawful use. On import, words such as “existing”, “ELU” or “s32” read as claimed; only an explicit “verified” or “s35” reads as verified. Against full authorised use, only a licence and a verified existing lawful use count as entitlements.

entries.title: Water use: taking (s21a) or storing (s21b)
entries.summary: A take is a volume a year; a dam’s storage is a row of its own, compared only with the dam’s capacity, never counted as a take.
entries.text: WARMS registers water per s21 water use, per property. Taking water (s21a) is a volume a year, compared with the unit’s modelled use. Storing water in a dam (s21b) registers the dam’s storage: the row has no volume (it is shown as “Storage only (s21b)”), is always surface water, and is compared only with the capacity of the dam the run modelled, never counted, capped or scaled as a take. A take can also state a storage beside its volume. Other s21 uses (21(c) to 21(k)) are refused on import, as is a row whose use or unit can’t be read: they are never guessed. Whether filling a dam is also an s21(a) take is a question for the catchment’s hydrologist.

entries.title: Licence conditions
entries.summary: Months of use, a maximum rate and conditions in words. Only a cap run keeps to the months and the rate; the words are only shown. (m³/s)
entries.text: A licence may limit when and how fast water is taken. Each volume can record the months water may be taken in (none ticked means none stated: all year), a maximum rate in m³/s, and up to 20 other conditions in the licence’s own words. The list sums them up in one line, such as “Oct–Mar only · at most 0.05 m³/s · 2 conditions”. Only a run whose allocation mode is cap keeps to the months and the rate: the unit takes nothing from that source in a closed month, and at most the rate × 86 400 m³ a day. The plain comparison and a full-allocation run don’t read them, and conditions in words are only shown, never applied.

entries.title: Importing registered volumes (WARMS)
entries.summary: A CSV of a WARMS extract or the template, matched to units by registration number, property or name. Removable as one import.
entries.text: WARMS has no public interface: a CMA or DWS sends an extract. Import reads a WARMS extract or the app’s CSV template (download it from the Import sheet). For a WARMS extract you record how you obtained it, the DWS or CMA letter or terms. The file is a CSV, comma or semicolon separated, UTF-8, up to 2 MB and 5 000 rows; save a spreadsheet as CSV first. Columns are found by their headings; one the importer doesn’t know is listed as not read, never guessed. Each row is read by its water use (21(a) or 21(b)) and its unit; a row that can’t be read for sure is a row problem and isn’t imported, and an extract with no water-use column is refused whole. A heading that looks like an ID number, passport, phone or email column refuses the whole file before anything is stored. Rows are matched to units by the same registration number as an earlier import, then the same property, then a hydrological unit or water user whose name equals the row’s farm (ignoring case and spacing); two units with the same name match neither. The preview lists rows with problems first, then unmatched rows with a picker. The same file can’t be imported twice into a project, and Remove this import deletes the file’s record and every row it brought.

entries.title: Modelled use vs registered volume
entries.summary: Each unit’s modelled use per water year beside its registered volume: above, within or below the band. Modelled, not metered. (m³ a water year)
entries.text: For a run, per hydrological unit or water user, water source and water year (October to September). Modelled use is the run’s supply summed over the year, from the unit’s own dam, the river and boreholes: groundwater is what boreholes pumped (to the crops or into the dam), and surface water the rest, less borehole water pumped into the dam and drawn out again in the same year. A dam beside the river (filled by River to dam or a top-up off-take, with none of the upstream river flowing into it) is measured at the intake, as its licence states the volume taken there: the surface use is what was taken from the river (River to dam, the top-up, and river water used without passing the dam), less what spilled back the same day, at most that day’s diversion (the run’s `intake_take`). What it then drew from the dam is shown beside it, not added. Water another unit got from such a dam was counted at its intake, so it isn’t counted again there (`received_at_intake`). A run from before engine 1.82.0 reads by the draws: run the model again. Water a unit’s dam rules pump out of the catchment is its surface use too, as a draw from its dam (the licence impact board counts it the same way). On a dam beside the river it was counted at the intake, so it is only in the draws shown beside the take. A cap run limits it to the unit’s surface volume. A dam on the river also shows its dam losses each water year (its evaporation plus the seepage that doesn’t return), marked not counted, so its whole effect on the river is visible. They are never counted against the registered volume, judged or capped: storing water is a water use of its own (s21(b)), apart from taking it. A dam beside the river shows none, since its take at the intake already holds what the dam later loses. Registered volume is each volume in force × the days it is valid that year ÷ the days in the year. Each year reads above registered (modelled use more than the volume × (1 + the band)), within band, below registered, no registered volume (use with nothing in force) or no use, none registered; the band is ±10 % unless the project sets another. A part year (a run that covers only part of a water year) compares those days with the volume prorated to them, is marked part, and isn’t counted with the whole years. A forecast run is compared on its record only. Volumes not matched to a unit, or on a unit the run doesn’t have, are counted, not compared. It is not a finding: modelled use is modelled, not metered, and a registered volume can be missing, out of date or held by someone else. The Reserve, other users’ priority and licence conditions aren’t applied here, only in a cap run. The Allocations page uses the project’s volumes and band now; an evidence report uses those each run stored, so an older run can differ.

entries.title: Registered storage vs dam capacity
entries.summary: A unit’s registered dam storage (s21b) beside the capacity the run modelled: over, under or unregistered. Arithmetic only. (m³)
entries.text: For a unit with a dam, the sum of its registered storage (its s21(b) rows, and storage stated on a take) is set beside the dam capacity the run modelled, with the difference (capacity minus registered storage). It reads over when the dam is larger than the storage registered for it, under when smaller, and unregistered for a dam with no storage registered, banded like a year’s use. It is arithmetic only. A registered storage is never part of the volume a year’s use is compared with, and whether filling the dam is also a take is a question for the catchment’s hydrologist.

entries.title: What the cap held back
entries.summary: In a cap run, the days a unit went short because its year’s volume was used up, it hit the maximum rate, or the month was closed. (days)
entries.text: A run made with the allocation mode cap says which limit held use back. For each unit, source and water year it counts the days the source took all the room it had and the unit still went short, split into days the year’s volume was used up, days at the maximum rate and days outside the months of use, beside the years the volume was used up (“The cap held use back on 80 days in 1 water year: 80 with the volume used up.”). The Allocations page shows it under the picked unit’s water years, the run’s summary CSV has an allocation cap table, and an evidence report prints it as “What the cap held back”, with “Not capped” for a source the run didn’t cap. Unlike the comparison, it counts the whole run, a forecast included. A run from an engine older than 1.40.0 has only the years: run the model again for the days.

entries.title: Who sees registered volumes
entries.summary: Owners and editors see every volume and name; viewers only totals held by 5 or more users, unless an owner allows more. Names never.
entries.text: Owners and editors see every volume, number and date, and the registered users’ names, and they make every change. Viewers see totals per water source held by 5 or more registered users (the volume and storage in force today, and a run’s use against them by water year), and never a name. An owner can let viewers see each farm’s volumes under What viewers see; do so only if every viewer works for, or was appointed by, your organisation, since viewers can be outsiders (an NGO commenting on an application). Farmers see only their own farm’s totals on their farm page, with no name or registration number. Share links, pack links and the verify page show no volumes. An issued evidence pack names the applicant’s own units; every other unit is in totals at 5 or more units, with no names. The history records registration numbers and counts, never names.

entries.title: Water year
entries.summary: October to September, the South African hydrological year. Monthly tables in this app run Oct … Sep.
entries.text: Monthly inputs (A-pan evaporation, crop factors, pragmatic EWR) are entered in water-year order, starting with October. Month pickers (transfer months, dry-season months) show one toggle per month in the same Oct … Sep order.

entries.title: Units: m³/day, m³/s, M.m³
entries.summary: Flows and volumes are m³/day inside the model. 1 m³/s = 86 400 m³/day; 1 M.m³ = one million m³. (m³/day, m³/s, m³, M.m³)
entries.text: Gauge and logger flow series are usually supplied in m³/s and converted to m³/day on the way in. Dam capacities and storage are in m³. Mean annual runoff is often quoted in M.m³ per year. A quick check: 1 m³/s = 86 400 m³/day, 1 l/s ≈ 86 m³/day, and 1 000 m³/day ≈ 11.6 l/s.

entries.title: Days in February
entries.summary: Days used for February when a monthly volume is turned into a daily rate. 28.25 gives a 365.25-day year. (days)
entries.text: Monthly crop requirements are divided by the days in the month to get a daily demand. Use 28.25 to average over leap years (the workbook’s default) or 28 for a strict 365-day year.

entries.title: Simulation window
entries.summary: Optional first and last day to simulate. Leave empty to run from the first to the last day with rain.
entries.text: Narrow the window to study a drought or to match a calibration period. Dams start from their initial storage on the first simulated day, so allow a warm-up period before the dates you care about.

entries.title: Calibration window
entries.summary: The period and observed flow record the outlet’s fit is scored on (a gauge location has its own). Empty = every day with an observation.
entries.text: Hydrologists usually calibrate on a period with reliable observations rather than the whole record; a Water Balance Tool workbook has its own calibration date range and flow choice. Choose which observed series to compare against (gauge or logger); left empty, the gauge record is used if there is one, else the logger. This window is the outlet’s (At the outlet, under the calibration locations); each gauge location has its own window in its row. The fit statistics and the annual volume table only count days inside this window.

entries.title: Calibration locations
entries.summary: The outlet and each gauge with a record; a ticked one fits GR4J for the units draining to it, in dependency order. None is required.
entries.text: One parameter set rarely fits a whole catchment: a wet mountain headwater and a dry lowland drain differently. Every place with a flow record of its own can be a calibration location: the outlet, and each gauge inside the network. None is special and none is required. A ticked location fits GR4J for the land units draining to it, on its own record; those units, with the location, are its zone. Calibration → Calibration record lists the locations. Tick Calibrate here on a row to calibrate there. A ticked gauge’s zone holds the land units draining to it that aren’t in a ticked location further upstream; a ticked outlet’s holds every unit left above it. Untick a location and its units join the next ticked location downstream. Each gauge’s row has its own calibration window, excluded periods, record and treatment of suspect days in its fold; the outlet’s are the fields under the table, with the gauged ranges, gap filling, missing and low-flow periods that only the outlet’s records have. Units with no ticked location downstream (below the lowest ticked gauge with the outlet unticked, or on an ungauged branch) take what the rest rule says: the nearest ticked location upstream on their river (the default for a new project; spatial proximity is the best-performing donor choice in large comparisons, Oudin et al. 2008, Parajka et al. 2013), the headline location’s parameters, or the catchment parameters (GR4J parameters, under Flow calibration). With no location ticked every unit runs on the catchment parameters, and Fit automatically has nothing to fit. The headline is the location whose statistics a run reports as its calibration statistics, and the one the uncertainty ensemble and the automated calibration rules vary. Pick it with the Headline radio, or leave it automatic: the outlet when it is ticked, else the ticked gauge with the largest area above it. Fit automatically fits the locations one at a time in dependency order: a location is fitted after every location whose units drain through it, and after any location a unit above it takes its parameters from, so each is fitted with the ones it depends on already in place; the headline goes last among those ready. The card lists the order, and refuses before it starts when no location is ticked, a location has no unit draining through it, or units borrow each other’s parameters in a circle. Until a location is fitted its units run on the catchment parameters, and the run says so. A gauge with fewer than 2 complete water years, or no dry year to test on, gets a note: its parameters rest on too short a record to trust alone. A flow record whose Measured at names a gauge no longer in the model, or a node that isn’t a gauge inside the network, or a second outlet record of a kind (a run reads only the first by name), can’t be calibrated on; the page flags it with a link to its Measured at on Data. Zones work because each unit runs its own GR4J (Per unit flow generation, the only method). The Network and the Map colour each unit by its zone, a run scores every ticked location on its own record (in or out of sample by its own fit), and the report, the evidence pack and Compare runs list every location. These choices are provisional, pending the client hydrologist’s review.

entries.title: Gauge vs logger agreement
entries.summary: Flags water years where the observed gauge and the logger disagree by more than the set ratio, on enough shared days.
entries.text: Two instruments on the same river should roughly agree. Each water year, the gauge volume is compared with the logger volume on the days both have a reading. A year is flagged when the ratio is below the lowest ratio or above the highest ratio (defaults 67 % and 150 %), and only when the year has at least the minimum number of shared days (default 90). A flagged year usually means a problem at one instrument, so choose the record you trust as the calibration flow series. The thresholds only change which years are flagged, never the model results. The Data tab’s Data checks also list negative values, outliers and flat stretches in each series, catchment rain that reads 0 where it looks missing (a zero blocks the CHIRPS fallback a blank day gets), and water years whose catchment rain reads far below CHIRPS.

entries.title: Data quality limits
entries.summary: The checks Data and runs report: negative values, outliers, flat stretches, rain read as 0 that looks missing, breaks against CHIRPS.
entries.text: Settings → Data quality holds the limits of the checks the Data tab and every run report. The gauge-vs-logger ratios, the outlier factors (a value this many times the 99th percentile of a series’ positive values, 5 for rain and A-pan, 10 for flow) and the flat-stretch lengths (5 days of one rain value, 7 of A-pan, 14 to 90 of flow depending on the flow and the record’s resolution) only decide what is flagged. The zero-rain and low-vs-CHIRPS limits change results, because a run treats a flagged zero run as missing (CHIRPS fills it) and leaves a flagged water year out of the CHIRPS factor fit. By default a zero run is flagged with 60 or more days in the series’ six wettest months, and a water year when its catchment / CHIRPS ratio is below half the record’s usual one. The alternatives come from a hydrologist review for semi-arid catchments: judge a run by the share of the usual annual rain it missed, check it against CHIRPS (a run CHIRPS reads as dry too may be a real dry spell and is not flagged), compare each year with the years around it instead of the whole record, and ask more CHIRPS rain of a year in a wet catchment before judging it. They are off until tested on a semi-arid record with a known drought. A fit made under other limits says its forcing changed.

entries.title: Reporting window
entries.summary: The period the curtailment report (equitable shares and EWR cuts per hydrological unit) averages over. Empty = the whole run.
entries.text: Pick a critical period — a dry season or a drought year — to see how much each hydrological unit would need to reduce for irrigation to balance and the EWR to be met in that period. A window partly outside the run is clipped to it. On Hydrological units, the Reporting window picker above the curtailment table shows the same tables over another period (the last 7, 14 or 30 days, the whole record or a custom range) without changing this setting or re-running: anyone who can see the run can use it.

entries.title: Assurance of supply
entries.summary: How reliably each hydrological unit’s irrigation demand was met over the reporting window: by days, by volume and by water years. (% ; days; m³)
entries.text: Two measures per hydrological unit and other water user (engine 0.32.0). Days met: the share of days with demand when the whole demand was supplied (days without demand don’t count). Water years met: the share of complete water years (1 October to 30 September inside the reporting window; a part year at either end is left out, engine 1.11.0) whose supply reached the annual threshold (Settings, default 90 %, a project choice rather than a standard). After Hashimoto et al. (1982), a failure is a run of consecutive demand days not fully met: the table gives the number of failures, their mean and longest length (resilience) and the mean and largest deficit per failure (vulnerability). The definitions are pending review by the project hydrologist.

entries.title: Allocation mode
entries.summary: What registered volumes do to a run. The baseline only compares use with them; a scenario may cap use at them or scale demand to them.
entries.text: The Allocations tab stores the volumes registered or licensed per unit and water source. WARMS registers per s21 water use: a take (s21a) is a volume a year; a dam’s storage (s21b) is a row of its own, shown as Storage only (s21b) and never counted as a take, only against the dam’s capacity. In the baseline they only sit beside a run: the tab compares each water year’s modelled use with them, for the unit you pick beside the list, and for every unit at once under Show all units’ water years at the foot of the page. Licence data never drives the baseline: its use comes from the crops, demands, pumps and boreholes you enter, so the Settings tab’s allocation mode is always compare only. Two modes (engine 1.18.0) make the volumes part of a run, and only a scenario can choose them (Change a setting → Allocation mode), to ask “what if use were capped at the licences” or “what if every licence were taken in full”. Cap: each unit’s surface-water use (from its dam, its river pump and off-take water) and groundwater use (pumped to the crop and into the dam) per water year (October–September) stays within its registered volumes. The budget is the whole year’s volume, so a unit may take it early and then goes without; its boreholes cover what a capped surface can’t, within the groundwater volume. A source with no registered volume isn’t capped, and nor is a day on which none of the unit’s licences of that source is in force, before its first starts or after its last ends; the use on those days doesn’t count against the year’s volume, which is prorated to the licences’ days (a licence from 1 September caps September at 30/365 of it). The run warns, naming the units and days, so check the licence dates (engine 1.70.0; before, a year with no licence in force was capped at 0). A demand-sized off-take into a capped unit takes only the demand its cap still allows. Full allocation: each unit’s demand (crops and other demands together) is scaled, year by year, so it asks for exactly its registered volume (both sources), keeping its own seasonal pattern. It shows the river if every registered or licensed volume were taken in full (a registration is not an entitlement), the background for a cumulative assessment. A demand level (a seasonal outlook’s or a demand sweep’s), a scenario’s Scale demand and the abstraction sensitivity case apply after that scaling (engine 1.70.0), so 80 % means 80 % of the registered volume. A unit without a volume, or a water year with no licence in force (engine 1.70.0), keeps its modelled demand, and a level then applies to that. A cap also keeps to the licence conditions: no water from a source in a month outside its licence’s months, and at most its maximum rate a day (the rate × 86 400 m³). Full allocation doesn’t apply them, and conditions written in words are only shown. How the cap counts water drawn from a dam that boreholes filled is pending the hydrologist.

entries.title: Allocation comparison band
entries.summary: How far modelled use may sit from a registered volume and still count as within it: ±10 % by default. (%)
entries.text: A water year whose modelled use is more than the registered volume × (1 + band) reads “above registered”, less than × (1 − band) “below registered”, anything between “within band”. It changes only how the comparison reads, never the run’s water. The ±10 % default is a provisional default (2026-10-01), not yet confirmed by the catchment’s hydrologist: it allows for meter and model error, and is not a legal tolerance.

entries.title: Stress class
entries.summary: A month’s supply as a class: Low (≥ 95 % of demand supplied), Moderate (≥ 85 %), High (≥ 70 %), Severe (≥ 50 %) or Critical.
entries.text: The classes and thresholds come from an experimental node-based workbook, which reported them per hydrological unit and per month. A month is Low with at least 95 % of its demand supplied, Moderate with 85 %, High with 70 %, Severe with 50 %, and Critical below that. The app grids them per hydrological unit, per other water user and for all of them together, water year by month, over the whole run. A month without demand has no class.

entries.title: Water account
entries.summary: Per water year: what entered the river network, where it went, what the dams kept, and a residual that should be 0. (m³)
entries.text: In: natural flow, rain on the dams, groundwater pumped and net transfers. Out: runoff removed by land cover, natural flow no hydrological unit received (when no unit has an area; on runs before engine 1.105.0, flow shares not summing to 1), consumptive irrigation (supplied − return flow), other users’ net take, dam evaporation, dam seepage lost from the catchment, stream depletion from boreholes and the outflow at the outlet. A dam storage reset, when one is set, counts on the In side. In − out − change in dam storage is the residual, float noise. Seepage that rejoins the river below the dam is shown as a memo. The EWR required and met at each site, per water year, is under the EWR by month grid on EWR.

entries.title: Network
entries.summary: How the hydrological units connect: each drains into exactly one hydrological unit downstream, ending at the outflow gauge.
entries.text: The network is a tree. A hydrological unit can receive water from several upstream hydrological units but sends all of its outflow to one downstream hydrological unit; a river that splits (bifurcation) is not modelled directly — use a transfer, or merge the hydrological units. The model works out the calculation order itself, upstream first, so each hydrological unit sees its upstream neighbours’ outflow on the same day.

entries.title: Hydrological unit
entries.summary: Any point of the network: a unit with land (runoff, an optional dam, demands), a gauge or an other water user. Exports call it a node.
entries.text: A hydrological unit is any point of the network, of three kinds: a unit with land (usually a farm, but also a sub-catchment or a town with land of its own, with its runoff, an optional dam and demands), a gauge (a measuring point) and an other water user (a town or industry that only draws water from the river, with no land of its own). The workspace, the farmer view, the farmer emails and the shared view say hydrological unit, naming the kind where it matters; the exports (CSV and workbook) and the API call it a node, and a unit with land a farm. It is not a unit of measurement (m³, l/s). Model each unit with land as the land it occupies. The same kind covers three cases, set by its parameters: • Farm (or sub-catchment) — crops, a dam if it has one, return flow. • Stand-alone dam — no crop areas (so no irrigation or return flow), all of its runoff (and upstream inflow, if the dam sits on the main stem) captured by the dam, no diversion. • Natural (unused) area — no crops, no dam capture, no diversion: it simply passes its runoff downstream.

entries.title: Gauge
entries.summary: A measuring point that only passes flow through and reports it, with its EWR check unless it isn’t an EWR site. No runoff, dam or demand.
entries.text: Use gauges where you want to read the simulated flow, for example at a weir with a record. A gauge is also an EWR site unless you untick “EWR site” (engine 1.5.0): its flow is checked against the EWR of everything upstream of it, and a shortfall there is charged to the hydrological units above it. Add gauges at the Reserve determination’s EWR sites to protect upstream reaches; untick one that only records flow (a weir that is no Reserve site), so it charges nobody and a Reserve rule table there is skipped. It still shows its flow and EWR shortfall. The last gauge in the network is the outflow gauge, always an EWR site.

entries.title: Other water user
entries.summary: A town, industry or unlisted irrigator that takes water from the river at its place in the network, with no land or dam of its own.
entries.text: Water taken by users that are not modelled hydrological units would otherwise be handed to the hydrological units and the EWR, over-stating both. An other user has a monthly demand (m³/day), a share of what it takes that comes back below it the same day (treated wastewater) and a priority. It takes only from the river where it sits: what reaches it from upstream, after anything upstream has taken its share. It is charged for EWR shortfalls below it like a hydrological unit, by its net impact (what it takes less what it returns). Other users are outside the irrigation equitable-share benchmark. A non-priority user is curtailed for the EWR (Curtailment tab, "Other water users"); a priority one only by its fixed restriction %, when it has one.

entries.title: User priority (Priority / Non-priority)
entries.summary: Priority (the default): units and non-priority users upstream pass its demand first. Non-priority: it takes what reaches it after them.
entries.text: A priority user’s demand is a requirement every hydrological unit upstream of it passes before it fills its dam or irrigates, shared between those hydrological units by their natural MAR shares (the hydrological unit diverts less, then lets inflow and its own runoff pass below the dam). A non-priority user upstream of a priority one leaves the priority demand in the river too. A non-priority user takes only what reaches it. Hydrological units have no protected claim, so a non-priority user upstream of a hydrological unit still takes first: position in the river decides. A municipal allocation is usually a priority user, which is the default for a new other water user. So adding one changes what every hydrological unit upstream of it gets, as a dam release rule would. A priority user is curtailed for the EWR only by its fixed restriction %, when it has one; the rest of its charge is reported and left standing, never moved onto the farms.

entries.title: Share returned (other user)
entries.summary: Share of what an other water user takes that comes back to the river below it the same day, such as treated wastewater. (%)
entries.text: A town returns part of what it abstracts through its wastewater works. That share joins the river directly below the user on the same day; the rest is consumed. 0 % means nothing comes back.

entries.title: Fixed restriction (Priority user)
entries.summary: Share of a Priority user’s demand it gives up when restricted, in a curtailment and under the drought restriction. Blank is none. (%)
entries.text: A priority user can carry a fixed restriction: the share of its demand it gives up when restricted. Blank (or 0) is uncurtailed, the default. • In a curtailment (Curtailment tab, "Other water users"): it is cut for its EWR charge by at most this share of its demand, and never more than it took. The rest of its charge stands; it is never moved onto the farms. The row is marked "fixed %, no basic-needs floor". • Under the drought restriction rule (Settings): while the rule is at a level that cuts some part of the hydrological units’ demand, it asks the river and its boreholes for its demand less this share, and the hydrological units upstream pass only that for it.
