One with no reading on any of them, or with no MAP while scaling is on, can’t help: it is greyed out and says why. Use Up and Down to reorder, Remove to drop one, and Add a source for another (at most 8). An empty list sends the gaps to the next fallback. • Satellite rain is never a unit’s station, only the fill. A station’s CHIRPS for its checks is read at its own coordinates, or, without them, from the unit it stands in. A unit with No station runs as before stations (see Flow generation). Tick several units to give them one station and patching priority at once. Changing a unit’s station changes the rain GR4J runs on: refit afterwards. Unreliable periods (Model settings → Rain gaps, under Flagged rain) can be marked on any rain record, not only a station: a unit’s own gauge and the alternative catchment gauge too. A run reads those days as missing, so the record’s next source stands in: for a station its corrected CHIRPS, for a unit’s own gauge its own CHIRPS, levelled, then the next link of its rule, for the alternative gauge the next source of its rain-source period. A station’s and a unit gauge’s are blanked after their zero-run and accumulation checks, so a marked period never looks like a blank outage. A station’s count only while it is assigned. The catchment gauge’s own days are the missing periods under Flagged zero runs. The stored series never changes.

entries.title: The catchment’s rainfall station
entries.summary: The catchment rain from a station × catchment MAP ÷ its MAP, its gaps patched in the order you set; none = the rain series as before. (mm/day)
entries.text: Under Model settings → Flow generation, The catchment’s rainfall station sets where the catchment rain comes from: the rain demand and the dams read, and the rain GR4J runs on for a unit scaled from the catchment gauge or with no rain of its own. No station (the default) keeps the catchment rain series, as before stations. With a station it follows the same rule as a unit’s station (see A unit’s rainfall station): • On the station’s days the catchment runs on its rain × catchment MAP ÷ station MAP, held between 0.25 and 4; untick Scale to catchment MAP to run on its rain as recorded. The catchment MAP is the one entered under Catchment MAP with its source, else the land units’ area-weighted mean MAP; with neither (a unit has no MAP) the ratio is 1, with a warning. • On its gaps and unreliable days the first source in Then patch gaps from with a reading fills in: another station × catchment MAP ÷ that station’s MAP, or CHIRPS, corrected: the catchment’s CHIRPS corrected month by month against the rain of the station chosen under Gaps: CHIRPS corrected against (its own by default) at the catchment’s MAP. CHIRPS alone is the default; an empty list sends the gaps to the forecast, else they are dry. • Each station in the list says how many of the main station’s gap days it fills over the run’s days before any forecast, or why it can’t help (no record, no MAP, or no reading on any of those gaps): such a station is greyed out. Under a catchment station the areal rainfall correction, the rain-source periods and the gap-filling product are not read: the station and its patching priority replace them, and the run warns. Changing the station changes the rain GR4J runs on: refit afterwards.

entries.title: Actual evaporation (AET)
entries.summary: Water the catchment actually evaporates each day in GR4J, in mm: never more than the potential evaporation. (mm)
entries.text: The part of potential evaporation that rain meets directly, plus what the soil-moisture store can give up. On dry days with a dry store it falls well below PET.

entries.title: Automatic calibration (Fit automatically)
entries.summary: Searches the runoff model’s parameters for the best fit to the observed record, then tests the fit on days it never saw.
entries.text: The search is DDS (Tolson & Shoemaker 2007): it tries a set number of model runs, perturbing all parameters at first and fewer as it homes in, and never leaves each parameter’s allowed range. It runs several separate searches (Starts, default 5), each from its own seed, and keeps the best; nearly equal scores with scattered parameters mean the record can’t pin them down. Every run scores the whole model, hydrological units and dams included, against the observed record over the calibration window. Pick what to optimise (the objective) by what the fit will feed, before seeing any score: KGE′ (the default) for the overall water balance, peaks and events; a year-balanced KGE′ when a few wet years would dominate; for EWR, low-flow and assurance decisions the mean of KGE′ on Q and on 1/Q when the low flows are well rated, or the non-parametric KGE when the rating at the extremes is uncertain; NSE on √Q or log Q mainly to compare with older studies. Don’t fit several objectives and keep the best-looking score: scores of different objectives don’t compare, and choosing after seeing them overfits. Check a low-flow fit for volume too, with the WR2012 fit statistics and KGE′ beside it. The fit alone says little. Validation fits again on the first half of the record and scores the second half, then fits on the driest water years and scores the wettest (listed by water year, since they interleave). When the project has a reference gauge on another river covering those years, the years are ranked dry → wet by it, a regional index that is never scored; otherwise by the record’s own flow. The result also says how representative the record is: how many water years it covers and where their rain sits among the run’s long-term rain. With both a gauge and a logger record you can also score the fit against the record it wasn’t fitted to, a second instrument. Those columns are the honest measure. The main scores show a 90 % range in brackets, from resampling whole water years: a wide range means the record can’t pin the score down. A second table sets the model beside two simple benchmarks on the same days, the mean flow every day and each calendar day’s average flow; a model that can’t beat the second adds little beyond the seasonal cycle. With a short record that is mostly drought, the result says so: wet-year behaviour is then weakly constrained. Nothing is saved until you apply the result and save the form.

entries.title: Objective (what a fit optimises)
entries.summary: The score the search maximises. Choose it by what the fit will feed, before seeing any score: KGE′ by default, a low-flow one for EWR.
entries.text: The optimiser searches for the parameters that score best on one objective. Each weighs the record differently, so the same data can give different parameters: KGE′ (Kling et al. 2012, the default) combines correlation, bias and variability. It keeps the overall water balance and follows peaks and events. Simulating the mean flow every day scores about −0.41. Year-balanced KGE′ is the mean KGE′ over the water years with at least 30 scored days, so each year counts once and a few wet years can’t dominate the score. Non-parametric KGE (Pool et al. 2018) uses the Spearman rank correlation, the shape of the flow-duration curve and the bias. It reads the order and the distribution of the flows rather than their exact values, so it is less sensitive to rating error at the extremes. NSE on √Q weights medium flows; NSE on log Q (with 1 % of the mean observed flow added, so zero flows are allowed) weights low flows. The mean of KGE′(Q) and KGE′(1/Q) scores half on the flows and half on their inverses, so recessions and low flows count as much as the peaks and the water balance, and neither end is traded away. How to choose: by what the fit will feed, before you see any score. For the overall water balance, peaks and events, KGE′. When a few wet years would dominate the record, year-balanced KGE′. When the fit feeds an EWR, low-flow or assurance-of-supply decision, a low-flow-sensitive objective: the mean of KGE′(Q) and KGE′(1/Q) when the gauge’s low flows are well rated, or the non-parametric KGE when the rating at the extremes is uncertain. NSE on √Q or log Q mainly to compare with older studies that used them. Never run several objectives and keep the one whose score looks best. Scores of different objectives aren’t comparable (a KGE′ of 0.7 and an NSE on log Q of 0.7 say different things), and picking after seeing them is the overfitting the calibration rules exist to stop. To try several objectives honestly, list them in the calibration rules: every fit is then judged on the same selection score on a held-out test, chosen in advance. A low-flow fit should still be checked for volume: read the WR2012 fit statistics and KGE′, reported beside every fit, before trusting its annual flows.

entries.title: Validation tests (held-out scores)
entries.summary: Scores on days a fit never saw: the record’s second half, the wettest years after fitting the driest, or a second instrument.
entries.text: A score on the days the parameters were fitted to shows how well they fit, not how well they predict. Each validation test fits on one part of the record and scores another part it never saw: Split-sample (Klemeš 1986): fit on the first half of the scored days, score the second half. Dry → wet (differential split-sample): with at least 4 water years of 180 or more observed days, fit on the driest half of those years and score the wettest. It is the hardest test for a catchment modelled through drought. The years interleave, so the test is listed by water year, not as a date range. When the project has a reference gauge on another river, the years are ranked dry → wet by it, as a regional index that is never scored; otherwise by the record’s own flow. Other observed record (independent record): the parameters fitted to one record, scored against the other, for example the logger when the fit used the gauge. It costs no extra fit and tests the fit against a second instrument rather than a second period. Expect validation to score below the fit. A validation score more than 0.2 below its calibration score, too few years to test wet years, or wet years barely wetter than the dry ones each get a note. These columns, shaded in the results, are the honest measure of a fit.

entries.title: Search: model runs, starts and seed
entries.summary: How hard the optimiser looks: model runs per search (1 500), separate searches from their own seeds (5), and a seed that makes it repeat.
entries.text: Model runs per fit (default 1 500, from 50 to 10 000) is the budget of one DDS search: how many candidate parameter sets it runs the whole model with. Starts (default 5, at most 10) are separate searches of the whole record, each from its own seed; the best is kept. When two or more starts score within 0.01 of the best but a parameter spreads over more than 10 % of its range across them, the result says the record can’t pin that parameter down. The seed makes the search repeatable: the same data, engine version and seed give the same fit. More runs or starts rarely rescue a poor fit. The record, not the search, usually limits it, and a flat ridge between X1 and X3 only gives an arbitrary point on the ridge more precisely. Under the calibration rules the seed, starts and model runs are rules too, so re-running with seed after seed until one scores well is a rule change, with its own revision.

entries.title: Benchmarks (mean flow and climatology)
entries.summary: Two naive simulations scored on the same days: the mean flow every day, and each calendar day’s smoothed average. A model should beat both.
entries.text: A score means little without something to beat. The table scores two naive simulations on the same days as the model. The mean flow repeats the period’s mean observed flow every day (KGE′ about −0.41, NSE 0). The climatology gives each day the average observed flow on that calendar day, smoothed over a centred 15-day window so it keeps the seasonal cycle but not single storms. On a split-sample or dry → wet validation period both benchmarks are built from that test’s calibration period and applied to the validation days, as a forecast made without the validation flows would be. In a strongly seasonal catchment the climatology is hard to beat, and a model that doesn’t beat it adds little beyond the seasonal cycle.

entries.title: Score range (90 %, by water year)
entries.summary: The bracketed range beside a score: its 5th–95th percentile with whole water years resampled 1 000 times. Wide = the record can’t pin it.
entries.text: Daily scores carry a large sampling error, mostly from a few wet spells. The range in brackets beside KGE′, NSE and the low/high-flow KGE′ comes from a block bootstrap: whole water years are drawn with replacement (days within a year aren’t independent), the resample is scored, 1 000 times, and the range is the 5th to 95th percentile. The draw is fixed, so the range is reproducible. It needs at least 3 water years with 30 or more scored days each; with fewer there is no range. Three years is a floor, not a recommendation: a short record gives a wide range, which is the point. Two fits whose ranges overlap widely can’t be told apart by the record.

entries.title: How representative the record is
entries.summary: How many water years a fit scored and where each year’s rain sits in the long-term record: dry, near normal or wet.
entries.text: A few years from one climate state can’t support the flow’s variability, its seasonal pattern or a high-flow calibration, however good the scores look. So every fit states the record’s length and where its years sit in the long-term rain: the run’s own rain over the whole run, complete water years only (rain on at least 95 % of the days). Each scored water year shows its scored days, its rain and its percentile among the long-term years. Below the 33rd percentile it is dry, above the 67th wet, otherwise near normal; with fewer than 10 complete long-term years no year is classed. The summary gives the scored years’ mean rain against the long-term mean, and the notes say what the record can’t show, for example “every classed year dry: it can’t show how the model behaves in wet years”.

entries.title: Uncertainty bands (behavioural ensemble)
entries.summary: How far a run’s results move across every parameter set and forcing the data can’t rule out: 5–95 % bands, never below 30 kept sets.
entries.text: One calibrated run gives one number for EWR days not met, curtailment and the annual volumes, but many parameter sets fit the record nearly as well, and the pan coefficient, the rain and the observed record are uncertain too. The ensemble samples them all: a Latin hypercube across the parameter bounds (never the optimiser’s own path), a shift of the pan coefficient (GR4J), station rain with CHIRPS infill or CHIRPS alone, and the gauge or the logger to judge against, where the project has both. A set is kept only if it passes the rule printed next to the bands: a skill score (KGE′ by default) on the first half of its record, the WR2012 flag on its natural flow, and the low-flow bias. The bands are the 5th to 95th percentiles of the kept sets; with fewer than 30 kept none are shown. The second half of the record is held out: the share of its observations inside the daily band is the coverage, and below 70 % the band is too narrow to trust. The server fixes the rule and draws the seed before anything runs, keeps every ensemble started, and re-runs members to check a result before storing it, so a band can’t be picked after the fact. Run comparison bands the difference between two runs member by member: the extra impact of an application, with its own uncertainty.

entries.title: Declared uncertainty rule (evidence)
entries.summary: The ensemble an evidence report may cite: its size, bounds, pan shift and the tests a set must pass, declared before any band is seen.
entries.text: An ensemble’s bands depend on its rule: how many parameter sets it samples, how far it may roam, how far it shifts the pan coefficient, and the skill score, WR2012 flag and low-flow bias a set must pass to be kept. Tried after the bands are seen, those choices could be tuned until a band looks kind to an application. So the project declares the rule first, under Settings › Evidence. An evidence report then cites the first complete ensemble whose options match the rule exactly, and names it; with no rule declared it cites none. The History tab records who declared or changed the rule and when, and a change means a new ensemble must be run to it before a report can cite one. The rule starts from the ensemble’s own defaults: 300 members, typical bounds, pan ±0.1, KGE′ at least 0.5, WR2012 flags up to “query”, low-flow bias within ±50 %.

entries.title: Bounds (automatic calibration)
entries.summary: How far the search may roam per parameter: wide (each parameter’s full calibration range) or typical (Perrin et al.’s published 80 % range).
entries.text: A short or drought-heavy record often can’t pin down X1 (production store) and X3 (routing store): the fit lands outside where GR4J parameters usually sit, because too little of the record constrains them. "Typical" restricts the search to Perrin et al.’s (2003) 80 % range over 429 catchments (X1 100–1200 mm, X3 20–300 mm, X4 1.1–2.9 days), which can make an under-constrained fit land somewhere plausible instead of at an extreme of the wide range. It is a constraint on the search, not evidence the catchment truly falls inside it: read the fit and validation scores either way, and prefer the wide range when the record constrains the parameters well. Recorded with the fit record.

entries.title: Regional GR4J prior
entries.summary: GR4J’s parameters in similar, nearby gauged basins (donors): a start for an ungauged catchment, or a penalty or search box in a fit.
entries.text: The Regional prior card, under Fit the parameters on the Calibration page, builds for the catchment (or one calibration zone), GR4J’s parameter ranges from donor basins: gauged basins in the region, each recalibrated on the same CHIRPS v3 rain and dPET evaporation the app uses. The donors most like the catchment (area, mean annual rain, aridity) and nearest to it are kept, weighted by both, and each parameter’s p10, p50 and p90 are taken over them; X1’s range comes from the soil water capacity instead when that relation has skill. The leave-one-out skill says how well the method predicts a donor’s parameters from the others, against simply taking their median: at 0 or below the prior has no skill, and is labelled so. Three uses. “Start from the prior” writes the medians into the parameters, for a catchment with no flow record to fit (saved at once, as a settings revision naming the donors). In Fit automatically, a penalty pulls the fit toward the medians (its weight is in score units: at 0.1 a parameter at its p10 or p90 costs about 0.08 of KGE′), or the search keeps to the p10–p90 box, or both. Off, a fit is as before. The fit record and an evidence pack name the prior, its donors and the donor set’s hash.

entries.title: WR2012 check
entries.summary: Compares simulated natural flow with the naturalised flow WR2012 publishes for the quaternary, scaled to the modelled catchment. (MAR Mm³/a; monthly means Mm³ per month; area km²; MAP mm)
entries.text: WR2012 (Water Resources of South Africa 2012) gives each quaternary catchment a naturalised mean annual runoff (MAR) and mean monthly flows: the river as it would be with no hydrological units, dams or abstraction. Enter them from the study for the quaternary this project lies in, with the period they cover and where they come from. The app doesn’t ship WR2012 data. Each run then compares its simulated natural flow, never the outflow, with the reference. The reference is scaled to the modelled catchment by the area ratio (the default), or, if you choose it and the quaternary MAP is entered, by the area and the rainfall ratio (the run’s mean annual rain ÷ the quaternary MAP). Runoff doesn’t scale in proportion to rain, so treat the rainfall scaling as a first estimate. The report gives the MAR ratio over the complete water years both cover and over the whole run, the 12 monthly ratios with the dry-season months marked, and the correlation of the monthly pattern. A MAR that differs by 10 % is noted, by 25 % (or 15 % wetter) is queried, and by 50 % makes the run unusable for EWR findings until it is explained. The thresholds are editable. Monthly means are in million m³ per month (not m³/s) and should add up to the MAR within 5 %. A MAR larger than the rain on the quaternary (MAP × area) is rejected.

entries.title: WR2012 MAR penalty (calibration)
entries.summary: Optional: automatic calibration also pulls the simulated natural MAR towards the scaled WR2012 MAR. Off by default.
entries.text: Switch it on in Calibration → Fit the parameters, in the Fit automatically card (WR2012 MAR penalty); it needs the WR2012 check’s reference MAR, and its weight and MAR band are set under the WR2012 check while it is on. When it is on, Fit automatically adds weight × |ln(simulated natural MAR ÷ scaled WR2012 MAR)| to the loss it minimises, so a wetter and a drier MAR by the same factor cost the same. It only touches the annual volume, not the daily pattern. When two published natural-MAR estimates disagree, tick “Use a MAR band instead of one target”: the penalty is then 0 inside the band (already at the modelled catchment’s scale) and weight × |ln(simulated MAR ÷ the nearer bound)| outside it. The result shows the fit with the penalty and the same fit without it, with the weight, so you can see what matching WR2012 costs the fit to the observed record. A short or impacted observed record can disagree with WR2012 for good reasons; the penalty is a nudge, not a constraint.

entries.title: WR2012 fit statistics
entries.summary: Five statistics of annual and monthly flow, observed against simulated, each with its % difference and a good-fit band. Never optimised. (Mm³ ; %)
entries.text: South African practice with the WRSM/Pitman model judges a calibration on five statistics of observed and simulated flow, beside the hydrograph and the flow-duration curve. The app reports them for the fit, each validation test and every run’s calibration, on the same scored days as the other statistics. The scored days are summed per calendar month; a month counts when at least 90 % of its days are scored, and a hydrological year (October to September) only when all 12 months count. Over those complete years: MAR (mean annual runoff), the mean of log10 annual runoff, the standard deviation and the log standard deviation of annual runoff, and a seasonal index (how unevenly the flow falls across the months: 0 is even, 183 all in one month). Each has a % difference, simulated against observed (+ = simulated higher), and is within its band when the difference is smaller than it: MAR 4 %, mean of logs 4 %, SD 6 %, log SD 6 %, seasonal index 8 %. Those bands, and the seasonal index’s exact form, are yet to be confirmed against the WR2012 manuals, so the table calls them indicative bands until they are. The table never changes a result and no fit optimises it; it is the volume check to read beside a fit to low flows.

entries.title: Calibration exclusions
entries.summary: Water years or date ranges left out of every calibration score, each with a reason that runs keep on record.
entries.text: Use one for a period whose data you can’t trust: a suspect rain year, the gauge after a known break, an outage. Excluded days are left out of Fit automatically and of the run’s calibration statistics alike; the model still simulates them. A water year runs from 1 October to 30 September. A reason is required, every run stores the exclusions it applied, and comparing two runs lists any exclusion added, removed or re-reasoned, so dropping an awkward period always leaves a record.

entries.title: Missing periods of one flow record
entries.summary: Periods of one flow record read as missing: its scores, the fit and its checks skip them, and its gap fill may fill them.
entries.text: Use one when a single flow record can’t be trusted for a while, a weir silted up or a logger reading drift, but the other records can. Unlike a calibration exclusion, which leaves the days out of every record’s scores, a missing period blanks the days of that one record wherever a run reads it: its calibration statistics, Fit automatically, the EWR test on the record and the plausibility checks all skip them, and the record’s quality flags call them missing. If the record is gap-filled, a filled day there is infilled like any other, and scored or not as the infilled treatment says. The stored series never changes, and the model still simulates the days. A reason is required, runs store the periods they applied, and comparing two runs lists any period added, removed or re-reasoned.

entries.title: Quality flags (per-day)
entries.summary: Each observed day is in the gauged range, above or below it, over a low-flow threshold, suspect, infilled or missing. Fits set flags aside.
entries.text: A gauge measures water level; a rating curve turns it into flow, and the curve is only checked against field gaugings over the range they cover. Above the highest gauging the flow is the curve extended by judgement, often out by 40 % or more on South African weirs, so a fit that chases those peaks chases the extrapolation. Enter the highest and lowest gauging of each record, with where they come from, under Calibration record. Each observed day then gets one flag: in the gauged range, above the highest gauging, below the lowest (above zero; a dry weir reads zero reliably), suspect (an outlier or a non-zero flat stretch by the Data checks, under the limits in Settings → Data quality, or zero flow the river-stops rule doesn’t trust), infilled (a gap-filled value) or missing. Fit automatically censors days above the highest gauging by default: the model only has to reach the highest gauging on them, however high the record reads. Below-rating, suspect and infilled days are left out. The fit shows its scores on all days beside the fit on the clean days, and a data-quality panel with the share of days by flag, the rain on the scored days (gauge reading or infilled) and what the record can’t support, with how wet the scored years were under it. The run’s own calibration statistics still score every observed day, except a reading above a low-flow period’s threshold (below). Changing a gauged range or a treatment marks the fit record “Quality flags changed since fit”. Zero flow can be the river stopping or a logger that failed. Tick the months the river is known to stop under Months the river stops: a zero stretch that overlaps them is trusted and scored as long as it runs no more than 30 days beyond them on each side (a drought year’s longer dry season), and one wholly outside them is suspect whatever its length. With no months ticked, a zero stretch of up to 30 days is trusted and a longer one is suspect. Check suspect zero flow with the client, and record a logger failure as an exclusion period. When a record’s high flows are wrong for a while but its low flows are good, add a period under Low flows only (beside the calibration exclusions): the record, the dates, the flow up to which readings are valid, a reason and a source. Inside it a reading above that flow is flagged “above a low-flow period’s threshold” and left out of the fit, the run’s statistics, its EWR test on the record and the plausibility checks, never censored, since a wrong high reading doesn’t say the flow was at least that much. The human-use class is defined but not yet derived.

entries.title: Calibration rules (automated calibration)
entries.summary: Rules saved before any fit is seen: which years to leave out, which fits to try and which one to keep. The fit then picks itself.
entries.text: Each pass of calibrate → review → refit normally needs a person, who chooses the years to leave out, the forcing and the fit to keep after seeing the scores. Chasing the score that way overfits, and an assessor can’t tell a principled choice from a convenient one. Calibration rules make those choices in advance. A water year is left out when more than a set share of its observed days carry a quality flag, and each such exclusion names the rule as its reason. Each listed pan coefficient is fitted with each set of bounds and objective, every fit with the split-sample and dry → wet tests, by a search (seed, starts, model runs) that is part of the rules too. The fit kept is the one with the best score on a held-out test, never the in-sample score, among those whose natural MAR is inside the WR2012 band (when there is a reference) and whose parameters are in the typical range. If none passes, none is kept, and the reasons are listed. Choose the objectives and the selection score by what the fit will feed, as for any fit: KGE′ for the overall water balance, a low-flow-sensitive score for EWR and licensing decisions. The server runs the saved rules, one background job per fit, and computes every score itself. Applying the kept fit is the server’s too: it saves the parameters with a record of the rules and every fit tried, runs the model and, when the rules say so, the uncertainty ensemble around the fit. Each change to the rules raises their revision, and a fit made under an older revision can’t be applied, so a rule can’t be adjusted once its result is seen. The rules can also run by themselves when new data arrives, and apply their fit while signed off. The default rules are drafts until the hydrologist signs them off: they type their name as a signature, and saving dates it and records their account in the History tab. A fit picked under draft rules is marked as not evidence.

entries.title: Selection score (which fit the rules keep)
aliases: keep the fit with the best
entries.summary: The one score, on one held-out test, that every fit the rules try is compared on. The best passing fit is kept. Match it to the use.
entries.text: “Keep the fit with the best … on the held-out test” is what picks the kept fit. Every fit the rules try (each pan coefficient × bounds × objective) is scored on this one score, on this one test, so fits made with different objectives are compared on common ground; the best that passes the filters is kept, the first on a tie. It is never an in-sample score: a fit whose record doesn’t allow the chosen test isn’t kept, rather than falling back to its score on the fitted days. The tests are those every fit runs. Dry → wet (the default) fits on the driest half of the water years and scores the wettest half. Split-sample fits on the first half of the scored days and scores the second. The other observed record scores the fit against the second instrument (the logger when the fit used the gauge), so it needs both records. Match the score to the use, as you would the objective: the default, KGE′ on the dry → wet test, for the overall water balance; for EWR or licensing decisions a low-flow-sensitive score (the mean of KGE′(Q) and KGE′(1/Q), or the non-parametric KGE when the low-flow rating is uncertain) on the dry → wet test. Decide it with the rules, before any fit is seen; changing it afterwards is a rule change, with a new revision.

entries.title: Flagged-year exclusion rule
entries.summary: Leaves a whole water year out of every fit when more than this share of its observed days carry a quality flag. Default 20 %. (%)
entries.text: Over the calibration window and outside the stored exclusions, each water year’s share of its observed days that carry a quality flag (above or below the gauged range, suspect or infilled) is counted. A year above the share is left out of every fit the rules make, on top of the project’s own calibration exclusions, with a reason that names the rule and the count, for example “200 of 365 observed days flagged (54.8 %), more than 20 %”. Inside the years kept, the quality flags’ own treatments still decide which days are scored. Untick it to leave no year out by rule.

entries.title: Filters a kept fit must pass
entries.summary: A fit is only kept if its natural MAR is inside the WR2012 band and its parameters are in the typical range. If none passes, none is kept.
entries.text: Natural MAR inside the WR2012 band: the simulated natural MAR with the fitted parameters must sit inside the calibration penalty’s MAR band when both ends are set, otherwise within the WR2012 check’s query threshold. Without a WR2012 reference the filter can’t be applied, and the report says so rather than failing every fit. Parameters in the typical range: every fitted parameter inside Perrin et al.’s (2003) 80 % range, the typical bounds. Both are on by default. A fit that fails either isn’t kept, whatever its score, and the report lists why. If no fit passes, none is kept: change the rules, not the result.

entries.title: Calibration rules on new data
entries.summary: What happens when new observed or rain data arrives: nothing (default), run the rules and keep the report, or also apply the kept fit.
entries.text: When new days of observed flow or rain arrive (an upload, a feed or an ingest), the server can run the saved calibration rules by itself, at most once per debounce. “Run the rules and keep the report” leaves the result for an editor to apply. “Run the rules and apply the kept fit” also saves the kept fit and runs the model, but only while the rules are signed off; under draft rules it only reports. The tick box beside it decides what applying a kept fit does next: run the model with it and the uncertainty ensemble around it, centred on the fit’s bounds and objective, so the range of results from parameter sets that fit nearly as well comes with every new fit.

entries.title: Fit record
entries.summary: What “Apply to form” stores with fitted parameters: how the fit was made and how it scored on days it never saw.
entries.text: The record keeps the runoff model, objective, bounds, seed, starts, model runs per fit, calibration window, exclusions, the record fitted to, the forcing (pan coefficient, A-pan, CHIRPS bias correction and the rain-gap settings), the engine version and the time, with every score: the in-sample fit and the split-sample, dry → wet and independent-record validation. The same inputs, engine version and seed give the same fit, so anyone can reproduce it. Each run keeps the record in effect, so its results show which fit produced their parameters. Change a fitted parameter by hand and the record is marked “Parameters edited since fit”: it no longer describes them. Change the forcing and it is marked “Forcing changed since fit”: GR4J’s parameters are only valid for the evaporation and rain they were fitted under. The in-sample score is the fit to the calibration period; judge the parameters by the validation scores.

entries.title: Catchment area (rain)
entries.summary: Area, in km², that rain falls on (mm to m³). Empty = the units’ summed areas, which a run always uses once a unit has land. (km²)
entries.text: Each hydrological unit makes its runoff over its own area (Per unit, the only method), so once a unit has land the units’ areas are the catchment’s and this override is not used: the run warns if it is set and differs. It applies only to a model with no unit with land. 1 mm over 1 km² = 1 000 m³.

entries.title: Rain threshold
entries.summary: Daily rain at or below this (mm) doesn’t reduce irrigation demand. GR4J uses all the rain. The workbook’s default is 2 mm. (mm)
entries.text: Filters out drizzle that the soil absorbs, so it doesn’t reduce irrigation demand (“Rain threshold for demand”). GR4J uses all the rain. The workbook’s default, and a new project’s, is 2 mm. In the legacy runoff model (removed in engine 1.0.0) the same thresholded rain also drove runoff (quirk Q6).

entries.title: Base flow
entries.summary: The slow, groundwater-fed part of river flow that recedes gradually between storms, in m³/day. (m³/day)
entries.text: GR4J has no separate base-flow store: its routing store carries most of the storm flow too. Where the app needs base flow (Low flows judged on) it separates it from the flow with the Lyne–Hollick filter. The Base flow column of a daily table belongs to a legacy run (engine < 1.0.0): there base flow receded day by day along the recession curve, and a big enough rain pulse reset it to the pulse size.

entries.title: Legacy runoff model
entries.summary: The workbook’s rain → peak → recession routine, removed in engine 1.0.0. Runs made with it still open, labelled, but can’t be re-run.
entries.text: The workbook’s empirical model: rain above the threshold made a peak a · rain^b × catchment area × a summer or winter factor (a summer month, or a winter month before a big storm switched it to winter response), which then receded along a recession curve, next to a slowly receding base flow. The engine audit found that it does not conserve water: one small storm could return several times its own volume as flow, so it was never evidence and engine 1.0.0 removed it. Runs made with it before then still open read-only, badged “Workbook comparison”: they can be compared and exported, but not re-run, nominated as evidence, signed or published. Their daily table keeps the model’s own columns (summer flag, rain flow, response flow, base flow). A project still set to it runs GR4J, with a warning to check the GR4J parameters.

entries.title: EWR (Environmental Water Requirement)
entries.summary: The flow that must stay in the river to keep the ecosystem in its target condition. (m³/day)
entries.text: In South Africa the National Water Act’s term is the Reserve: its ecological part, often called the ecological Reserve, is the water kept to protect aquatic ecosystems (the other part is basic human needs). Older studies call it the IFR (instream flow requirement). It is derived per river for an ecological category, typically with the Desktop Reserve Model. This model checks every day whether the simulated flow meets it.

entries.title: Pragmatic EWR
entries.summary: The workbook’s simplification: one fixed m³/day per month at the outlet, instead of a requirement that varies with wetness. (m³/day per month)
entries.text: Reserve tables vary the requirement with how wet the month is, which is hard to plan for on a farm. The Water Balance Tool workbook instead picks one value per month — typically a percentile of the Reserve flows without high flows, converted to m³/day — so farmers know in advance how much to leave in the river. Enter the 12 monthly values, Oct … Sep. The catchment value is checked at the outflow gauge and split into per-unit shares by each unit’s natural MAR share; each gauge is checked against the shares of everything upstream of it.

entries.title: Hydrological unit EWR share
entries.summary: The unit’s part of the pragmatic EWR (EWR × its natural MAR share), added up down the river to give the EWR each point must pass. (m³/day)
entries.text: The daily series is the cumulative EWR: the hydrological unit’s own share plus the cumulative EWR of the elements directly upstream, as the workbook’s Element sheets compute it (quirk Q4). A gauge is checked against the same sum, and the outflow gauge against the full EWR. Who is charged for a shortfall is the EWR charge, not a hydrological unit’s own share.

entries.title: EWR shortfall
entries.summary: How far flow falls below the EWR on a day (negative = not met), in m³/day. Zero when the EWR is met. (m³/day)
entries.text: At the outflow gauge it is simulated outflow minus the pragmatic EWR on days it falls short; at a gauge, the flow there minus the EWR of everything upstream. Who is charged for it is the EWR charge.

entries.title: EWR charge
entries.summary: A hydrological unit’s share of the EWR shortfall at the EWR sites below it, pro rata to its net impact that day. (m³/day, shown as a positive volume charged (negative in the daily series))
entries.text: The EWR is assessed at EWR sites: the outlet and every gauge marked as an EWR site (the default). On a day a site is short by D, each hydrological unit upstream of it has a net impact e = inflow + runoff + transfers − outflow (its consumptive use, storage gain and exports; a transfer counts only when it leaves the site’s catchment). The hydrological units are charged D in proportion to the positive impacts, but never more than the sum of those impacts: the rest is natural, because natural flow was already below the EWR. A hydrological unit that added water that day (a dam release, return flow) is neither charged nor credited. A hydrological unit above several sites carries the largest of its charges, not the sum, because a cut upstream raises the flow at every site below it; the site that sets it is its binding site, stored with the run each day (engine 1.5.0). A hydrological unit short on its own reach is not charged while every EWR site is met. Add gauges at the Reserve determination’s EWR sites to protect upstream reaches. A cut can be taken up by a dam between two nested sites; only a re-run with the cuts applied shows that. The curtailment report uses the charge (engine 0.17.0). Before, it used the reach shortfall, which could charge a hydrological unit more than it took or for low flow nobody caused. Decided on a simulated CMA-assessor recommendation (2026-09-24), pending the real assessor and hydrologist. Every table and export shows the charge as a positive volume charged (m³/day), and its irrigate-less and store-less parts the same way; the changes it asks for (supply cut, total change) are negative, a reduction. Only the daily series (ewr_charge, ewr_charge_irrigation) keep the workbook’s sign, negative on a day with a charge.

entries.title: Irrigate less / store less
entries.summary: The EWR charge split by what the hydrological unit can change: its irrigation, or its storage and pass-through. (m³/day; l/s)
entries.text: For a hydrological unit charged A on a day, c = supplied − return flow is its consumptive irrigation and o = e − c the rest of its impact (storage gain and net export). The irrigation part is A × c ÷ (c + max(o, 0)); the rest is “store less / pass inflow”. A hydrological unit with no irrigation therefore gets no irrigation cut: its charge is a storage or release condition. The supply cut that removes the irrigation part is irrigation part ÷ (1 − r), with r the return flow (the share of the water supplied that comes back to the river, at most 1 − the irrigation efficiency): cutting supply by ΔG removes ΔG × (1 − r) of consumptive use, since the returned water comes back to the river.

entries.title: Equitable share of supply (fairness benchmark)
entries.summary: Σ supplied ÷ Σ demand: the share of its demand each hydrological unit would get if supply were shared in proportion. Not an allocation. (% of demand; m³/day)
entries.text: Over the reporting window, the catchment supplied this share of the total demand. A hydrological unit’s equitable share volume is that same share of its own demand, and “above (−) / below (+) equitable share” is that volume minus what it was supplied. The differences cancel across the hydrological units. It is a fairness benchmark only: it assumes water can move freely between hydrological units, and ignores where a hydrological unit sits in the network, its storage, licensed or registered volumes and existing lawful use. A positive value is not water the hydrological unit can get: a surplus downstream can’t reach a hydrological unit upstream. Not an allocation or licence condition. Under the National Water Act, sharing in a shortage runs through authorisations (s43 compulsory licensing; Schedule 3 item 6 restrictions, which DWS gazettes as % limits on authorised use per sector). A network-aware allocation based on licensed or registered volumes is future work; model demand is not an entitlement, and raising crop factors or areas raises a hydrological unit’s benchmark.

entries.title: Demand left
entries.summary: Share of a hydrological unit’s demand left to irrigate once supply is shared fairly and the EWR supply cut is made. (% of demand)
entries.text: Volume left ÷ demand, where the volume left is the equitable share minus the EWR supply cut, and never below 0. Shown as a whole %: “no demand” for a hydrological unit without demand, “—” when demand is under 1 m³/day (a % of almost nothing isn’t meaningful), and “<1%” or “>99%” at the ends so neither rounds to 0 or 100. The summary CSV keeps the exact value and a demand_pct_note column. When the EWR supply cut is larger than the hydrological unit’s equitable share, the volume left is 0 and the table flags “EWR cut exceeds this hydrological unit’s equitable share”. The workbook labels this column “reduction of demand required”, but it is the share left.

entries.title: Curtailment targets (total change)
aliases: to balance and meet the EWR
entries.summary: How much each hydrological unit’s supply would change to share water fairly and meet the EWR. Negative = reduce. Not a restriction. (m³/day; l/s)
entries.text: The curtailment table reads the run over its reporting window, as daily averages, one row per hydrological unit: its demand and what it was supplied; its equitable share volume and how far its supply sits above (−) or below (+) it; its EWR charge, split into irrigating less and storing less or passing inflow, with the supply cut that meets the irrigation part; and the total change, which also removes that cut. Negative means reduce. The volume left, and the demand left as a share of demand, never go below 0, nor below the unit’s basic-needs floor. Units that must cut are highlighted; 1 l/s = 86.4 m³/day. Other water users are listed apart, by priority, with what they took and returned, their EWR charge, their supply cut and the charge left standing. The EWR sites table gives each site’s days not met and shortfall, and how much of it was charged to the units upstream and how much was natural. These are model targets for discussion, not official restrictions or allocations: only a notice from a body with the legal power to make one, such as the responsible authority or the WUA, is.

entries.title: Share the pain
entries.summary: Each group’s supply as a share of its own demand in two steps: what it got, and what is left once its EWR charge is met. (% of demand)
entries.text: The board above the curtailment table reads the same window in two steps, each as a share of the group’s own demand: 1. Today, what it was supplied, and 2. EWR met, what is left once each unit’s EWR charge is met (between 0 and 100 %). The equitable share is one sentence above it, not a step: every unit would get the same share of its demand, the same water in total as today, shared equally. When the units’ total demand is too small, the board says the share means nothing. Other water users have their own rows, outside the equitable share, each marked priority (not curtailed) or non-priority (curtailed). Every figure is the curtailment table’s; the board only lays them side by side. Runs & results shows it; the printable report doesn’t.

entries.title: Report PDF
entries.summary: Download PDF prints the page in your browser; Generate PDF has the server print the same pages, to download or by email.
entries.text: Download PDF on a report prints the page with your browser’s own print dialog (choose Save as PDF); a Chromium-based browser also prints the running footer on every page. Generate PDF and Email me the PDF queue the same report for the server, which prints the same pages to A4 in a headless browser; the bar follows the job until the PDF is ready to download, or emails you the link. The link needs you to sign in, and a generated PDF is kept for 7 days. On the Project page, Scheduled reports emails the latest run’s report PDF to chosen members every week or month, sent as the editor who last saved the schedule. A report PDF is not evidence on its own: it isn’t hashed or registered anywhere. An evidence pack’s PDF is, and the verify page shows its hash.

entries.title: Reach shortfall (workbook AB)
entries.summary: The workbook’s incremental shortfall: a hydrological unit’s shortfall minus those directly upstream. A diagnostic only. (m³/day)
entries.text: MIN(AA − Σ AA of the elements directly upstream, 0), as the workbook’s Element sheets compute it. It shows where along the river the flow falls below the accumulated EWR, but it does not add up to the outlet shortfall, never credits a hydrological unit that adds water, and can charge a hydrological unit for a reach the next hydrological unit makes good. From engine 0.17.0 it no longer drives curtailment: the EWR charge does.

entries.title: Days EWR not met
entries.summary: Outlet: days flow was below the EWR. A hydrological unit: days it was charged for a shortfall at an EWR site below it. Also as a share. (days; fraction 0–1)
entries.text: The headline measure of how often the river fails. Look at when the failures happen, too: a few summer weeks every year differ from a multi-year drought. For a hydrological unit it counts the days the hydrological unit was charged for a shortfall at an EWR site below it (engine 0.17.0; before, the days its reach shortfall was below 0).

entries.title: EWR rule table (the Reserve’s assurance rules)
entries.summary: The Reserve’s EWR as a table: per month, the flow required at each assurance level, read at the natural flow’s percentile. (Mm³ per month or m³/s; % points 0–100)
entries.text: A South African Reserve determination (the Desktop Reserve Model and its revised form) gives the ecological water requirement as a table: for each month, the flow required at each assurance level, or “% point” (10 %, 20 % … 90 %, 99 %). Assurance is the share of time the flow should be equalled or exceeded, so 10 % is the requirement in wet conditions and 99 % the drought flow. The gazette pairs it with the natural flow at the same points. Enter one table per EWR site: the outlet, or a gauge placed at the determination’s EWR site. Say where it comes from, the hydrological unit (Mm³ per month, or the month’s mean m³/s), whether it is the total flow or low flows only, and where the natural-flow percentile comes from: the run’s own natural flow at the site (ranked among the same month in every year of the run), or the table’s natural flows. The scale multiplies every value, for a table given for a larger or smaller catchment than the site. Paste the 12 month rows from a spreadsheet or a PDF, with the heading row of % points if you have it; month names in the first column put rows in order. The table adds a monthly compliance report. The pragmatic EWR drives the daily EWR charge and curtailment unless the Settings choice “EWR charge follows” is set to the rule tables. The outlet’s table is a separate input from the daily EWR’s percentile tables, even when both come from one .rul: monthly compliance reads the table, the daily EWR its own tables, and a gazetted table beside a desktop .rul is a legitimate pair. When the outlet’s grids are the same as the daily EWR’s .rul tables shown above them, they fold under one line saying so (the REC and the other fields stay shown, and the fold opens to edit them); when they differ, a line says which reads which.

entries.title: Monthly compliance with the Reserve rules
entries.summary: Share of months whose simulated flow met the Reserve rule table’s requirement for that month’s natural condition. (share of months; Mm³; months)
entries.text: For each complete calendar month, the month’s natural flow at the EWR site (the upstream hydrological units’ runoff, before any dam or abstraction) is placed on that month’s natural flow duration curve. The EWR is read from the rule table at the same % point, interpolated between points, and the month is met when the simulated flow at the site is at least that. A naturally dry month is held to the drought flow; a wet one to more. The requirement depends only on natural flow, so more abstraction can only lose months. The report gives the share of months met (the headline), per month of the year, the deficit volume, the longest run of consecutive months not met and the FDC check: whether the simulated flow duration curve of each month lies on or above the EWR curve at each % point. Days below the pragmatic EWR stay alongside as a second measure. With fewer than 10 years of a month the percentiles are coarse, and the run says so. The daily series ewr_rule is each month’s requirement per day.

entries.title: Maintenance and drought low flows
entries.summary: The low-flow part of the Reserve: the base flow a river needs in normal years (maintenance) down to the least it needs in a drought. (Mm³ per month or m³/s)
entries.text: The Desktop Reserve Model gives two assurance tables for a site: the total flow (low flows plus high flows) and the low flows alone, each per month at the 10 % … 99 % points. The low flows fall from the maintenance low flow at the wetter points to the drought low flow at 99 %. Enter the low-flow table beside a total-flow table and each month is judged twice at the same natural percentile: against the total and against the low flows. A month that meets its low flows but not the total failed only its high flows (the heat map shows ◐); one below its low flows (●) is the more serious failure. The difference between the two requirements is the month’s high-flow part. As a provisional default, not yet confirmed by the catchment’s hydrologist: both are judged on the month’s total flow volume, unless the Settings choice “Low flows judged on” is set to base flow.

entries.title: High flows: freshets and floods
entries.summary: Reserve high-flow events: a peak flow held for some days, a number of times each water year, in given months. (m³/s; days; events per water year)
entries.text: Reserve determinations ask for high flows as well as low flows: small freshets that reset the riverbed and cue fish to spawn, and larger floods that scour pools and reach the floodplain. Each component here is a name, the months it may peak in, a peak (m³/s, daily mean), the event’s duration in days from the rise to the end of the recession (not days held at the peak), and how many such events a water year needs. The check runs on every complete water year at the site. An event is a run of days at or above half the peak that reaches the peak, first in one of the months, and lasts at least half the duration: what a flood hydrograph of that peak and duration, drawn as a triangle, spends above half its peak. Two peaks count as two events only if the flow falls below half the peak between them. A year is asked for no more events than the site’s natural flow had that year: a dry year that would have had no flood is not failed for it, while a dam that holds back a flood the river would have had is. The table’s scale multiplies the peak too.

entries.title: What the EWR charge follows
entries.summary: The daily pragmatic EWR (default; provisional, not hydrologist-confirmed), or at a site with a rule table the month’s requirement. (m³/day)
entries.text: The EWR charge (each hydrological unit’s share of the shortfall at the EWR sites below it) and the curtailment it sets follow a daily requirement at each site. By default that is the pragmatic EWR, as in the Water Balance Tool workbook. Set it to the Reserve rule tables and, at a site with a rule table, each complete calendar month’s requirement from the table (the one the monthly compliance report judges, the daily series ewr_rule) becomes the daily requirement for that month’s days. A site without a table, and a part month at either end of the run, keep the pragmatic EWR, and the run says how many days that was. The EWR required and met at each site (under the EWR by month grid on EWR) follow the same choice. The shortfall the charge followed at such a site is the daily series ewr_charge_shortfall; the pragmatic EWR, its days not met and the observed-record agreement stay as they are. Which the charge should follow is a question for the hydrologist and the assessor, so the pragmatic EWR stays the default.

entries.title: How the EWR is split between units
entries.summary: Each unit’s EWR share is its natural MAR ÷ the units’ total, from its own GR4J runoff. (fraction 0–1 (shown as %))
entries.text: The EWR at the outlet is shared out between the hydrological units, and each unit’s share is its own EWR requirement: the EWR sites below it add the shares of everything above them, and the EWR charge, curtailment, hands-off EWR flows and the drought restriction’s EWR trigger all read those requirements. It is shared one way only: by each unit’s natural MAR. A unit’s natural MAR is its own GR4J natural runoff from its own rain, over the run’s complete water years (October to September), or the whole run when it has none, never a forecast’s days; its share is that ÷ the units’ total, so the shares add up to 100 %. A wetter unit carries more of the EWR than its area alone would give it. Because each site adds the shares above it, the requirement at a site follows the natural MAR of everything upstream of it. The shares come from the units’ own runoff (Per unit, each unit’s rainfall station, its MAP or CHIRPS). A unit with no rain of its own runs on the catchment rain, so its share follows its area; the run names those units, and so do Run readiness and Model settings. The run records each unit’s share in its summary. The MAR period is a provisional choice, pending the hydrologist. Before engine 1.105.0 this was a choice, the flow share by default; older runs keep the split they ran with. Engines 1.105.0 to 1.108.x also offered Fragmentation, where the same shares split one catchment GR4J run’s flow; it was retired in engine 1.109.0.

entries.title: The daily EWR at the outlet
entries.summary: Where the outlet’s daily EWR comes from: the pragmatic EWR, the DRM TAB file, or the DRM percentile tables, scaled to the model. (m³/s in the tables; m³/day in the run)
entries.text: The outlet’s daily EWR is what every day is judged by: it is split between the hydrological units by each unit’s natural MAR, and the shortfalls, the EWR charge, curtailment and the compliance grid all follow it. It can come from one of three places. The pragmatic EWR (the default): one flow per month, as in the Water Balance Tool workbook. The DRM TAB file: the Desktop Reserve Model summary’s monthly “Total Flows, Maint.”, entered in m³/s (a .tab file’s Mm³ a month are converted over each month’s days, February 28), the same flow every day of the month. The DRM percentile tables: the rule-curve (.rul) output’s natural duration curves and a Reserve table at the ten % points, either the total Reserve flows (the file’s first table, with high flows; the default) or the Reserve flows without high flows, your choice; loading a .rul fills all three tables. Each day, the natural flow at the outlet (net of the natural bed losses when they are on) picks its place in that month’s natural flows, and the chosen Reserve flow is read there, interpolated between points, held at the wettest point above it and scaled with the flow below the driest. The other Reserve table is kept and shown, and drives nothing. The tables are usually for a larger catchment than the model, so every value is multiplied by a scale factor: the modelled area ÷ the table’s area (the default for a new source), or the model’s natural MAR at the outlet ÷ the table’s MAR. Settings shows the tables scaled to the model under the ones you entered, once the factor is known. Each run works its factor out from its own natural flow, says in its warnings and summary which EWR it was judged by, and shows the tables as it read them under its summary. The file you load is kept with the values it gave, for the record: the whole .tab (its header, the annual flows, the IFR summary and the monthly table, all seven columns, with the column the TAB flows are marked) and the .rul’s name, date, unit and Recommended Ecological Category. No run reads them. If you change a TAB flow after loading, Settings says the file is shown as it was loaded.

entries.title: Low flows judged on
entries.summary: The month’s total flow (default, the hydrologist’s choice), or its base flow (a one-pass digital filter), so a flood can’t hide low flows. (Mm³ per month or m³/s)
entries.text: A low-flow requirement (a table that covers low flows only, or the low-flow part of a total-flow table) is judged against one figure for the month. By default that is the month’s total flow volume, so a month with a flood can pass its low flows even though the river ran short the rest of the month. Set it to base flow and the month is judged on its base flow instead: the simulated flow at the site with the quick flow taken out by the Lyne–Hollick digital filter, run once forward with α = 0.995, as Hughes, Hannart & Watkins (2003) separate daily flows in the study that recalibrated the Desktop Reserve Model’s base-flow parameters (α 0.995 is the value found for daily flows in most South African catchments; up to 0.997 in some). Earlier engine versions ran the filter three times, forward, backward and forward, which gives less base flow. The total-flow requirement is still judged on the month’s total flow, and the natural-flow percentile still comes from the natural flow. The catchment’s hydrologist judges the low flows on the total flow (2026-10-10), so it stays the default.

entries.title: Plausibility checks
entries.summary: Six checks a reviewing hydrologist makes on a run (fewer on older runs): they only warn, and never change a result.
entries.text: Every run makes six checks and shows them in the Plausibility checks panel on Calibration, in its warnings and in the summary CSV: 1. natural flow is at least the observed flow plus the modelled net abstraction, in every water year; 2. EWR days not met, split between good-rain years (rain mostly from the catchment station) and fallback-rain years (mostly CHIRPS, forecast, spread or blank days); 3. the double-mass curve of observed flow against rain, to tell new use upstream from a failing gauge; 4. dry-season low-flow duration curves of the gauge, the logger and the model, overlaid with the latest run of each other runoff model; 5. recession diagnostics: how fast the record and the model fall in rain-free spells (runs from engine 1.19.0); 6. hydrological signatures: base-flow index by two filters, the low-flow duration curve’s slope and bias, and the skill on held-out recessions (runs from engine 1.55.0). The dry season is the six calendar months in a row with the lowest mean flow: from the calibration record, else the other observed record, else the simulated natural flow. The thresholds are fixed in the engine, for the hydrologist to confirm.

entries.title: Natural flow ≥ observed + abstraction
entries.summary: Observed flow plus what the network took out upstream is the natural flow the record implies; it can’t exceed the simulated natural flow. (Mm³ per water year)
entries.text: On each water year of the calibration record (300 or more observed days, calibration exclusions left out), the observed volume O plus the modelled net abstraction A rebuilds the natural flow the record implies. A is natural flow less the simulated outflow, from the network’s own water balance, split into use net of return flows (irrigation, other users, boreholes), dams (storage gained plus evaporation less rain on the dam) and land cover. A year fails when O + A exceeds the simulated natural flow by more than 10 % of the observed volume, the annual error of a well-rated gauging weir (at least 1 % of the record’s mean volume, so a near-dry year doesn’t fail on noise). Since A is natural less simulated outflow, that is the same as the simulated outflow falling short of the observed by that much. A failing year points to natural flow simulated too low (rain, parameters), abstraction over-estimated, or a problem in the record that year.

entries.title: Good-rain and fallback-rain years
entries.summary: EWR days not met, split by whether the water year’s rain came mostly from the catchment station or from fallback rain.
entries.text: A day’s rain is a station reading when the catchment rain series has a value the run used as recorded. It is fallback rain when bias-corrected CHIRPS or forecast rain filled it (a blank day, a zero run treated as missing, a listed missing period, a reading set aside after a blank outage), when a multi-day accumulation was spread onto it, or when nothing filled it and it ran dry. A water year is a fallback-rain year when more than half its rain, or more than half its days, were fallback; every other year is a good-rain year. The panel gives the share of days the outlet EWR was not met in each group and, with a Reserve rule table, the share of months met. The run warns when the groups differ by 10 percentage points or more: part of the EWR result may then come from the rain source rather than the river. It can also be real climate, such as a station out of action through a drought.

entries.title: Double mass: observed flow vs rain
entries.summary: Cumulative observed flow against cumulative rain: a kink means the catchment’s use or the gauge changed.
entries.text: While the catchment, its development and the gauge stay the same, cumulative observed flow plotted against cumulative catchment rain is a straight line; its slope is the runoff ratio. The check uses the calibration record’s water years with 300 or more days having both flow and rain and at least 100 mm of rain (10 such years or no result), and finds breaks as the rain-vs-CHIRPS double-mass check does. The runoff ratio falls in a run of dry years on its own, so each break is compared with the simulated outflow over the same days, which has the same rain and fixed development. A change the model shows too is the rain’s. A fall the dry season takes more of points to new use upstream (abstraction and filling dams take a larger share of low flows); a fall the wet season takes more of, or a rise, points to the gauge (a rating change, or floods bypassing or drowning the weir). It is a hint: check the gauge’s records and the development history.

entries.title: Dry-season low-flow duration curve
entries.summary: The flow duration curve of dry-season days only, for the gauge, the logger and each model’s simulated flow. (m³/s)
entries.text: Each curve gives the flow equalled or exceeded on a share of the dry-season days (Q90: 90 % of them). The gauge and the logger are drawn dashed, each on its own days; the simulated outflow and natural flow cover every dry-season day of the run, and the latest run of each other runoff model is drawn beside them when it used the same dry season. "Simulated outflow over" switches the model’s curve to one record’s days only, for a like-for-like comparison. The run warns when, on the calibration record’s dry-season days, the simulated Q90 is more than twice or less than half the observed. Low flows are where a gauge is least certain (±50–100 %), so a factor of 2 is beyond gauging error. Flows under 0.001 m³/s count as 0.001.

entries.title: Recession diagnostics
entries.summary: How fast flow falls in rain-free spells (−dQ/dt against Q), in the record and in the model on the same days. (m³/s; m³/s per day)
entries.text: After rain stops, a river falls at a pace set by how its catchment drains. The check picks those spells out of the calibration record: flow falling day after day for at least 5 days, with at most 1 mm of catchment rain on each day and the day before, starting the second day after the peak, and no missing, zero or excluded day. On each day it takes the rate of fall, −dQ/dt, and plots it against the flow Q on log–log axes, for the record and for the simulated outflow on the very same days, and fits a straight line to each: −dQ/dt = a·Q^b. b = 1 is a single linear store (an exponential recession); a larger b a store that drains faster when full. The run warns, as an indicative check, when the model recedes more than twice as fast or slow as the river at the observed points’ median flow, or when b differs by more than 0.5, which points to the routing and groundwater parameters (GR4J X2 and X3) or to abstraction in dry spells. With fewer than 8 spells the fit is too thin to judge, and the run says so instead. The segment rules and the rate estimate (exponential time stepping) follow the TOSSH toolbox’s defaults.

entries.title: Hydrological signatures
entries.summary: Base-flow index by two filters, the low-flow duration curve’s slope and bias, and skill on held-out recessions. (ratio; %)
entries.text: The calibration statistics say how closely the model follows the river day by day. These three signatures ask something else: does the model behave like the river in dry weather, where the water in a dry season comes from? They compare the record the calibration statistics score (the headline calibration location’s) with the simulated outflow on the same days. They only report and warn; none changes a result. Base-flow index (BFI): the share of the river’s flow that is base flow, the slow drainage from groundwater and soils that keeps a river running between rains, as against quick flow straight after rain. 0.6 means 60 % of the water arrived as base flow. Nobody measures base flow, so a filter separates it from the flow record, and two filters are used: the one South African Reserve work uses (Hughes, Hannart & Watkins 2003: α 0.995, β 0.5, one forward pass) and Eckhardt’s (a 0.98 and a ceiling BFImax of 0.25, his value for perennial rivers on hard-rock aquifers). Each runs over every stretch of 30 or more recorded days, the record and the model over the same stretches. Eckhardt’s index can’t exceed its ceiling, so read it as a comparison between the record and the model, not as the river’s own index. A model whose BFI is too low dries up too fast after rain; too high, it holds its flow too long. The run warns when the two differ by more than 0.15 by either filter. Low end of the flow-duration curve: rank every day’s flow from high to low. Q70 is the flow exceeded on 70 % of days, Q95 the flow exceeded on 95 %, the river in a drought. The slope between them, ln(Q70 ÷ Q95) ÷ 0.25, says how steeply the flow falls away in the driest quarter of days: steep for a river that nearly stops, flat for one fed by steady groundwater. The table shows the observed and simulated slopes and the simulated slope’s bias in %. The low-flow volume bias (%BiasFLV, Yilmaz et al. 2008, the same measure the fit uses) looks at the lowest 30 % of days: how far each curve’s flows sit above its own lowest flow, on log flow, the model’s against the river’s. 0 is a match; the further from 0, either way, the less the model’s driest days look like the river’s. The run warns when either is beyond ±50 %. Skill on held-out recessions: a recession is a rain-free spell in which the river falls day after day. Every third one, in date order, is held out. On each held-out spell the simulated fall from its first day is scored against the river’s, as a skill against no fall at all: 1 is perfect, 0 no better than a flat line, below 0 worse. For comparison, the river’s own recession curve, fitted on the other spells only, is scored the same way (the Observed column): a model close to it recedes about as well as the river’s own law predicts. The model’s parameters were fitted on every scored day, the held-out spells included, so this is a check of shape, not a true blind test. With fewer than 8 spells there are too few to judge; with 8 or more, the run warns below 0. The limits are provisional, set in the engine for the hydrologist to confirm.

entries.title: EWR test against observed flow
entries.summary: Does the model fall below the EWR on the days the observed river did? A 2×2 table of observed days, with scores. (days; ratios)
entries.text: A gauge or logger measures the same river the outlet EWR test uses, so on each observed day the observed flow takes the test too. Hit rate: share of the river’s failures the model also has (1 ideal). False-alarm ratio: share of the model’s failures the river didn’t have (0 ideal). Frequency bias: the model’s share of days below the EWR ÷ the observed share (1 ideal). Use it to judge which runoff model’s EWR count to trust.

entries.title: Desktop Reserve Model
entries.summary: Software (“Desktop Version 2”) that produces monthly Reserve flow tables by percentile for a river’s ecological category.
entries.text: Its tables — with and without high flows, in M.m³ per month at the 10 %–99 % points — are the usual starting point for the pragmatic EWR.

entries.title: Ecological category
entries.summary: The A–F class of river condition; the Reserve is set for a target category of A–D (A = natural, F = critically modified).
entries.text: The higher the target category, the more flow the Reserve keeps in the river. A river’s present state can be E or F (seriously or critically modified), but those aren’t management targets: the lowest category a Reserve is set for is D.

entries.title: Catchment rainfall
entries.summary: Daily catchment-average rainfall in mm. The first choice for driving natural flow and effective rain. (mm/day)
entries.text: Each day the model uses the first available of catchment, CHIRPS and forecast rainfall. Missing days are left empty, not zero.

entries.title: Final catchment rainfall
entries.summary: The daily rainfall a run works from after filling gaps: catchment rain, else bias-corrected CHIRPS, else forecast rain, in mm. (mm/day)
entries.text: One value per day from the first source that has one. CHIRPS is the corrected value when the CHIRPS bias correction is on. Rain used is the same rain, with blanks as 0; the rain threshold only applies to irrigation demand. A day with no value from any source is left empty; the model treats it as dry. In the daily CSV export it sits beside CHIRPS as uploaded and bias-corrected CHIRPS, so the filled days can be checked against both.

entries.title: Drought index (SPI, SPEI)
entries.summary: How unusual the last 3, 6 or 12 months were, in standard deviations from the median: SPI from the rain, SPEI from rain less evaporation.
entries.text: The Summary’s Drought index card says how dry or wet the catchment has been, from the latest run’s own final catchment rainfall and potential evaporation, for the last whole month of its history (never a forecast day). • SPI (Standardized Precipitation Index): the rain over the last 3, 6 or 12 months, set against every other year’s total over the same months. A gamma distribution is fitted to each calendar month’s totals (zero totals counted apart), and the total’s probability under it is written as a standard normal value. • SPEI (Standardized Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index): the same for rain less potential evaporation, with a log-logistic distribution, so a hot dry spell reads drier than its rain alone. The usual classes: 2 or more extremely wet, 1.5 to 2 very wet, 1 to 1.5 moderately wet, between −1 and 1 near normal, −1 to −1.5 moderately dry, −1.5 to −2 severely dry, −2 or less extremely dry. Values are shown between −3 and 3. The distributions are fitted over 1991–2020 when the record has at least 25 of those 30 years in every calendar month, else over the whole record, and the card names the years. A calendar month needs at least 20 years to be fitted, so a shorter record has no index. A month with a missing day has no total, and no index covers it. SPEI needs the run’s potential evaporation, which only a GR4J run records. 3 months reads the season’s soil moisture and farm dams; 12 months reads the big dams and groundwater. The project list and the team page show the card’s headline, the driest index, as a badge beside each catchment. It is stored with each run, so a run saved before the badge existed shows a dash (“No drought index for this run”).

entries.title: CHIRPS rainfall
entries.summary: Satellite-and-station daily rainfall (Climate Hazards Group). Used on days without catchment rainfall. (mm/day)
entries.text: Useful to fill gaps or extend a short gauge record. At catchment scale CHIRPS can read well below (or above) a local gauge, so by default the model scales it by a factor per calendar month, fitted where both records have a reading, on the days it fills in (see CHIRPS bias correction).

entries.title: CHIRPS bias correction
entries.summary: Scales CHIRPS rain, on days it fills in for blank catchment rain, by a catchment ÷ CHIRPS factor for the calendar month.
entries.text: For each calendar month the factor is the catchment rain divided by the CHIRPS rain, summed over the days both have a reading. Suspect catchment rain is left out: a water year far below CHIRPS as a whole, and one by one the days of flagged zero runs, of periods listed as missing (see Zero-rain runs) and of multi-day accumulation windows (see Multi-day rain accumulations). Zero runs you keep dry stay in, as confirmed readings, unless CHIRPS reads a lot of rain over them; then that water year stays out and the run warns. A month with fewer than 90 shared days, or less than 50 mm of CHIRPS on them, uses the factor pooled over all months; with too little overlap for even that, CHIRPS is used as it is and the run says so. Factors are kept between 0.25 and 4. Only CHIRPS that is actually used is scaled. Catchment rain and forecast rain are never changed. Each run lists the factors and the number of days corrected in its warnings, and outputs the corrected CHIRPS (CHIRPS × its month's factor, on every day, not only the days it filled in) as a daily series beside CHIRPS as uploaded, with the day's monthly factor in the next column, in the series explorer and the daily CSV export. The run's summary CSV lists the 12 factors with their source (own month, pooled, or none) and the shared days behind each, then the water years and days left out of the fit and why. Comparing runs notes when the factors differ. Rain used shows which value the model took each day. Choose "Raw CHIRPS" only if the CHIRPS series you loaded is already corrected to the catchment; otherwise it would be corrected twice. Not in the workbook, which used raw CHIRPS.

entries.title: CHIRPS fit period
entries.summary: Which years the CHIRPS factors are fitted on: the whole record, or water-year ranges you list, each with a reason.
entries.text: When the double-mass check finds that the catchment / CHIRPS ratio changed part-way through the record, one set of factors fitted over every year is a blend of the eras, so a gap in one era is filled at the wrong ratio. The fit period decides which years the factors come from. Whole record (the default) fits one set over every year, as before. Listed water years fits one set per range you list, each only on its own years and each with a reason; years outside every range are left out of every fit, and a gap there takes the nearest range (the later one on a tie). Put each break where the station records or the CHIRPS version say it is. Propose from the double-mass breaks fills the list with one range per segment the check finds. It is only a proposal: the check's break years are estimates that can be a year or two off (the five-year minimum segment and dry years move them), and a break that is partly CHIRPS's (a product change, or drift against other products) moves them too. Check each range against the station history and rewrite its reason before saving. Split only when the step is large against the standard error of each era's ratio (its year-to-year scatter over the square root of the number of years), or a Pettitt or Buishand test calls it, not merely against the year-to-year scatter.
