Within each range the usual rules hold: a month needs 90 shared days and 50 mm of CHIRPS, else it takes its range's pooled factor, else the factor over all the listed ranges together; factors stay between 0.25 and 4. Periods listed as missing under Zero-rain runs, and flagged zero runs that CHIRPS fills, stay out of every fit. Each run names the range whose factors filled each gap and the years each set was fitted on; the summary CSV lists every range's factors; comparing runs notes a changed fit period, range or reference window; and a fit record flags "Forcing changed since fit" when the fit period changes. Not in the workbook.

entries.title: CHIRPS quantile map
entries.summary: Opt-in: gives the CHIRPS that fills gaps the catchment rain’s wet-day frequency and intensity, keeping each month’s total.
entries.text: A monthly factor fixes the level of CHIRPS but not its shape: a 0.05° cell is wet on more days than a gauge, with fewer heavy falls, and a runoff model turns heavy days into flow. With the quantile map on, the CHIRPS that fills a gap is reshaped too. It is fitted per calendar month on the same shared days as the factors (the fit period). Where CHIRPS × factor is wet (at or above the wet-day threshold, 1 mm by default) more often than the catchment rain, its own threshold is raised until the two wet-day rates agree; its wet days are then mapped, quantile by quantile, onto the catchment's wet days, its days below the threshold go dry, and every calendar month is scaled back to its factor-corrected total. So the frequency and the spread of the falls change, and the volume doesn't, month by month. A month with fewer than 30 wet days on either side uses its three-month season; a season too thin keeps the factor alone, and the run warns and names the months. A CHIRPS series drier than the catchment keeps the wet-day threshold: the map can't make wet days. It applies only with bias correction on, and it is off by default, so a run without it is unchanged. Each run lists what it mapped in its warnings and its summary CSV, outputs CHIRPS after the map as a daily series, and pins the fit with the factors; comparing runs and a fit record both flag a change. Not in the workbook.

entries.title: Gap-filling product
entries.summary: Which product fills blank catchment-rain days (CHIRPS, ERA5-Land, or both), and IMERG Late for the last few days, each on its own fit.
entries.text: Which product fills the days the catchment rain is blank. CHIRPS (the default) fills them as it always has. CHIRPS, then ERA5-Land where CHIRPS has none keeps CHIRPS and falls back to ERA5-Land only on a blank day CHIRPS has no value for. ERA5-Land instead of CHIRPS fills every blank day from ERA5-Land. ERA5-Land is the Copernicus reanalysis of the land surface at 0.1°, about 5 days behind; ERA5, which it reruns, matched South African gauges best of the open products day by day (daily r 0.57 against 0.25 for CHIRPS), most of all in winter frontal rain like the Western Cape's, where CHIRPS is weakest. IMERG Late (NASA's satellite rainfall, about 14 hours behind) can fill the last few days, before CHIRPS' first values appear: only days after the last reading of the product chosen above, never a gap inside the record. Each product, and each IMERG version, is corrected to the catchment rain on its own monthly fit, with the same minimum sample and limits as CHIRPS's; ERA5-Land also gets a 1 mm wet-day threshold and a quantile map, which take its drizzle away. Both come from our copy of the rain data over the CHIRPS feed's cells, on the feed's next fetch: a CHIRPS series no feed writes has none, and the run says so. Under a catchment rainfall station the setting isn't used. Each day's rain source says which product filled it (5 ERA5-Land, 6 IMERG Late, with its version), the run lists each product's days, factors and double-mass check, and the Data tab draws the products beside CHIRPS. Their credits go with their values everywhere. The choices are provisional, pending the hydrologist's review. Not in the workbook.

entries.title: Double mass: catchment rain vs CHIRPS
entries.summary: Cumulative catchment rain against cumulative CHIRPS: a kink means one record changed, e.g. a station opened, closed or moved.
entries.text: Two records of the same rain should keep a steady ratio, so cumulative catchment rain plotted against cumulative CHIRPS is a straight line. A kink means one of them changed: a rain gauge opened, closed or moved, the catchment average was built differently, or CHIRPS changed. The check adds up each water year on the days both have a reading (leaving out zero runs treated as missing and periods listed as missing), and needs 10 years with at least 300 such days and 100 mm of CHIRPS. It fits up to two breaks, each segment at least 5 years long, and reports a break only when the slope changes by 20 % or more and a statistical test (Pettitt, or the gain in fit) says it is more than one odd year. The chart shows the curve, the whole-record line (dashed) and the segments (solid), with each segment's slope, and below it how far the curve departs from the whole-record line each year. The check alone changes nothing: a break doesn't say which record is wrong, so the CHIRPS factors are fitted over the whole record unless Settings → Rain gaps → CHIRPS gap filling → Fit ranges lists water-year ranges to fit them on (it can propose ranges from these breaks for you to check). A run warns when CHIRPS fills gaps in a segment whose ratio differs by 20 % or more from the ratio of the factors that filled them, because those days may then run too wet or too dry; with listed ranges it names the range whose factors filled each gap. The run's summary CSV has the table.

entries.title: Zero-rain runs treated as missing
entries.summary: In long wet-season runs of zero catchment rain, days CHIRPS reads more than 2 mm on count as missing, and bias-corrected CHIRPS fills them.
entries.text: A zero is a reading, so a gap in the rain record exported as zeros stops CHIRPS filling it, and the catchment runs dry for weeks in its wettest months. The Data tab flags these runs: 60 or more zero days in the series' six wettest months. By default a run treats a flagged run's days as blank where CHIRPS saw rain, more than 2 mm (the threshold is a setting), so bias-corrected CHIRPS, then forecast rain, stand in, exactly as on any blank day. On a day CHIRPS reads 2 mm or less the gauge's 0 is kept as a dry day, since CHIRPS reports too many light-rain days; a day with no CHIRPS reading is still treated as blank. The rain series you uploaded is never changed. If the hydrologist confirms a flagged run was a real dry spell, add it under Keep dry: its days stay 0 mm, and they count in the CHIRPS factor fit as readings (a flagged run that is filled is left out of the fit day by day). If bias-corrected CHIRPS reads more than the larger of 50 mm and a quarter of the catchment's usual annual rain over a kept-dry run, the keep-dry looks doubtful: each run warns and leaves that water year out of the fit. Run as recorded keeps every flagged run dry, as the workbook does. Also treat as missing covers other bad periods whatever they read, such as the gap days inside a year that reads far below CHIRPS. Those days are also left out of the CHIRPS factor fit. Each run lists every period it filled, the rain that replaced it and any days with nothing to fill them, in its warnings and in the summary CSV. The daily column "Catchment rain treated as missing" is 1 on each day filled. Comparing runs lists any change to these settings. Not in the workbook.

entries.title: Gap filling of observed flow
entries.summary: Short gaps in a gauge or logger record interpolated, longer ones filled from another record × a fitted ratio; in a run only.
entries.text: A gauge or logger record has gaps: a flood took the logger, a download was missed. Calibration → Calibration record → Flow gaps can fill them, in a run only: the record you uploaded is never changed, and nothing is filled until you turn it on for a record. Interpolation fills a gap of up to a few days (5 by default) between the readings either side, on a log scale: a recession falls by a steady fraction a day, so a log-scale line follows it where a straight one would overstate the flow. A longer gap is never interpolated, because a flood inside it would be missed. From another record fills a longer gap (up to 60 days by default) from the other record on the same river (the logger for the gauge, or the reverse) or from the reference gauge on a neighbouring river, scaled by the ratio of the two records' totals on the days both have a reading. The donor is refused when they share fewer days than the minimum (365 by default) or their daily flows don't rise and fall together (a correlation below 0.5). A filled day is never higher than the highest the record itself ever measured. By default no statistic reads a filled day: the calibration scores, the fit, the EWR test on the observed record and the plausibility checks use measured days only, and the filled days are shown on the Data tab's chart, in the run's warnings, and in the daily columns "Observed flow gap fill" (1 = interpolated, 2 = from another record) and "Observed flow: filled gap days only". Each filled day is flagged infilled; to score them, set Infilled days to "Score as recorded" under the quality flags (one control for the fit and the run). A fit that scored filled days is flagged when the filling changes. Not in the workbook.

entries.title: Series source and unit
entries.summary: Where a series' values came from (a station, agency, file or feed) and the unit they were given in before the app converted them.
entries.text: Each series can say where its values came from: a DWS station number, the agency, the file, or the data feed that wrote it. The Upload form asks for it, and an editor can change it on the Data tab. The unit a file was given in (l/s, ML/day, cm …) and the factor that converted it to the unit the app stores (m³/s for flow, mm for rain) are recorded by the upload itself: a series stored in m³/s that was uploaded in l/s says so, which is how a thousandfold unit mistake is found. Days merged into a series that already has values keep the series' own source and unit. The model never reads either. A run records them with its inputs, so comparing runs says when a series now comes from somewhere else, and a fit records its calibration record's, so a fit is flagged when that record's source or unit changes.

entries.title: Multi-day rain accumulations
entries.summary: Several days of rain read on one day after blank days: the total is spread back over those blank days in proportion to CHIRPS.
entries.text: When nobody reads the rain gauge for a few days, the unread days are often left blank and the whole total entered on the day it was read. The total is right; the days are wrong: a dry spell, then one day far wetter than it was. Viney & Bates (2004) found these untagged accumulations throughout long daily records. A run flags a reading as an accumulation when it is at least 20 mm, follows 3 to 7 blank days of catchment rain, bias-corrected CHIRPS reads less than a quarter of it on that day and the days either side (CHIRPS can be a day early or late), and CHIRPS over the blank days (leaving out the day just before) reads at least half of it. The window is those blank days plus the reading day. Only blank days count (from engine 1.84.0): a day recorded as 0 is a reading, so it ends the run, and a large reading after days of 0 is real rain and stays on its day. Up to engine 1.83.0 days of 0 counted like blanks. A storm after unread days CHIRPS was dry over is left alone too. More than 7 blank days in a row is an outage (a logger down, or a gauge nobody read for weeks), and days listed as missing count as blank here: it is not a window's run. A reading of 20 mm or more straight after an outage, on a day CHIRPS was nearly dry after CHIRPS rained over the outage, could be the outage's rain or one day's, and the record can't say which. From engine 1.70.0 the run sets such a reading aside: CHIRPS fills its day as it fills the outage, it is left out of the CHIRPS factor fit, and the run warns, naming it. Spreading it would put weeks of CHIRPS rain under one reading; keeping it on its day would count an unread gauge's rain twice. Before 1.70.0 a blank stretch of any length counted towards the run, and such a reading was spread over the outage's last 92 days. By default the run keeps the recorded total and spreads it over the window in proportion to bias-corrected CHIRPS. Those days are not also filled from CHIRPS as blank days (which would count the rain twice), and they are left out of the CHIRPS factor fit. If CHIRPS reads no rain over a window at all, its total stays on the reading day. The rain series you uploaded is never changed. In Settings → Rain gaps → Flagged rain → Multi-day accumulations, Accumulated readings chooses between spreading (the default) and Run as recorded (one day), as the workbook does. Keep as recorded lists readings you know were one day's rain (a thunderstorm CHIRPS missed, or a logger back from a fault on a stormy day): a detection or a set-aside reading whose day falls in one stays as recorded, and counts in the CHIRPS fit. Also spread lists windows by hand, ending on the reading day: list the days an unread gauge’s total covers to spread a set-aside reading over them. A period listed as missing, or a keep-dry period, wins over a detection that touches it; listing an outage as missing doesn't stop the reading after it being set aside. Each run lists every window in its warnings and its summary CSV, and the daily column "Catchment rain from a multi-day accumulation" is 1 on each day spread. Comparing runs lists any change to these settings. Not in the workbook.

entries.title: Rain source periods
entries.summary: Dates when catchment rain comes from another gauge × monthly factors instead of the catchment series; its gaps take a named fallback.
entries.text: Use a rain-source period when the catchment series stops describing the catchment for a stretch of years (a gauge moved or closed, the average was rebuilt) and another gauge covers it, such as an in-catchment automatic station. Within the period, each day's rain is that gauge's reading × its month's factor; the catchment series is not used there and stays out of every factor fit. Factors. Normally 12 fixed values (Oct … Sep, 0.25–4) with where they came from: who fitted them, over which dates, and how. Or Fit: the gauge is scaled to the catchment series' level in a reference era you name, measured against a reference series that doesn't contain the gauge: factor = (catchment ÷ reference in the reference era) ÷ (gauge ÷ reference in the period). Use a gauge-free reanalysis such as ERA5 as the reference. CHIRPS is refused once you tick "CHIRPS ingests this gauge", because the fit would then be circular. Gaps. A day the gauge has no reading takes CHIRPS × the CHIRPS factors by default, or a named reanalysis × factors fitted on the catchment series over its own era; then forecast rain. With "CHIRPS ingests this gauge" ticked, name a reanalysis fallback. Daily intensity. A factor fixes the monthly volume, not how the rain falls: one automatic gauge has more intense days than an average of several gauges, and GR4J turns heavier days into more flow. Every run reports the share of the period's rain on heavy days (20 mm or more) against the catchment series' share in a reference era, and warns when they are more than 5 points apart. Tick "Quantile-map its wet days" to map the gauge's wet days (at or above the wet-day threshold, 1 mm by default) onto the catchment series' wet days over the water years you name, month by month (a month with fewer than 30 wet days on either side uses its three-month season; a season still that thin keeps the factor alone). Each month's total stays exactly what the factor gives, so the map changes the spread of the falls, not the volume, and not how many days are wet. Each run warns once per period with the day counts and factors, adds a daily "Rain source" column (0 catchment, 1 alternative gauge, 2 CHIRPS, 3 reanalysis, 4 forecast) and a block in its summary CSV, and comparing runs sets the periods side by side. A saved calibration is flagged "forcing changed since fit" when the periods change. Not in the workbook.

entries.title: Alternative catchment gauge
entries.summary: A second catchment rain record (mm/day), e.g. an in-catchment automatic station. Read only inside a rain-source period. (mm/day)
entries.text: Upload it as its own series kind. Outside every rain-source period (Settings → Rain gaps → Flagged rain → Rain source periods) the model never reads it. An automatic station often logs hourly: upload the hourly file and pick how to add it up into days. Manual gauges are read at 08:00 and the reading booked to the day before, so choose 08:00 to 08:00 to line it up with a manual record; the series records the choice. Its product and version (e.g. the station network) can be recorded with it.

entries.title: Reanalysis rainfall
entries.summary: A gauge-free gridded rain product such as ERA5 (mm/day): a reference for a rain-source fit, or the fallback for its gaps. (mm/day)
entries.text: ERA5's precipitation is a model forecast that assimilates no rain gauges outside the United States, so a local gauge change can't enter it: a good yardstick for scaling a replacement gauge to the catchment record's level. The model reads it only when a rain-source period names it. Free without an account from the Open-Meteo archive API.

entries.title: Daily A-pan evaporation
entries.summary: A daily Class-A pan record (mm/day), e.g. a nearby station: replaces the monthly A-pan means on the days it has a value. (mm/day)
entries.text: Upload it on the Data tab as its own series kind (mm, cm or inches, stored in mm). Where it has a value it is that day's A-pan for crop demand (A-pan × crop factor), dam evaporation (A-pan × lake factor) and, when GR4J's PE is pan coefficient × A-pan, the runoff model. Days without a value, with a negative value or outside the record use the monthly A-pan means (Settings → Demand), and each run says how many days did. A monthly PE row for GR4J replaces both for the runoff model only.

entries.title: Daily reference evapotranspiration
entries.summary: A daily FAO-56 reference ET record (mm/day): GR4J’s PE, as it stands, under a monthly PE row on the days it has a value. (mm/day)
entries.text: Set up an AgERA5 daily reference evapotranspiration data feed (Data → Data feeds) over the catchment's grid cells or a box around it, or upload a station's own daily ET₀ as this series kind. GR4J reads it only when its potential evaporation is a monthly PE row (Calibration → Flow calibration), such as the dPET climatology from the map: on each day the series has a value it is that day's PE as it stands, with no pan coefficient; every other day uses the row, and each run says how many days did. Under pan coefficient × A-pan it is not read, and the run says so. Crop demand and dam evaporation never read it: they keep A-pan. The feed reads our own copy of AgERA5 v2.0 (Copernicus, CC BY 4.0), about a week behind and copied a month at a time. For the newest days AgERA5 doesn't have yet it takes ET₀ we compute with FAO-56 Penman-Monteith from NASA POWER's daily weather (CC BY 4.0), and replaces those days with AgERA5's once its month lands. Adding or replacing the series after a GR4J fit marks the fit “Forcing changed since fit”.

entries.title: Forecast rainfall
entries.summary: Forecast daily rain in mm: fills gaps in the record, and runs past its end only in a forecast run, to look ahead a few days. (mm/day)
entries.text: Used on days neither catchment rain nor CHIRPS has a value. An ordinary run stops where the observed record ends, so forecast rain past it only reaches a forecast run, whose summaries leave those days out. Treat results on forecast days as indicative only.

entries.title: Observed flow
entries.summary: Measured flow at the outlet (gauge record, or a logger), in m³/s. Scores the calibration and the EWR test; it never drives the model. (m³/s)
entries.text: Converted to m³/day and compared with the simulated outflow on days both exist. The calibration record (Calibration → Calibration record, “Compare with”) picks which one; left on the default, the gauge record is used, else the logger, and a run with both says so in its warnings. With both records, the hydrograph shows both (engine 0.39.0): the calibration record as a solid line, labelled “calibration record”, and the other dashed. Only the calibration record is scored.

entries.title: Reference gauge (other catchment)
entries.summary: A gauge on another river: a regional wet/dry index. Runs never read it; Fit automatically ranks water years by it, never fits to it. (m³/s)
entries.text: A workbook’s gauge column may hold a record measured elsewhere, or one rescaled for part of its span. Such a record is not observed flow for the modelled river, so it is kept as its own series kind: runs never calibrate or validate against it, never compare it with the logger and never use it in the EWR comparison. Use it to rank wet and dry years: Fit automatically ranks the dry → wet test’s water years by it when it covers them. The importer stores it this way with --gauge-as-reference, and its scaling options undo a known rescaling.

entries.title: Date (daily preview)
entries.summary: One row per day, from the first day of the earliest loaded series to the last day of the latest. A blank cell means no reading.
entries.text: The rows come from the input series themselves, not from the simulation period: the table starts on the first day any loaded series has and ends on the last. Each series column shows its value for that day exactly as uploaded; a blank means that series has no reading that day, or the day is outside its period. A shaded value carries a data-check flag (negative, outlier or flat-line), found with the same rules as the Data checks, and screen readers read the flag with the value. The days read day first (1 Oct 2021). The search box narrows the rows by a date (2015, Mar 2015, 14 Mar 2015, or year first, 2015-03) or by a value in the visible series (> 20, = 0); Missing only and Flagged only keep the days where a visible series is blank or flagged. Lining every input up by day is the quickest way to see a gap in one record that another fills, or a spike only one instrument recorded.

entries.title: Flow in m³/day (daily preview)
entries.summary: The flow series’ m³/s value × 86 400: the unit the model works in, so the day reads directly against simulated flows. (m³/day)
entries.text: Flow records are uploaded in m³/s. The model converts them to m³/day (1 m³/s = 86 400 m³/day) before comparing them with the simulated outflow, which is in m³/day like every flow and volume inside the model. This column is that conversion, day by day, blank where the record has no reading. Use it to read an observed day against the daily results or the daily CSV export without converting by hand. For gauge or logger flow this is the value calibration and the EWR comparison score against, when that record is the one chosen under “Compare with”. A reference gauge on another river is converted the same way, but the model never reads it.

entries.title: Rain used (daily preview)
entries.summary: The rain the model runs on each day: catchment rain if it has a reading, else bias-corrected CHIRPS, else forecast rain. (mm/day)
entries.text: It is worked out with the same code a run uses, so it is the rain that drives runoff and reduces irrigation demand. Catchment rain comes first, after the rain-gap settings: days of a zero run treated as missing count as blank, so CHIRPS fills them, and a multi-day accumulation is spread back over the days it covers. That is why this column can differ from the catchment rain column on a day that has a reading. Where catchment rain is blank, CHIRPS stands in (scaled by its month’s factor when the bias correction is on), then forecast rain. It is blank outside the simulation period (Settings, simulation start and end) and on days no source has a value, which the model treats as dry. It is the rain before the rain threshold for irrigation demand. Compare it with the uploaded columns to see which days were filled and from where; screen readers also read the source with each value.

entries.title: CHIRPS bias factor (daily preview)
entries.summary: The catchment ÷ CHIRPS rain factor for the day’s calendar month: what CHIRPS is multiplied by on days it fills a catchment gap. (× (ratio))
entries.text: Fitted from the loaded records for each calendar month: catchment rain divided by CHIRPS rain, summed over the days both have a reading, leaving out suspect catchment rain (see CHIRPS bias correction). A month with fewer than 90 shared days, or less than 50 mm of CHIRPS on them, takes the factor pooled over all months, and factors are kept between 0.25 and 4. A dash means no factor could be fitted, so CHIRPS is used as it is. The same factor shows on every day of that month in the simulation period, but it only changes a day where CHIRPS fills in for blank catchment rain, and not at all when Settings → Rain gaps → CHIRPS bias correction is set to Raw CHIRPS (it is then shown for reference only). A factor well away from 1 says CHIRPS reads consistently wetter or drier than the catchment record in that month.

entries.title: CHIRPS corrected (daily preview)
entries.summary: CHIRPS as the model reads it: × the month’s bias factor on days it fills blank catchment rain, as uploaded on every other day. (mm/day)
entries.text: Only CHIRPS the model actually uses is corrected. On a day with no catchment rain value (including the days of a zero run treated as missing) it is CHIRPS × that month’s factor; on a day catchment rain has a reading CHIRPS isn’t used, so it shows as uploaded. With Raw CHIRPS chosen, or no factor fitted, it is the uploaded value every day. Blank outside the simulation period. Beside the uploaded CHIRPS column it shows how much rain the correction added or took away on the filled days. It differs from a run’s corrected-CHIRPS output column, which applies the factor on every day.

entries.title: Excluded from calibration (daily preview)
entries.summary: Marks days inside a calibration exclusion (Calibration record): they don’t count in Fit automatically or in a run’s calibration scores.
entries.text: Comes from Calibration → Calibration record → Calibration exclusions: whole water years (1 October to 30 September) or date ranges, each with a reason. A day inside one reads Excluded, and screen readers also read the reason; every other day shows a dash. The model still simulates excluded days; only the scores leave them out, so Fit automatically and the run’s calibration statistics compare observed and simulated flow on the remaining days of the calibration window. Use it to check that an exclusion covers the days you meant, such as a gauge outage or a suspect rain year, and no more.

entries.title: View (daily preview)
entries.summary: Which columns the daily preview shows: All, one hydrological unit’s rain side by side, or a group (stations, catchment rain, flow).
entries.text: All shows every column, as the preview always has. A hydrological unit shows only what that unit’s rain is made of, side by side: its station as recorded, the station adjusted to the unit (× the ratio of the unit’s MAP to the station’s, three decimals in the header), each patch station raw and adjusted to the unit in its patching priority, the unit’s own CHIRPS as stored and bias-corrected, the rain a run reads and where each day came from, then any other series stored at the unit. Above the table it lists the twelve monthly CHIRPS factors, fitted for that unit against its correcting station’s rain adjusted to the unit’s MAP, or why that pairing was refused, and the patching priority with the days each source filled. A unit without a rainfall station, under per-unit rain, shows the links of its own chain instead: its own gauge after the checks, the catchment gauge adjusted to it (× its MAP ratio), its CHIRPS as stored and levelled as a run levels it, the rain used and which link each day came from, with the rule and its factors above the table. With per-unit rain off it shows only the series stored at it. The groups gather the rainfall stations, the average catchment rainfall (when Settings assigns the catchment a station) and every flow record with its m³/day and the calibration exclusions. The Columns checkboxes hide columns inside the view, and Missing only and Flagged only read only the stored series shown. The view is kept in the address while the preview is open, so a reload or a shared link opens the same view.

entries.title: Station raw (daily preview)
entries.summary: An area’s rainfall station as recorded, over the run window, beside the same rain adjusted to the area’s MAP. (mm/day)
entries.text: The station’s record as stored, cut to the run window, shown in a unit’s or the average catchment rainfall’s own view right before the same rain adjusted to the area. The difference between the two columns is only the MAP ratio, so reading them side by side checks the scaling day by day. Blank where the station has no reading. The All view leaves it out: the station is a stored series column there already.

entries.title: Station × ratio (daily preview)
entries.summary: An area’s rainfall station as recorded × the ratio of the area’s MAP to the station’s: derived when viewed, not stored. (mm/day)
entries.text: Shown for the average catchment rainfall and each land unit that reads a rainfall station (Settings → Flow generation). It is the station’s record as stored, multiplied by the ratio a run applies: the area’s MAP divided by the station’s MAP, or 1 when a MAP is missing or the scaling is off. Blank where the station has no reading. Nothing here is stored: it is worked out when the preview opens, with the same engine code a run uses over the inputs a run would read, so it changes as soon as a series or a setting does. It is the same column as “station × ratio” in the Data tab’s Full CSV. In a unit’s own view (the View select) its header names the station, the unit and the ratio to three decimals, and the station raw column sits beside it.

entries.title: Patch station raw (daily preview)
entries.summary: A station in an area’s patching priority as recorded, over the run window, beside the same rain adjusted to the area’s MAP. (mm/day)
entries.text: Each station in the area’s patching priority (Model settings → Flow generation: “Then patch gaps from”) as stored, cut to the run window, shown in the area’s own view after the main station’s lines and before its CHIRPS, in priority order. The header numbers it by its place in the priority, the same number the Rain used from column gives a day it fills, so a CHIRPS earlier in the list keeps its place. A station the run skips (no record, or no MAP while scaling to the MAP) has no lines. The All view leaves it out: the station is a stored series column there already.

entries.title: Patch station × ratio (daily preview)
entries.summary: A patch station’s record × the area’s MAP ÷ that station’s MAP: what fills the main station’s gaps from it. Derived when viewed, not stored. (mm/day)
entries.text: A patch station’s record × the area’s MAP ÷ that station’s own MAP (kept between 0.25 and 4, or × 1 with the scaling off), the ratio to three decimals in the header. On a day the main station has no usable reading, the run takes the first source of the priority with a value; when that is this station, the rain used is this column’s value and Rain used from names it. Derived when the preview opens, never stored: the Full CSV’s “patch N: <station> × ratio” column, which follows the station × ratio column in priority order.

entries.title: Area CHIRPS raw (daily preview)
entries.summary: The area’s own CHIRPS as stored, over the run window, beside the same CHIRPS bias-corrected against its station. (mm/day)
entries.text: The area’s own CHIRPS as stored (a unit’s CHIRPS feed, or the catchment CHIRPS for the average catchment rainfall), cut to the run window, shown in the area’s own view right before the bias-corrected line. Each corrected value is this one × the factor of its month, listed above the table. The All view leaves it out: the CHIRPS series is a stored series column there already.

entries.title: Area CHIRPS corrected (daily preview)
entries.summary: The area’s own CHIRPS × its month’s factor from the pairing with its correcting station: derived when viewed, not stored. (mm/day)
entries.text: The area’s own CHIRPS (a unit’s CHIRPS feed, or the catchment CHIRPS for the average catchment rainfall) multiplied by the factor of the day’s month, from the pairing a run fits between that CHIRPS and the area’s correcting station’s rain taken to the area’s MAP, so it sits at the area’s level. It fills a day the station has no reading when CHIRPS comes first in the area’s patching priority with a value that day. The column is missing when the area has no CHIRPS, and blank when the pairing is refused, so its gaps are not corrected. Derived when the preview opens, never stored: the Full CSV’s “CHIRPS corrected” column. Unlike the catchment’s CHIRPS (corrected) column, it applies the factor on every day. In a unit’s own view (the View select) it reads “bias-corrected (f(m) against” its station, follows the CHIRPS raw column, and the twelve factors are listed above the table.

entries.title: Area rain used (daily preview)
entries.summary: The rain a run reads for the catchment or a land unit under its station, gaps filled: derived when viewed, not stored. (mm/day)
entries.text: The rain a run reads for this area, to the bit: the station × ratio where the station has a reading, else the first source of its patching priority with one (another station × its ratio, or the corrected CHIRPS), else the next fallback, else nothing (read as dry, 0). For a unit without a station, the first link of its per-unit chain that has a value: its own gauge, the catchment gauge × its MAP ratio, its levelled CHIRPS, then the catchment rain. For the average catchment rainfall it is the catchment rain demand and the dams read; for a land unit, its per-unit rain. It covers the run window only. It is computed when the preview opens with the engine’s own code over the inputs a run would read, not stored, so it is never older than the series and settings. The Rain used from column says, day by day, which source it came from.

entries.title: Rain used from (daily preview)
entries.summary: Where each day of an area’s rain used came from: the station, a patch station by name, corrected CHIRPS, the next fallback or none.
entries.text: Each day of the area’s rain used names its source: station (the station × ratio), patch 1: and the station’s name (a patch station × its ratio, numbered by its place in the patching priority), corrected CHIRPS (the station had no reading, or the day was set aside), next fallback (nothing in the patching priority had a value that day either) or no source, which a run reads as dry. The Full CSV writes the same as station, patch 1: <station>, chirps, fallback or none. For a unit without a station the sources are the links of its chain: own gauge, catchment gauge × MAP ratio, own CHIRPS (levelled), catchment rain, forecast or no source (unitGauge, gaugeMap, unitChirps, catchment, forecast, none in the CSV). Read down it to see where a long record leans on CHIRPS, or where an area had no rain at all.

entries.title: Own gauge, checked (daily preview)
entries.summary: A unit’s own rain gauge after the catchment’s checks and its unreliable periods, as a unit without a station reads it: derived when viewed. (mm/day)
entries.text: A unit’s own rain gauge (the rain series sited at the unit) after the same checks the catchment rain gets, zero runs and accumulations, and with its unreliable periods blanked, cut to the run window. It is what a unit without a rainfall station reads first, so a day blank here and recorded in the stored gauge column was set aside by a check. Blank where the gauge has no usable reading. Derived when the preview opens, never stored: the Full CSV’s “own gauge, checked” column.

entries.title: Catchment gauge × MAP ratio (daily preview)
entries.summary: The catchment rain × the unit’s MAP ÷ the gauge’s MAP, as a unit without a station reads it: derived when viewed, not stored. (mm/day)
entries.text: The catchment rain × the unit’s MAP ÷ the catchment gauge’s MAP (Settings → Flow generation → Units without a station), the ratio three decimals in the header and kept between 0.25 and 4. A unit with no gauge of its own reads it first; one with its own gauge reads it after its own CHIRPS. Shown only when the ratio applies: the unit has a MAP, the gauge MAP is set and there is catchment rain. Derived when the preview opens, never stored: the Full CSV’s “catchment gauge × MAP ratio” column.

entries.title: Unit CHIRPS levelled (daily preview)
entries.summary: A unit’s own CHIRPS levelled as a run levels it (to its MAP, or by the bias or reference factors), for a unit without a station. (mm/day)
entries.text: A unit’s own CHIRPS multiplied as a run multiplies it: by its MAP ÷ its CHIRPS mean annual rain, or by the catchment’s monthly bias factors, or by the reference gauge’s monthly factors and k_unit; the header says which. Raw CHIRPS runs as stored when nothing can level it, and a CHIRPS that totals 0 mm every year is not read at all, so the column is missing. Derived when the preview opens, never stored: the Full CSV’s “CHIRPS levelled” column. The CHIRPS raw column beside it is the series as stored.

entries.title: WR90 / WR2012
entries.summary: The Water Resources of South Africa studies (1990, 2012): S-pan evaporation, MAP and naturalised flow per quaternary catchment.
entries.text: The standard national source for the monthly evaporation and naturalised-flow inputs.

entries.title: Quaternary catchment
entries.summary: The smallest standard South African catchment unit (e.g. A21A), used to look up WR90/WR2012 data.
entries.text: A model catchment usually lies within one quaternary or spans a few.

entries.title: MAP and MAR
entries.summary: Mean annual precipitation (mm/yr) and mean annual runoff (M.m³/yr): the long-term averages of rain and river flow. (mm/yr; M.m³/yr)
entries.text: MAP varies across a catchment, which is why each hydrological unit can have its own MAP: it sets the level of the unit’s rain, and with it the unit’s natural MAR share of the flow and the EWR. (The Water Balance Tool workbook split unit areas into high- and low-MAP zones instead; that split was removed in engine 1.105.0.)

entries.title: Catchment map
entries.summary: The project’s geography: boundary, parcels, dams, gauges and rivers. It proposes values; none reaches the model until you accept it.
entries.text: The Map tab draws the catchment boundary, farm parcels, dams, gauges and rivers over a basemap of OpenStreetMap data served from the app’s own storage (without one, a plain background). The Network stays the model’s schematic of what drains into what; the map is the geography, and a model builds and runs without it. The map proposes and you decide. A polygon’s area enters a hydrological unit only through Use and a confirmation; a quaternary’s values, a dam’s capacity or full-supply area, a unit’s cultivated area and the boundary’s evaporation each enter only through their own Use; a delineated catchment reaches the map only through Accept; a reach of the river network becomes a project river only through Add to the map as a river. Each accepted value is a model or settings revision naming where it came from, so History and the run comparison show it. Everything on the map is also in the feature list and table beside it: points can be placed by typing coordinates, shapes pasted as GeoJSON or WKT, and areas still typed on the Network. Measure (distance, or area and perimeter on the WGS84 ellipsoid) and Download GeoJSON (the features as one WGS84 file) are there for viewers too.

entries.title: GeoJSON upload
entries.summary: Map features from a GeoJSON file in WGS84 longitude/latitude, checked on the server; any problem refuses the whole file.
entries.text: The server reads and checks the file whatever the browser did, and refuses the whole file on any problem, listing them per feature. It takes WGS84 longitude/latitude only (EPSG:4326, as GeoJSON requires): a file naming another CRS, or with coordinates outside ±180 / ±90 (a projected Lo or UTM file), is refused with a request to reproject it; nothing is guessed. Coordinates are 2D; the types are Point, LineString, MultiLineString, Polygon and MultiPolygon. Rings must be closed, have an area, and not cross or touch themselves or each other; the parts of a MultiPolygon may share an edge but not overlap beyond slivers of 0.1 %, so no area counts twice. At most 5 MB, 500 features and 50 000 positions a feature. Only a name (from name, Name, label or title), a description and a reference are kept; every other property is dropped, since attribute tables can carry owners’ names or ID numbers. The same file can’t be imported twice into a project. A file may mix kinds. The review proposes each feature’s kind from a kind, type or layer property, else from its shape (a line a river, a point a gauge, a polygon a farm parcel, the largest polygon holding every other feature the catchment boundary), and the node of the same name it stands for; check every row before importing. A file holds at most one boundary, and replacing the current one needs its own tick. Shapefiles aren’t read: export the layer as GeoJSON in EPSG:4326 (in QGIS, Export → Save Features As). Paste a shape takes the same GeoJSON, or WKT, for one shape while drawing.

entries.title: Area from the map
entries.summary: A polygon’s area on the WGS84 ellipsoid, worked out by the server. Use sets a hydrological unit’s area to it, as a model revision. (km²)
entries.text: Every area is worked out on the server, never taken from the browser: the geodesic area on the WGS84 ellipsoid (an equal-area projection of the ellipsoid, where a ring’s area is exact), not a mean-radius sphere, which is up to about 0.5 % off at South African latitudes. Measuring a shape on the map gives the same figure. Use … km² on a farm parcel or an area (an “other” polygon) sets a hydrological unit’s area to it, after a confirmation, and saves it straight away as a model revision naming the feature, so the model must have no unsaved edits. The unit then shows its area as from the map, until you type over it or the feature is deleted (the area stays; the link goes). Reshaping or splitting the polygon doesn’t change the unit’s area until you press Use again. A dam’s water surface and the catchment boundary are never offered. The area is the unit’s catchment area, the land whose runoff it receives, so the polygon to use is the unit’s sub-catchment, not its irrigated land. A polygon delineated from the elevation model stores the area of the cells it came from, which can differ slightly from its simplified outline’s.

entries.title: Gross or effective area (pans)
entries.summary: Gross: the whole delineated area. Effective: less what drains into pans (closed depressions), if you model them as not contributing. (km²)
entries.text: Delineation fills every closed depression and routes it to the outlet, so in pan veld the catchment it proposes is the gross one. It also reports how much of it drains into pans: closed depressions at least 1 m deep and 0.1 km² in floor that hold at least 100 mm of their own catchment’s runoff. Storage behind a dam wall, a depression a mapped river flows out of over a wall, and one the register or the map has a dam in are not counted as pans. Gross (the default) is the whole area, pans’ catchments included, as WR2012’s quaternary areas and a gauge’s published catchment are, so it can be checked against them; and the pans come from the elevation model alone, so a false one taken out silently would remove real catchment. Effective is the area less what drains into pans, for a hydrologist who models the pans as non-contributing (WR2012’s endoreic areas). The choice is never silent: the button and the confirmation name the area taken, the unit records which, and the revision says so. The polygon keeps its gross outline and area. For an off-channel dam, the proposed runoff-to-dam share follows the area taken, so the same water reaches the dam either way. A drawn, imported, split or reshaped polygon has no pans figure and offers no choice.

entries.title: Snap to features
entries.summary: A corner placed within 12 px of another feature’s corner or edge lands exactly on it; Follow edges also takes the corners between.
entries.text: While drawing, placing a point, dragging a corner or adding one on an edge, a position within 12 px of another feature’s corner lands exactly on that corner; failing that, within 12 px of its edge, on the edge. A corner wins over a nearer edge, so a shared corner is met exactly. Every feature on the map is a target except the one being edited, and a ring marks where the pointer would snap. Enter at the keyboard crosshair snaps the same way. Follow edges (on with snapping, for a new shape or line): two corners in a row snapped to the same outline take that outline’s corners between them, the shorter way round. A parcel drawn against its neighbour or the boundary then shares their edge corner for corner, with no gap or overlap for the map’s checks to find. Turn it off, or hold Alt for one corner, to cut straight across.

entries.title: Map search
entries.summary: Finds gauging stations, registered dams, quaternaries and then place names, and moves the map there. Nothing is drawn or saved.
entries.text: The box over the map’s top edge finds something to move the map to before drawing, delineating or starting a model, from the app’s own server (no outside geocoder sees what you type). It searches, in this order: gauging stations by code or name, the register of dams by number or name, quaternary catchments by code (at most 5 of each), then places from the gazetteer, towns, farms, rivers, pans, peaks and areas (at most 10). Every word typed must start a word of the name, in any order, ignoring case and accents; a code matches from its start. Within each group the whole name comes first, then names that start with what you typed; among places, towns come before farms, rivers and water, and among towns of one name the seat of government first. One match moves the map at once; several are listed, and picking one moves the map. A quaternary is framed whole; a point is centred, so a delineation or a point placed from the keyboard lands on it. Nothing is drawn or saved. The project’s own features aren’t searched: the feature list beside the map holds them. Place names come from a gazetteer (GeoNames) that the server’s operator loads. Where none is loaded, the search says so and still finds gauges, dams and quaternaries; the towns the basemap draws aren’t searchable.

entries.title: Trace a dam
entries.summary: Proposes a dam’s outline from satellite water occurrence (JRC Global Surface Water, 1984–2024) around a click inside its water.
entries.text: Click inside a dam’s water (or enter coordinates) and choose the share of satellite observations a cell must be water in to count: 10, 25 (the default), 50 or 75 %. The server reads the water occurrence around the point (about 8 km, grown once), moves a click within 60 m of water onto it, takes the cells at or over the share that touch the clicked one by an edge (two dams meeting at a corner stay two), fills islands and outlines them. Water reaching the edge of the window, dry land and a point outside the data are refused with a reason. The outline comes back as a drawing to adjust, nothing stored. Saved, it keeps how it was traced (the dataset, the share, the click, and whether you adjusted it) in its description and history; the server traces again to check an unadjusted outline. It is the water’s edge as the satellite saw it over 1984–2024, not the full supply level: a dam that seldom fills traces smaller at a high share, so a lower share takes in the edge a full dam reaches now and then. The share is your call. The data is JRC Global Surface Water occurrence (about 30 m cells); credit “Source: EC JRC/Google”.

entries.title: Map checks
entries.summary: Warnings where the map and the model disagree: units with no parcel, features outside the boundary, overlaps, areas 10 % apart.
entries.text: Warnings only: none stops a save or a run. Each names its features as buttons that select them on the map. The checks: a hydrological unit no farm parcel is linked to; a parcel, dam, point or line with a vertex outside the boundary (within 10 m of the line counts as on it); two farm parcels whose insides overlap (shared edges and slivers within 5 m don’t count); the units’ areas added up more than 10 % off the boundary’s area; a unit whose typed area is more than 10 % off its linked parcels’ area; and, with river lines on the map, a gauge more than 100 m from every river line. They read the project’s own features only: a reach of the river network counts once it is added to the map as a river. Distances are great-circle, areas the server’s.

entries.title: Results on the map
entries.summary: Colours each parcel and dam polygon by one run’s figure: days short, curtailment, dam level or use against allocation, in words too.
entries.text: Each farm parcel, and each dam polygon through its unit, is coloured by one run’s figure, using the app’s own bands: Days short (the default: demand days in the reporting window not fully met, banded at 95 % and 70 % of days met), Curtailment (the cut the curtailment table asks of the unit), Dam level (end of run: 60 % full or more, 30–60 %, under 30 % or at its minimum) and Use against allocation (above the registered volume in any whole water year is short). Gauges and EWR sites say whether the EWR was met. Kind goes back to the features’ own colours. The run is the published one for everyone; an editor can pick any run, and sees the newest when none is published. A parcel not linked to a unit, or with no figure, takes the “no figure” colour, so a parcel’s own green never reads as OK. The colour is never the only cue: the legend, the card and the table say each figure in words.

entries.title: Elevation model (DEM)
entries.summary: Copernicus GLO-30, a 30 m global elevation model: it shades the Relief layer, and delineation routes water over it.
entries.text: Over South Africa the elevation model is Copernicus GLO-30, a 30 m global digital elevation model, served as map tiles (Mapterhorn’s build). The Relief layer shades hills from it, for the eye only. Delineation, the terrain channels, sub-catchments and Start or Divide from the map read the same model on the server; without one there, those tools are not offered. It is a global satellite model, not a survey. In flat land a divide can be hundreds of metres out and a catchment can come out joined to, or cut from, its neighbour. Flats, dams and pans drain towards their outlet by construction; canals, pipelines, culverts and transfers between basins are invisible to it. Check a proposal against the relief, the mapped rivers and the quaternary outlines before accepting it. Every proposal names the dataset and its fingerprint, and a delineated polygon carries the Copernicus licence notice.

entries.title: Delineation
entries.summary: The catchment draining to a point on a river, from the elevation model: depressions filled, flow routed cell to cell (D8), outlined. (km²)
entries.text: Delineate proposes the catchment that drains to a point you click on a terrain channel (the elevation model’s own rivers): the catchment’s outlet, or just below a dam wall. The point goes on the terrain channel nearest it. The server reads the elevation model in a window around the point (about 34 km, grown to about 100 km while the catchment reaches its edge), fills depressions, routes each cell’s flow to its steepest neighbour (D8), collects every cell upstream of the outlet and outlines them as one polygon, simplified to about a cell. Mapped rivers play no part: the outlet sits on a terrain channel and the outline follows the terrain alone. A larger catchment goes to a background worker (windows up to about 200 km); one still cut off there, or one reaching missing data, is refused rather than cut off. A main stem too large for any window is refused with the advice to divide it with sub-catchments. The proposal lists its area, how far the outlet moved, the cells, what drains into pans and the effective area, and the dataset and method. Accept as the catchment boundary (replacing a current one only with its tick), Accept as an area (to link to a unit and Use), or Reject. An accepted boundary is a map feature only: the model’s units don’t change until you Start or Divide the model from the map. Each delineation takes a few seconds; a project can make 30 an hour.

entries.title: Terrain channels
entries.summary: The rivers as the elevation model routes them, drawn while delineating: the lines to click. Mapped rivers can sit hundreds of metres off.
entries.text: While Delineate or Sub-catchments is on (and dimmed behind a proposal waiting for a decision), the map draws the elevation model’s own channels, wider for a larger area upstream: every cell with at least 1 km² draining through it, routed the same way delineation routes. These are the lines to click: the outlet always goes on one of them. Mapped rivers (the river network, the basemap’s waterways) can sit hundreds of metres off the channel the elevation model routes along; they are for reference only and never move the outlet. The outline of a delineated catchment follows the terrain channels. Zoom in to see them: they are drawn for a view at most about 0.35° across. A channel entering the view from far beyond carries less area here than it really drains.

entries.title: Outlet placement on the channel
entries.summary: A clicked outlet goes on the nearest terrain channel (terrain channels in the map’s key) within 150 m; mapped rivers never move it.
entries.text: The outlet always sits on a terrain channel: the server puts the point on the nearest cell within 150 m that has at least 1 km² draining through it (terrain channels in the map’s key). Nearest, not the most-drained, so a click on a tributary beside the main river stays on the tributary. With no terrain channel that close, the point is refused: click on one of the terrain channels. Mapped rivers (the river network, the basemap’s waterways) never move or choose the outlet, since the elevation model’s rivers often run somewhere else than the mapped ones. When a channel draining 100 times more runs within 1 km, you are asked (Use that channel or Keep my point); the point is never moved there by itself. The proposal says how far the point moved, and Start and Divide place every abstraction point and gauge by the same rule (one with no terrain channel near it is left out, with the reason). A dam polygon takes its most-drained cell, unless it is marked off-channel or only clips a much larger river.

entries.title: Sub-catchments, one per click
entries.summary: Each click on a river gets the land that drains to it before reaching any other click: its incremental catchment, from the terrain.
entries.text: Sub-catchments, one per click divides the land by clicking the rivers, with no boundary and no roles to set first. Each click is an outlet, placed on the nearest terrain channel as delineation places one. Its piece is its incremental catchment: the cells whose water reaches it before any other click. A click upstream carves its piece out of the one below; the lowest click takes what lies between. Each piece drains into the first click its flow meets; a click on another river, or on the same cell as another, is dropped with the reason. A click whose catchment runs past the routed window (about 100 km across) is an inflow point: it gets no piece, and the water from above it enters the piece below, which is how a reach of a large river is modelled anyway. Click the main stem where the modelled reach starts and where it ends. Nothing is stored while you click. Save routes the clicks again on the server and saves each piece as an area, named by its click, with its outlet, where it drains and the area upstream in its description; link each to its unit and Use its area. At most 50 clicks; inflow points aren’t saved.

entries.title: Start the model from the map
entries.summary: On an empty model: a unit from each boundary you put on the map, with its area and order, and the dams and pumps inside it linked to it.
entries.text: On a model with no hydrological units yet, editors get Start the model from the map: a sheet of four steps. Put the catchment boundary on the map (delineate it, draw it or upload it), and each unit’s own boundary (draw or upload them, or save sub-catchments from clicks); say what each feature is (a unit’s boundary, a dam that is part of its unit’s composite dam, its unit’s river pump, another water user with no land, a gauge in the network, or not in the model) and which gauge is the outlet; then review the proposal; then add the data. The units follow your boundaries: each unit’s area is its boundary’s. A dam or an abstraction point is never a unit of its own. The dams inside a unit’s boundary make up its composite dam and the abstraction points its river pump: each is linked to the unit, and the composite dam’s volume, the area draining to it and the pump’s capacity stay yours to enter (the register of dams is a reference only, since many farm dams are unregistered). With an elevation model on the server, each unit is placed at its boundary’s outflow and drains into the first unit its flow meets; the cells reaching that outflow check the boundary’s area, with a warning when they differ by more than a tenth. The rest of the catchment (the catchment less the units) can be a unit of its own. Without an elevation model, every unit drains into the outflow gauge until you set the order. Each value is a tick: only what you tick is written, as one model revision, with each ticked unit’s area its boundary. The last step links the data proposals in order: rain from the boundary, the nearest gauging stations, each unit’s composite dam, land cover, then a run.

entries.title: Divide the model from the map
entries.summary: For a model with units: proposes each unit’s area from its boundary and what it drains into, beside its value now.
entries.text: For a model that already has hydrological units, with an elevation model on the server and exactly one outflow gauge. Say which unit each unit’s boundary on the map stands for (a point can stand for another water user, and a gauge with no node can become a new gauge node). A dam or an abstraction point never divides a unit: the unlinked ones inside a unit’s boundary become its composite dam and its river pump, linked on apply. The routing of Start from the map then proposes each unit’s area (its boundary’s, checked against the elevation model) and what it drains into, each shown beside the unit’s value now, and the rest of the catchment to a unit, a new unit or nobody. Only what you tick changes. A ticked value that changed in the model since the proposal, or a boundary redrawn since, is refused rather than overwritten unseen. A unit with no boundary in the division keeps its values.

entries.title: Dam siting: on the river or off-channel
entries.summary: Whether a dam sits on the river or is filled by a pump or furrow. A water user placed at the dam in Start or Divide goes by it.
entries.text: Set on a dam outline’s card. Not said (the default) lets the outline decide: a point placed at the dam goes at its most-drained cell, the wall when the river runs through the reservoir, unless the outline only clips a much larger river. On the river puts it on the river’s channel. Off-channel (filled by a pump or a furrow) finds the dam’s own outflow, ignoring the river however much of the outline it runs along, and goes where that outflow joins the river. The terms follow DWS practice: a dam registration distinguishes off-channel storage, which is filled from a river it doesn’t sit on. Since units follow your boundaries, a dam in Start or Divide is part of its unit’s composite dam and is never placed, so the siting only places another water user at the dam; the composite dam’s shares of upstream inflow and of runoff are yours to enter on the unit.

entries.title: River network (HydroRIVERS)
entries.summary: Mapped river reaches with Strahler order and area upstream, for reference; add a reach to the project’s rivers one at a time.
entries.text: The River network layer draws mapped river reaches around the catchment (or the view, before there is a boundary), dashed, wider for a higher Strahler order. The list beside the map gives each reach’s order and area upstream; a picked reach adds its length, a modelled mean flow (a WaterGAP long-term mean, never a gauged one) and its source. The real data is HydroRIVERS v1.0 (WWF HydroSHEDS), which holds rivers with at least 10 km² upstream or 0.1 m³/s mean flow at about 500 m resolution: it misses the smallest farm streams, and its lines can sit a few hundred metres off the real channel, so check a reach against the relief and the basemap. At most 1 000 reaches are drawn, the smallest dropped first. Add to the map as a river copies one reach into the project’s rivers, named after the reach (rename it on its card) with its source; then the map’s checks measure gauges against it and drawing snaps to it. Mapped rivers also help place a delineation’s outlet, but never shape its outline.

entries.title: Quaternary lookup (propose from the map)
entries.summary: Finds the quaternary catchment holding a point and proposes its area, MAP, MAR and monthly flows for the WR2012 check, value by value.
entries.text: Calibration → WR2012 check → Propose from the map finds the quaternary catchment that contains a point (the boundary’s centre, a gauge on the map, or coordinates you type) and lists its reference values (code, area, MAP, naturalised MAR, reference period and monthly means, with the dataset’s source) beside what the form holds. Each Use puts one value into the form only; Save keeps it. Check each against the study before you rely on it. The Map tab’s Quaternary catchments layer draws the loaded outlines around the project and lists their codes; click one to pick it out. A catchment spanning several quaternaries needs the values combined by hand. The operator loads the dataset: the DWS quaternary outlines with the WR2012 values from their own download, since the WR2012 redistribution terms are not published. The app ships only invented quaternaries, and a proposal from them is marked as synthetic.

entries.title: Synthetic test data
entries.summary: Invented reference data the app ships for development and tests. Anything proposed from it is marked; never use it for a real catchment.
entries.text: The reference datasets behind the map’s proposals (quaternaries, gauging stations, the register of dams, the river network, land cover, the evaporation grid, the water occurrence and the elevation model) are loaded by the operator from their own downloads, because their licences or the repository’s public nature keep real data out of the app’s code. What ships instead is invented: a handful of quaternaries and gauges in a drainage region that doesn’t exist (Z), invented dams, reaches, cropland, evaporation, water and terrain around the example catchment, each with a source saying SYNTHETIC. Anything proposed from them carries a warning (“Synthetic test data … never use them for a real catchment”), and data feeds reading the sample files instead of CHIRPS or DWS show a Sample data badge. Seeing either on a real project means the real dataset isn’t loaded on this server.

entries.title: Dam values from the register and the map
entries.summary: Registered dams within 1 km, their capacities for reference only, and a dam’s full-supply area from its polygon on the map.
entries.text: On the Dams page, for a unit whose dam is on the map (a polygon first, else a point): The register of dams, for reference. The registered dams within 1 km of the dam’s place on the map, nearest first (at most five), each with its register number, distance, capacity, wall height, completion year, river and farm. Matching is by distance only, because names on the register rarely match a farm’s dam name. A unit’s dam is its composite dam, the total of all its farm dams, and many farm dams are unregistered, so the register’s capacities are never used for it: its volume, and the area draining to it, are yours to enter. The register is the DWS Dam Safety Office’s list of registered dams, loaded by the operator. Full-supply area, from the dam polygon. The polygon’s area on the ellipsoid as the dam’s area when full, which the run then uses for the dam’s evaporation instead of the estimate from its capacity. A point has no area to propose. Use (the area only) asks first, then saves that one value as a model revision naming its source; the server derives it again, so a dam linked to another unit is refused. Draw the polygon at the full supply level, not the water’s edge on the day of the imagery.

entries.title: Cultivated area from land cover
entries.summary: Cultivated land from satellite in a unit’s parcels, dryland and fallow included: not irrigated area. Check it before you use it. (ha)
entries.text: In a unit’s planted-areas drawer, From land cover sums the area a land-cover map shows as cropland inside each farm parcel linked to that unit, the parcels together, and the boundary for reference. Pick an area (all the parcels or one) and a crop; Use sets that crop’s planted area on the unit, as a model revision citing the dataset. The data is ESA WorldCover 10 m (2021 v200), class 40 Cropland, pre-summarised by the operator into a grid of 0.0025° cells (about 250 × 230 m) holding each cell’s cropland share. A parcel’s figure is, over the cells it covers, each cell’s area × the share of it inside the parcel × its cropland share, so cropland is taken as spread evenly within a cell and a small parcel can be off by up to a cell’s cropland along its edge. Overlapping parcels count twice. It is cultivated land from satellite, not irrigated area. WorldCover’s cropland includes dryland (rain-fed) and fallow fields, so the figure can be well above what is irrigated: check it against the farm before you use it. Land cover doesn’t say what grows there either, so the crop is always yours to choose, and a parcel with several crops is split by typing afterwards. Nothing is applied until you press Use and confirm, and the area is used as it stands, with no fixed discount: if only part of the cultivated land is irrigated, type the irrigated area over it. The drawer says when the crop’s area has been typed over since. Orchards and vines. Where a crop-type grid is loaded (South African National Land Cover, SANLC: class 32 permanent orchards and class 33 permanent vines), the drawer also shows each parcel’s orchards and vines, summed the same way, and offers them under Area to use as one crop’s planted area. It doesn’t say which fruit or cultivar, nor whether it is irrigated. New since an earlier edition is the orchard or vine land that was neither then, the new plantings a licence application records; it is shown, never offered. SANLC’s terms are not yet recorded, so the live site shows no crop types until they are.

entries.title: Evaporation from the map
entries.summary: An evaporation grid’s 12 monthly means averaged over the boundary: ET₀ goes to GR4J’s monthly PE, A-pan to the A-pan row, unconverted. (mm/month)
entries.text: In Calibration → Flow calibration, under GR4J’s potential evaporation. Each month is the mean of the grid cells the catchment boundary covers, each weighted by its area × the share of it inside, rounded to 0.1 mm. Cells without a value (the sea) are left out and the share of the boundary they leave is shown as coverage; below 50 % nothing is proposed. What a grid holds decides where it goes, and nothing is converted. A reference evapotranspiration grid (FAO-56 Penman-Monteith ET₀) is proposed as GR4J’s monthly PE as it stands; the pan coefficient is then unused, and crop demand and dam evaporation keep reading the A-pan row. An A-pan grid is proposed as the A-pan row. ET₀ is a reference grass surface’s loss, not a pan’s; the pan coefficient between them depends on the pan’s siting, humidity and wind, so it stays your call. For an ET₀ grid the panel shows ET₀ ÷ saved A-pan per month as a cross-check only, flagged outside FAO-56’s typical Class A range of 0.6–0.85. The real grid is dPET (University of Bristol), daily FAO-56 PET at 0.1°, averaged by the operator into monthly means over a period such as 1991–2020. Use saves the 12 values as one settings revision citing the dataset; a GR4J fit made before is then marked “Forcing changed since fit”.

entries.title: Data feeds
entries.summary: Rain and gauge flow fetched daily into a series: CHIRPS, the CHIRPS-GEFS forecast or a DWS gauge. A missing day never erases data.
entries.text: Data → Data feeds, under the series. Each feed reads one source and merges its new days into one series once a day: CHIRPS daily rainfall (for listed grid cells, a bounding box, or the cells of the catchment boundary, area weighted), the CHIRPS-GEFS 16-day forecast, or a DWS gauge’s verified daily flow, or AgERA5 daily reference evapotranspiration (with NASA POWER on its newest days) for GR4J under a monthly PE row. A day the source has no value for never erases what is there, and a feed attached to a series that already holds data keeps those values and fills only the empty days (the form asks first, and suggests a separate series instead). Each card says its state in words: OK; Stale when its newest day is older than the source’s usual lag allows (12 days for CHIRPS; a forecast reaching fewer than 12 days ahead; 240 days for DWS); Failing when the last fetch failed, with the reason; Waiting before its first fetch; Off. A fetch that meets a changed page, a corrupt file or a sea cell fails loudly and writes nothing. Run now fetches at once, between the daily runs. Owners attach, switch off and remove feeds; editors can run them; viewers see their health. A Sample data badge means this server reads invented sample files, not the real sources. Feeds change the series only: a run reads them like any uploaded series.

entries.title: Rain from the catchment boundary
entries.summary: A CHIRPS feed averaging the 0.05° cells the boundary covers, each weighted by the share of it inside, rather than a box around it. (mm/day)
entries.text: Data → Data feeds → Attach a feed → Area The catchment boundary, from the map proposes a CHIRPS feed for the boundary on the map: the CHIRPS v3 cells (0.05°, about 5.5 km) it covers, each weighted by the share of it inside the boundary (clipped exactly, holes taken out) × the cosine of its latitude, with a table of the cells. A cell less than 0.1 % inside is left out. At most 100 cells in 25 rows, about 2 500 km²; a larger boundary needs feeds for its parts. Apply attaches a CHIRPS feed into the CHIRPS series, or gives the cells to a CHIRPS feed that holds no days yet. A feed whose series already has a record never gets new cells, since its days were averaged over the old ones: the proposal attaches a new feed into a separate series to compare. A run reads the first CHIRPS series by name, so that series is always named to sort after the record runs read: the record stays the run’s until you choose otherwise. Where runs read a record, the feed reads from its first day (rnl when that is before 1998), and an owner may instead Replace the record: the feed reads it again whole from its first day and takes its place once complete, the old values kept in the History. The daily product and start date can be changed before Apply. A boundary redrawn since you looked is refused rather than applied unseen; the Map says when the boundary has changed since its feed read it.

entries.title: Rain for each unit (CHIRPS feeds)
entries.summary: One CHIRPS feed per unit with land, averaging the 0.05° cells its parcel covers, area weighted, into that unit’s own rain series. (mm/day)
entries.text: Under Data → Data feeds → Attach a feed, the Area Each unit’s parcel (Rain for each unit) proposes one CHIRPS feed for each hydrological unit with land and a parcel on the map (its delineated or drawn area, linked to the unit). Each feed averages the 0.05° CHIRPS cells the parcel covers, each weighted by the share of it inside and by its area, and writes into that unit’s own rain series. One daily product serves every unit, end to end: rnl (from 1981, final days only) by default, or sat (from 1998, with preliminary days); a feed never splices one onto the other. Without a start date the feeds read from the product’s first day, so the MAP period has its years. Units without a parcel are listed, with a link to the map. Neighbouring small units often share cells, so their raw CHIRPS is nearly the same: what tells them apart is each unit’s MAP, which levels its CHIRPS. The series are read under Model settings → Flow generation, where they fill a station’s gaps or, for a unit with no station, are its rain.

entries.title: CHIRPS-GEFS forecast
entries.summary: A 16-day daily rain forecast on the CHIRPS grid, issued daily; each issue replaces the last in the forecast rainfall series. (mm/day)
entries.text: CHIRPS-GEFS v3 is a rainfall forecast from the Climate Hazards Center: the GEFS weather forecast bias-corrected to CHIRPS, on the same 0.05° grid, one issue a day of 16 daily values. A feed reads the newest complete issue for its cells or box and writes all 16 days into the forecast rainfall series, each issue replacing the last from its issue date on. An ordinary run stops where the observed record ends, so forecast days reach only a forecast run, where results on those days are indicative. Forecast rain also fills a day neither catchment rain nor CHIRPS has.

entries.title: CHIRPS product and version
entries.summary: Which CHIRPS a series holds: v2.0 (usual in the workbooks) or v3.0, sat or rnl. One series holds one; two are never spliced together.
entries.text: CHIRPS v2.0 and v3.0 differ by an amount that changes over the years, so one series holds one of them and two are never spliced together. Water Balance Tool workbooks were built on v2.0; the CHIRPS data feed writes v3.0, which comes as two daily products with the same pentad totals but different daily timing: sat (from 1998, with preliminary days two days after each pentad, replaced by finals about three weeks after the month) and rnl (from 1981, final days only, out with the sat finals about three weeks after each month, so its newest day is weeks old). Choose rnl for a record that starts before 1998. The workbook import and an upload ask which a CHIRPS series holds. A feed whose series holds another product or version, or an unrecorded one, refuses every fetch until an owner chooses Replace the series: it backfills the new record separately and swaps it in whole when caught up, and History keeps the old values. A fit then needs redoing, since the CHIRPS factors move.

entries.title: DWS gauge flow
entries.summary: A DWS river gauge’s verified daily mean flow in m³/s, from a data feed or an exported table. Verified data lags by months. (m³/s)
entries.text: The Department of Water and Sanitation publishes verified daily mean flow for its river gauges (codes like A2H012, H in the third place for a river gauge; reservoir stations are not read, since their daily table is spillway discharge from the dam level). Verified data is revised in arrears and lags by months, so use it to calibrate, not to run the catchment day to day. A feed re-reads a year before its newest day each time, and ten years on its first fetch; it counts as stale after 240 days without a newer day. When attaching a DWS feed, Nearest gauging stations lists the river gauges within 50 km of the catchment’s outlet (the outflow gauge on the map, else the boundary’s centre), nearest first, with river, distance and the years their record spans; Use fills the station code, and nothing is attached until you say so. Check the record covers the years you calibrate on. A daily table exported from the DWS hydrology site also uploads as it is. In both, a row whose quality code marks it missing, and a blank or negative placeholder such as −999, is a gap, never a zero; the upload lists the quality codes it saw.

entries.title: Data up to, and Behind
entries.summary: A series’ last day with a value. Rain or A-pan a run is driven by is Behind once that day is more than 7 days ago.
entries.text: Data up to is the last day a series has a value, not the last day it stores: blank days after it (a dead logger’s) are no data. The series a run is driven by (recorded rainfall and daily A-pan evaporation) are Behind once that day is more than 7 days before today; they are listed first, and their count is the number beside Data in the workspace. A forecast runs ahead, and observed flow only scores a run, so neither is ever Behind. Missing is the share of days in the series’ own stored span with no value (a record can store blank days before its first reading, which From, the first day with a value, leaves out), and Coverage by year shows where the gaps fall. When a driver series has changed since the latest run, or reaches past its end, the Data and Runs tabs say the results are older than the data.

entries.title: Day boundary of sub-daily readings
entries.summary: How several readings a day add up into days: 08:00 to 08:00, booked to the day it starts (the manual-gauge day), or midnight to midnight.
entries.text: A logger file with several readings a day is added up into daily totals before it is stored. 08:00 to 08:00 is the manual rain gauge’s day: the total read at 08:00 is booked to the day the interval starts. Midnight to midnight is the calendar day. Each timestamp is taken as the end of its interval, so a reading at 08:00 closes the day before. The series records the choice, and a rain-source period compares like with like, since a one-day shift between a manual gauge and an automatic station wrecks a daily fit while leaving monthly totals unchanged. The summary says how many readings a day it found and how many days have fewer, whose totals may be short.

entries.title: Append / update or replace
entries.summary: Append / update adds new days and corrects overlapping ones; Replace overwrites the whole series. Overwritten values stay in History.
entries.text: Uploading into a series that exists: Append / update adds the file’s new days and corrects the days both have, leaving the rest; Replace overwrites the whole series with the file. Before you upload, the form counts new, changed and unchanged days and the series’ span afterwards, and a file that changes stored days asks first, naming how many and between which dates (Show the changes lists each). The values it overwrites are kept: History’s Restore the earlier values brings them back.
