A new series of a kind that already has one is a second series: runs read the first by name, in character order (digits and capitals before lower case, so “RAIN-B” comes before “average”), and the form says which one runs will read.

entries.title: Edit a day, or paste rows
entries.summary: Set or clear one day of a series by hand, or paste date and value rows from a spreadsheet. Days typed in are marked as edited by hand.
entries.text: Edit a day, under a series’ chart, sets or clears one day of it: type the day, day first (2 Oct 2021, 2/10/2021 or 2021-10-02), type its value in the series’ unit (12.5 or 12,5), or leave it blank for no reading, and save. It is for correcting a bad reading or filling a gap; days outside the series come from a file or a paste. Each edit is kept in History like an upload (the values before it can be restored), and the day is marked edited by hand on the series row, in its details and as points on the chart, so an edited record never passes as the raw one. A data feed or an API key never writes over a day edited by hand; an upload or paste that writes the day takes the mark off, since the value is the file’s then. Paste rows in Add data takes a block of dates and values copied from a spreadsheet (or typed as date,value), read exactly like a file: the same Expected format, the same summary of new and changed days, and the same question before stored days are overwritten. A blank pasted cell leaves the stored day as it is.

entries.title: Workbook import
entries.summary: Turns a Water Balance Tool workbook into a project, read in your browser: network, units, crops, transfers, settings and Flow data series.
entries.text: Import workbook reads a Water Balance Tool workbook (.xlsm or .xlsx) in your browser (only the extracted project is sent) and makes it a new project: its network, hydrological units, crops, transfers, settings and Flow data series. Formulas and macros are never run, and the per-farm result sheets aren’t imported; the first run is the app’s own. The review asks what the workbook can’t say. Gauge column: whether the gauge measures another river (import it as a reference gauge, optionally undoing a scaling from a date). River pumping units: units the importer thinks pump from the river (the workbook can’t model that, so they were entered as a tiny dummy dam or none), converted to run-of-river supply if you tick it, with the pump capacities left for you to enter. CHIRPS column: which CHIRPS product and version it holds. Importer notes (notes and warnings, with sheet and cell) and the Unmapped report (what couldn’t be carried across as the workbook meant, such as a hand-written transfer formula) never change a value on their own: read them before relying on a run. They stay with the project as its import record on the Summary. A .json project file imports the same way.

entries.title: Fraction of demand supplied
entries.summary: Average supplied ÷ average demand over the run (1 = every drop of demand met). (fraction 0–1)
entries.text: A quick reliability measure per hydrological unit. It averages over wet and dry years; check the daily deficit to see when the shortfalls happen.

entries.title: Flow-duration curve (Q10–Q95)
entries.summary: Flow against the share of days it is equalled or exceeded. Q95 is the flow exceeded on 95 % of days: a low flow; Q10 a high one. (m³/s or m³/day)
entries.text: Each daily flow record (observed, simulated outflow, natural flow) is sorted from highest to lowest and plotted against how often it is equalled or exceeded, using Weibull plotting positions (rank ÷ (days + 1)), with linear interpolation between ranks. The table reads the curve at 10, 50, 90 and 95 %: Q50 is the median flow, Q90 and Q95 the usual low-flow indices. The curves only compare like with like when they rank the same days: when the observed record covers part of the run, the chart offers to rank only the days with an observation. A forecast run’s curves rank its history only. The curve says how often a flow occurs, not when: two records with the same curve can have their dry spells in different years.

entries.title: Run comparison (baseline and what-if)
entries.summary: A baseline beside up to two what-if runs. Every change is the what-if minus the baseline (B − A): green better, red worse.
entries.text: Compare runs puts a baseline (run A) beside up to two what-ifs (B, and a second when you add one); any run of any project you can see can take any place. It opens on the latest run against the published run, or against the run before it when nothing is published. What the change does gives the main outcomes for every run at once: the share of days the EWR wasn’t met, the share of demand supplied, the deficit, the units below 95 % supplied, the units whose supply moves most, dam storage at the end of the run, mean outflow, mean natural flow and the runoff coefficient. Full comparison then gives every detail for the baseline against one what-if. Every change is B − A, with a sign and ▲ or ▼. Green is better, red worse and grey neither (demand and flow are just different); the judgement is also in words, so colour is never the only cue. For percent bias closer to 0 is better; for the EWR frequency bias and the WR2012 ratios, closer to 1; for the Reserve, more months met. Dam storage at the end of the run gets no verdict: a bigger dam can end emptier as a share yet hold more. Results are daily averages over each run’s own period. When two runs cover different periods, or ran on different engine versions, part of the change comes from that, and the page says so. Compare runs over the same dates when the change should be your edit alone.

entries.title: How runs are matched
entries.summary: Runs line up by id first, then by name: a unit renamed between runs is still the same unit; across a copy the same name is the same unit.
entries.text: To compare two runs, each hydrological unit, gauge, crop and transfer of one has to be paired with its counterpart in the other. Within one project ids match, so a unit renamed between the runs is still the same unit and reads “Rooikloof (was Farm 1)”. A copied project gives everything new ids, so across a copy names match instead (trimmed, ignoring case); a unit both renamed and copied can’t be paired and is listed under Only in run A or Only in run B. Crop areas pair by unit name and crop name; transfers by id, then by their from → to route; boreholes and demand objects by id, then by their unit’s name and their own; irrigation systems by id, then by name; Reserve sites the outlet with the outlet and a gauge by id, then by name. A scenario keeps its base run’s ids, so every change lines up with its base: a unit the scenario added is only in run B, one it removed only in run A. When a unit you expected to compare shows under “only in”, a rename across a copy is the likely reason.

entries.title: Inputs that differ
entries.summary: Every difference between two runs’ inputs, in words: network, crops, transfers, settings and series, with who saved each change.
entries.text: Each run stores a snapshot of what it ran on: the settings, the whole model, and every driving series with its dates, its values and a hash of them. Inputs that differ compares the two snapshots and lists each difference in words, grouped by network, crops, transfers, settings and series (“Rooikloof: dam capacity 600 000 m³ → 750 000 m³”, “Calibration rain threshold: 2 mm → 3 mm”). A series edited in place is caught too: the days both runs cover are compared value by value (“values changed on 53 of the 366 days both runs cover; their total fell 15 %”), and a series’ new product or version is its own line. For two runs of one project, the earlier as the baseline, each model or settings line says which save set its final value, by whom and when, with the save’s reason. Runs of two projects, a what-if older than its baseline, and scenario runs carry no names; a scenario run’s changes are listed under Scenario overrides, each with its class. What it can’t see: runs saved before series values were stored compare a series by its hash only and say so, and runs saved before the hash existed show nothing for a series edited in place. A setting the app doesn’t know yet reads “Setting … changed”. If the results changed and the list is empty, an old run is the likely reason.

entries.title: Read as 0: a feature only one run has
entries.summary: A river pump, boreholes, a release rule or land cover in one run only reads as 0 in the other: that run moved none of that water.
entries.text: Some columns are stored only when a feature is on: a river pump, boreholes (groundwater used or pumped to the dam, stream depletion), a dam release rule, land cover, priority water users, a share of dam seepage that returns. When one run has the feature at a unit and the other doesn’t, the other moved none of that water, so the comparison reads it as 0 there and says so (“(none)”, “A: none (0)”, a note under the chart). A scenario that pumps from the river, compared with its base that only draws on the dam, is then its pumping against 0. Only those feature columns are filled, and only when the unit is in both runs as the same kind of element and the other run stored nothing under that name. Anything else one run lacks (observed flow, a calibration series, a core column an older run didn’t store) stays unknown, shown as a gap or “–”, never as 0.

entries.title: Takeaways (material changes)
entries.summary: Plain sentences under What the change does, only for material changes: a day a year below the EWR, 1 pp of demand supplied, 5 % of outflow.
entries.text: Under What the change does each what-if gets a sentence or two on what moved enough to matter: “What-if 1 puts the river below the EWR on 13 more days a year”, “Under What-if 1, Farm 4 gets −12 pp of its demand”. A change is material at one day a year below the EWR (the share of days not met × 365.25), one percentage point of the catchment’s demand supplied, a unit crossing 95 % supplied, five points of one unit’s supply, or 5 % of the mean outflow. A what-if with none “makes no material change to these outcomes”; the table above it still shows every change. When both what-ifs add days below the EWR, a line says which costs less and by how much. The days are the pragmatic EWR’s, not the Reserve rule table’s months. A what-if over other dates, or on another engine version, gets a line saying part of its change comes from that. The thresholds say where a sentence is worth writing; they are not a test of significance. For how sure a change is, see the paired uncertainty band.

entries.title: Paired uncertainty band (B − A)
entries.summary: The change between two runs under each parameter set of run A’s ensemble: the change’s own uncertainty, with what both share cancelled.
entries.text: Two runs’ own uncertainty bands overlap even when every plausible parameter set moves the result the same way, because most of each band is the catchment-response uncertainty both share. The paired band removes it. Every parameter set run A’s newest ensemble kept is run again, unchanged, on run B’s inputs, and B − A is taken set by set; the band is the 5 %, median and 95 % of those differences. For a licence application it is the change’s own impact with its uncertainty. The same inputs give exactly zero. The table bands the change in EWR days not met and in the shortfall (each with the share of sets in which B is worse), the outflow MAR, Reserve compliance in percentage points and each unit’s curtailment, then EWR days not met by month. Sets where B is worse is the share of pairs in which the what-if does more harm: a small median with a high share still means the change does harm under most of the parameter sets. It needs run A to have a stored ensemble, and both runs on one project, one runoff model and one period. An editor of B’s project computes it: the server copies A’s seed and rule, the browser runs the pairs, and the server re-runs the first pair and three at random before storing it. Runs of two projects get a note instead: the parameter sets describe one catchment.

entries.title: Ensemble rule: sample and acceptance tests
entries.summary: How an uncertainty ensemble is drawn and which parameter sets it keeps (skill, WR2012 flag, low-flow bias), fixed before it runs.
entries.text: Run an ensemble sets the rule a band is built to, and the server fixes it, with a seed it draws, before anything runs. Parameter sets (30–1 000, default 300) are the points of a Latin hypercube across the free GR4J parameters’ bounds; more give steadier percentiles and take longer, since each is a full model run in this browser. Bounds are the fit’s own when the parameters come from a fit, else Typical (Perrin et al.’s 80 % range); Wide samples further, and a range over a factor of ten is sampled on a log scale. Pan coefficient ± (GR4J) shifts each set’s whole monthly row by up to that much (default 0.1, at most 0.3), and is dropped when GR4J reads a monthly PE row. Where the project has both, half the sets use station rain with CHIRPS infill and half CHIRPS alone, and half are judged against the gauge and half against the logger. A set is kept only when it passes three tests: Lowest skill kept, the KGE′ (or the fit’s objective) it must reach on the first half of the scored record, default 0.5; Worst WR2012 flag kept, default query, so a set not usable for EWR findings is out (No WR2012 check turns it off); and Largest low-flow bias kept, the volume bias of the lowest 30 % of flows, default ±50 %. Set 0 is always this run itself, and This run’s own parameters says whether it passes. Parameter sets kept counts the sets that passed and why the rest failed; with fewer than 30 kept no band is shown. The second half of the record is held out: the share of its observations inside the daily 5–95 % band is the coverage, and below 70 % the band is too narrow to trust. A band is only as fair as its rule, so set the rule before looking; for an evidence report, run the rule the project declared.

entries.title: Sensitivity runs
entries.summary: EWR compliance re-run with one uncertain input changed at a time: rain, pan coefficient, dam evaporation, abstraction, starting storage.
entries.text: Some inputs the observed record can’t settle at all, and a fit would only trade them against its parameters: how much rain really fell, the pan coefficient, how much a farm dam loses to evaporation, how much is really abstracted, and how full the dams were on the first day. Sensitivity runs carry them through as factors. The central run is this run’s inputs as they stand; each factor is then run at its low and its high with everything else unchanged: rain × 0.9 and × 1.1 (every rain series, so the CHIRPS correction is unchanged), the pan coefficient and the dam evaporation factor × 0.85 and × 1.15, abstraction (every unit’s and user’s demand) × 0.7 and × 1.3, and every dam starting empty and full. That is at most 11 model runs, with the runoff parameters this run’s throughout. A factor that doesn’t apply (no dam, no demand, GR4J on a monthly PE row) is listed under Not run with the reason. At each EWR site each run gives the days the EWR is not met and the shortfall volume over the reporting window, and with a Reserve rule table the share of months meeting it. The tornado shows, for one site and one result, each factor’s low (blue) and high (orange) against the central run (the solid line), largest swing first; a factor’s swing is the gap between its low and high results. The table under it gives the same numbers. It is a live diagnostic: worked out in this browser from the run’s stored inputs, the same every time, and not stored. One factor at a time ignores their interactions, so two factors at their worst together can go further; the joint uncertainty of the runoff parameters is the uncertainty bands’ job. The ranges are defaults pending the catchment’s hydrologist.

entries.title: Sensitivity verdict and threshold
entries.summary: Meets, or below, the threshold when every sensitivity run agrees; not determinable when their range crosses it. 80 % by default. (% of days or months)
entries.text: The verdict judges one measure per EWR site: the share of months meeting the Reserve rule table where the site has one, else the share of days the pragmatic EWR was met. The envelope is the lowest and highest value over the central run and every factor’s low and high. Meets the threshold: the whole envelope is at or above it. Below the threshold: the whole envelope is below it. Not determinable with current data: the envelope crosses it, whatever the central value says. Nothing to judge: the site has no data. Neither a rule table nor the pragmatic EWR carries a pass mark of its own, so the threshold is the project’s choice: 80 % for both by default, a provisional decision not yet confirmed by the catchment’s hydrologist. Changing a threshold re-judges at once, without running again. A verdict of not determinable is a finding in itself: better data on the factor with the largest swing is what would settle it.

entries.title: Demand levels
entries.summary: Percentages of today’s demand to run side by side (100, 85, 70 by default); each scales every hydrological unit’s irrigation demand. (% of today’s demand)
entries.text: The outcome matrix and the seasonal outlook run the catchment at a few demand levels, typed as percentages separated by commas (0–200 %; up to 12 for the matrix, 6 for the outlook). Each level is one Scale demand change on every hydrological unit: 85 means every unit takes 85 % of what it would take, with crop areas unchanged. On a full-allocation run a level is that share of each unit’s registered volume. In the outlook the levels apply from the decision date only. The outlook also takes a monthly plan, a % for each month of the season, which ranks among the levels by the water it asks for. The levels are what the WUA might set as a restriction; the panels report how each fared and never pick one. Both run as background jobs on an ordinary run of the model (not a scenario or forecast run) and add no runs to the run list.

entries.title: Water-year class
entries.summary: Complete water years ranked by natural flow at the outlet and split into terciles (dry, normal, wet) or, with 25 years or more, quintiles.
entries.text: The classes are the catchment’s own: the run’s complete water years (1 October to 30 September, all inside the run) ranked by their total natural flow at the outlet. A part year at either end, or a year with a missing day, isn’t classed, since a part total would read as a dry year. With 25 complete years or more the years are split into quintiles (very dry, dry, normal, wet, very wet), else into terciles (dry, normal, wet); Settings › Outcome matrix can fix either. Each class is headed with its bounds in m³ of natural flow a year and its number of years. The bounds use Weibull plotting positions, as the Reserve’s natural flow-duration curve does. A year exactly on a bound goes to the drier class, and years with equal totals always share one, so classes can be uneven (8 years in terciles make 3, 3 and 2). Natural flow, not observed flow, sets the class, so the classes don’t move with demand.

entries.title: Outcome matrix
entries.summary: For each demand level and water-year class, how the river fared in those years of the record: a historical tally, not a forecast.
entries.text: One row per demand level, one column per water-year class of the base run. Each level is the base run re-run with every unit’s demand scaled (a demand sweep). Each cell reads the years of its class: with a Reserve rule table at the chosen site for every level, the share of months meeting the table over those years; otherwise the share of days below the pragmatic EWR at the outlet. The sentence in each cell counts years (“EWR met on every day in 2 of 3 dry years”), and its colour and words give the risk: lower, increasing or high. A class with fewer than three years reads Not enough years. Reserve site (the outlet, or a gauge with a rule table) is a project setting, so everyone sees the matrix the editor chose. The classes and the risk are worked out from the stored sweep, so changing them in Settings re-reads it without running it again. The matrix reports how past years went at each level. It doesn’t recommend a level: that is the WUA’s decision.

entries.title: Outcome risk cut-offs
entries.summary: Where a cell turns from lower to increasing to high risk: months met ≥ 90 % / ≥ 75 %, or days below the EWR ≤ 5 % / ≤ 20 %. (%)
entries.text: Each cell of the outcome matrix is labelled by cut-offs in its own measure’s direction, a value on a cut-off counting to the lower risk. On Reserve months met: lower risk at 90 % or more, increasing risk at 75 % or more, high risk below. On days below the pragmatic EWR: lower risk at 5 % of days or fewer, increasing risk at 20 % or fewer, high risk above. The days cut-offs are the portfolio traffic light’s; 90 % and 75 % of months are a judgement. These defaults are provisional, agreed with the client but not yet confirmed by the catchment’s hydrologist, and the matrix says so while they are in use. Settings › Outcome matrix sets the project’s own, per measure.

entries.title: Seasonal outlook
entries.summary: The season run from the catchment’s state on the decision date with each past year’s weather, at a few demand levels.
entries.text: An ensemble streamflow prediction (ESP). The base run’s state at the end of the day before the decision date (dam storage, soil water, the runoff model’s stores, boreholes’ volumes) is kept, and the season is run from it once per analogue year, with that year’s rain (and daily A-pan, where the project has one) in its own day-to-day order, and once per demand level. Every member starts from the same state, so the spread across years is the weather’s and the difference between levels is the demand’s. Per level the table gives the farm dams’ storage at season end, the share of hydrological unit demand met and the days below the pragmatic EWR (or Reserve months met, with a rule table at the site), each as the median with its 10–90 % range across the analogue years, and the years that met the requirement in full. With fewer than 10 analogue years there are no ranges and no planning figure, only each year’s values. Its skill comes from the starting state, not from knowing the weather: read it as how the season went from here in past years, not as a forecast. A lower demand doesn’t always mean fewer days below the EWR, because part of the water irrigated from a dam drains back to the river on dry days. The outlook runs without the drought restriction rule, since its levels are what such a rule would set.

entries.title: Analogue years
entries.summary: The past water years whose weather a seasonal outlook replays: each one the record holds whole, except the season’s own.
entries.text: An analogue year is a stretch of the record as long as the season, starting on the decision date’s day and month in that water year; season day one takes its first day, and so on, so no day is repeated or dropped. A season that crosses 1 October takes the end of one water year and the start of the next, labelled by the first. The rain is what the base run used (gaps filled, bias corrected), and the A-pan the daily series where the project has one. Every water year whose stretch lies wholly inside the base run, with rain on every day, is used, up to 40, except the season’s own year (in a hindcast it would be the answer). Every analogue year, under the table, lists each year’s results and the years left out with why: outside the record, a rainless day, the season itself, over the limit, a member that failed. Ten years is the fewest the ranges and the planning figure are given for.

entries.title: Decision date and season end
entries.summary: The first and last days a seasonal outlook covers; it starts from the state the day before. 1 October to 30 April by default.
entries.text: The season is the stretch the WUA plans for. The decision date is its first day: the outlook takes the latest such date the run’s state reaches, and every member starts from the run’s state at the end of the day before. The season end is its last day, at most 366 days on. By default 1 October to 30 April: the summer irrigation months of a winter-rainfall catchment, starting with the water year, when the wet season’s storage is known (confirmed with the client). Settings › Seasonal outlook sets the project’s own, with the planning share and the review date. Reserve months count only when the whole calendar month falls inside the season.

entries.title: Planning figure and planning share
entries.summary: The highest demand level that met the requirement in full in at least the planning share of analogue years (80 % by default).
entries.text: The levels are ranked by the water they ask for, highest first, so a monthly plan ranks by its volume, not by its place in the list. The planning figure is the first that met the requirement in full (every Reserve month met, or no day below the EWR all season) in at least the planning share of the analogue years: “70 %: met the EWR on every day of the season in 12 of 12 analogue years, the highest demand level to do so in at least 80 % of them”. The share is a project setting (Settings › Seasonal outlook), 80 % by default as confirmed with the client; a year at the cut counts. It is a count of past years, not a probability and not a recommendation: the WUA decides the level and publishes it as the restriction notice. With fewer than 10 analogue years there is no planning figure.

entries.title: Review triggers
entries.summary: For each band of total dam storage on the review date, the highest demand level the past years supported for the rest of the season.
entries.text: Turns a rule such as “above x m³ on 1 January, 100 %; between, 85 %; below, 70 %” into a computed table. Total farm dam storage on the review date is split into bands, by default the terciles of the storage the record had on that day each year. For each band the outlook is run again from the review date to the season end, starting with the dams at a storage in the band, and the band’s level is that outlook’s planning figure, or No level when none met the share. Each row gives the years met in full at that level and every level’s count. The review date is 1 January for the default season (the first of the month holding the season’s middle day), and Settings › Seasonal outlook sets the project’s own. Since the season usually starts after the base run ends, the table is drawn on the latest review date the record holds, as a rule for that day of the year: the rest of the state (soil, runoff stores) is that year’s. The WUA decides on the review date; the table only says what the past years supported.

entries.title: Publishing an outlook level to farmers
entries.summary: The level the WUA has set, published from an outlook: each linked farmer sees what it gave their own unit, until the season ends.
entries.text: Once the WUA has decided, an editor picks the Level the WUA has set from the levels the outlook ran and presses Publish to farmers. Each farmer linked to a hydrological unit then sees, on their farm page’s This season card, that level’s figures for their own unit only: the share of its demand met and its dam’s storage at season end as a share of capacity, across the analogue years. Publishing replaces the level published before, and Withdraw takes it down. The app never picks the level.

entries.title: Historical firm yield
entries.summary: The largest steady draft a dam meets on every day of the record, with the rest of the network running as modelled. (m³/day)
entries.text: The headline number of a storage application: how much a dam can supply. The app searches (by bisection) for the largest mean daily draft the dam meets on every day of the record, with the rest of the catchment running as modelled; a failure day is one whose supply falls short of the draft. The draft follows the draft pattern, scaled so its mean over the record is the yield. Work out the yield stores it for everyone, with the failures at that draft; the preview is worked out in this browser and not stored. The yield is the dam’s alone: its boreholes are left out of the search (they are a separate resource with their own registration), and so is the drought restriction rule (the yield is what the dam can give, not what a restriction asks of it). It is historical: it replays the one record the project has, and a yield from many synthetic records can be materially less reliable. A forecast run has no yield, since its tail runs on forecast rain. Under a scenario, Yield under this scenario works it out on the scenario’s model, so a raised dam can be read against its base.

entries.title: Yield at an assurance
entries.summary: The largest draft that fails in at most a set share of water years: 98 % fails in at most 1 year in 50. Firm allows no failure day.
entries.text: A firm yield allows no failure day at all, so one extreme drought in the record can set it alone. A yield at assurance p allows failures in up to 1 − p of the water years: the largest draft for which the water years (October start) with at least one failure day, divided by the water years in the record, is at most 1 − p. The panel offers firm, 98 % (at most 1 year in 50), 95 % (1 in 20), 90 % (1 in 10) and 80 % (1 in 5). A part year at either end of the record counts as a year here. A record shorter than the return period can’t show it: 1 year in 50 on a 30-year record allows no failure year, the same as firm. Pick the assurance the licence or the users ask for, and read the failed years with it.

entries.title: Draft pattern
entries.summary: How a yield’s draft is spread over the year: the same every day, or shaped like the unit’s own irrigation demand by month.
entries.text: Constant draws the same amount every day. Demand shapes the draft like the hydrological unit’s own abstraction demand, its mean for each month of the water year, so a dam that serves irrigation is tested drawing most in the months it is drawn on. Either way the shape is scaled to a mean of 1 over the record, so the yield is the mean daily draft whatever the shape. (The engine also takes 12 custom monthly factors; the panel offers these two.) Use the pattern the water will be drawn in.

entries.title: Storage–yield curve
entries.summary: The yield at 11 dam capacities from 0 to twice the dam’s own, at the chosen pattern and assurance: what a raise would add. (m³ → m³/day)
entries.text: Each point is the dam resized and its yield found as for the dam itself; the dam’s own capacity is one of the 11 points. A resized dam keeps its initial and minimum storage as the same shares of capacity, and its surface follows its own area–volume relation (the same basin filled to another level), so a bigger dam evaporates more, but less than in proportion. A dam with a survey curve is cut at the new top, or carried past it by a power law fitted to its top rows: an extrapolation, so a surveyed curve for the enlarged dam, entered on a scenario, is better evidence. The curve usually rises with capacity. Where it falls, that can be the model, not a fault in the search: a large shallow dam can lose more to evaporation than its extra storage gains, and a dam that starts below its minimum operating level supplies nothing until it fills, which takes a bigger dam longer. The panel says so rather than smoothing it.

entries.title: Forecast run
entries.summary: A run that carries on past the record on forecast rain. Its forecast days stay out of every total; the Forecast panel reads them alone.
entries.text: The days after a record often have a few days of forecast rain. An ordinary run stops where the record does. A forecast run runs on into the forecast, but every summary of the run (hydrological unit totals, curtailment, EWR days, calibration, the Reserve) covers only the days before the forecast starts, so yesterday’s forecast can’t change the figures farmers and regulators rely on. Charts draw the forecast days as a hatched band. The Forecast panel reads the forecast days alone: per hydrological unit the lowest dam level expected, the days short expected and the share of demand supplied, and at the outlet the days the EWR is at risk. Forecast rain is uncertain and so is everything modelled on it: read it as a guide to the coming days. A forecast run can’t be the base of a scenario, a demand sweep or an outlook, and has no yield.

entries.title: Preview of unsaved edits
entries.summary: The last run worked out again with your unsaved edits laid over it, in your browser, and compared with it. Nothing is saved or stored.
entries.text: With model or settings edits not yet saved, Preview on the save bar answers “what would these do?” before you save. It takes the newest run of the catchment’s own model (not a scenario’s), with the input that run read, lays only your unsaved edits over it, and runs it twice on this build’s engine, with and without them, so every difference is your edits’ and never an engine change since that run. The series are always the run’s: a change saved since the run, or new data, is not in the preview, which is why a saved run of the same edits can differ. It compares demand met, demand, shortfall, the units below 95 % supplied, mean natural flow, mean outflow at the outlet and the days the EWR is not met (and NSE, KGE and percent bias when the run has a record to score), then lists the units whose supply moved most. An edit with problems still to fix, or an item added after the run, is left out and named under “Not in this preview”. Nothing is stored, no run is used up, and your edits stay unsaved. With no run yet, run the model first.

entries.title: NSE (Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency)
entries.summary: 1 − Σ(obs − sim)² / Σ(obs − mean obs)². 1 is a perfect fit; 0 or below is no better than the observed mean. (dimensionless, −∞ … 1)
entries.text: Squared errors make NSE dominated by flood peaks, so a good NSE can hide poor low flows. Look at it alongside PBIAS and the hydrograph.

entries.title: PBIAS (percent bias)
entries.summary: 100 × Σ(obs − sim) / Σobs. Positive = the model is too dry; 0 is unbiased. The calibration panel says it in words. (%)
entries.text: Measures volume error regardless of timing — the fit that matters most for allocation questions.

entries.title: RMSE
entries.summary: Root-mean-square error between simulated and observed daily flow, in m³/s. Smaller is better. (m³/s)
entries.text: Has the units of flow, so compare it with the mean observed flow to judge its size.

entries.title: KGE (Kling–Gupta efficiency)
entries.summary: Combines correlation, bias and variability into one score; 1 is perfect. Less peak-dominated than NSE. (dimensionless, −∞ … 1)
entries.text: Often preferred to NSE because it separates timing, volume and variability errors.

entries.title: R² (coefficient of determination)
entries.summary: Share of the day-to-day variation in observed flow that the simulation follows (0–1). Ignores volume errors. (dimensionless, 0 … 1)
entries.text: R² is the square of the correlation between simulated and observed flow. A high R² with a poor NSE usually means the timing is right but the volumes are off — check PBIAS.

entries.title: log-NSE (low-flow fit)
entries.summary: NSE computed on the logarithm of flow, so it rewards a good fit in low flows rather than in floods. (dimensionless, −∞ … 1)
entries.text: Ordinary NSE is dominated by a few big floods. For irrigation and EWR questions the dry-season low flows matter most; log-NSE weights them evenly. A small constant (1 % of mean observed flow) is added before taking logs so zero flows are allowed.

entries.title: Volume error
entries.summary: Simulated minus observed volume over the window, as a % of observed: PBIAS with the opposite sign (+ = too wet). (%)
entries.text: The same information as PBIAS with the opposite sign: +10 % means the simulation is 10 % too wet. The annual volume table shows it per water year, which reveals whether an error comes from a few years or is systematic.

entries.title: Flow-duration signatures (high, mid-slope, low)
entries.summary: Bias of the top 2 % of flows, of the flow-duration curve’s slope from 20 to 70 % exceedance, and of the low 30 %. 0 is ideal. (%)
entries.text: Reported with every fit beside the efficiency scores, after Yilmaz et al. (2008). Each compares the simulated flow-duration curve with the observed one on the same days. High flows: the volume of the top 2 % of flows. Mid-slope: the slope of the curve between 20 % and 70 % exceedance, in log space, which says whether the model’s flows are as flashy or as steady as the river’s. Low flows: the bottom 30 % of the curve, in log flows above its minimum. They score the shape of the flow distribution, not the timing, so a fit can match them with the days in the wrong order. Read them as a check on whichever end of the curve the decision depends on: the low-flow signature for an EWR or low-flow question, the high-flow one for floods and dam spills.

entries.title: Annual water balance (calibration)
entries.summary: Observed and simulated volume per water year, over the days with an observation only, and how far apart they are. (Mm³ ; %)
entries.text: Each water year (1 October to 30 September) adds up the observed and the simulated flow over the same days: those with an observation inside the calibration window and outside the exclusions. A year with observations on less than 90 % of its days in the window is marked part year: it still compares like with like, but it is not that year’s runoff. The last column is the simulated volume against the observed, as a %; the foot of the table is the whole window, the volume error. A model that is right on average can still be too wet in dry years and too dry in wet ones, which this table shows and the scores hide.

entries.title: In-sample (calibration period)
aliases: parameters not from an automatic fit
entries.summary: Scores on the same days the parameters were fitted on. Only then are they in-sample; otherwise the label says why not. (label)
entries.text: Scores on the days a model was fitted on show how well it fits, not how well it predicts: judge fitted parameters by the fit’s validation scores. A run’s calibration scores are labelled in-sample only when its parameters came from Fit automatically for its runoff model, unchanged since, with the same calibration window, exclusions and flow record (engine 0.39.0). Otherwise the label says why not: “parameters not from an automatic fit” (set by hand, imported or left at their defaults), “parameters edited since the fit”, or “fitted on other days” (another window, other exclusions or the other record). Parameters tuned by hand against the record flatter the model as much as a fit does, so read hand-calibrated scores the same way. A run made before engine 0.39.0 says only “calibration period”.

entries.title: Even share
entries.summary: The share of what they needed that hydrological units across the catchment received. A fairness check, not water you are owed.
entries.text: Add up what every hydrological unit in the catchment needed, and what they all received. The even share is the second as a part of the first: if it is 89 %, hydrological units together received 89 % of what they needed. Your hydrological unit page puts your own figure next to it, so you can see whether you did a little better or worse than the catchment as a whole. It is a fairness check, not extra water for you: whether more water can reach your hydrological unit depends on where you are on the river and what is in your dam. It is only shown when there are enough hydrological units in the catchment that it can’t reveal a neighbour’s figures.

entries.title: The river’s reserve
entries.summary: Water the law keeps in the river so it stays healthy for everyone downstream.
entries.text: South African law sets aside some water in every river: the Ecological Reserve. The model checks, day by day, whether the river kept that much water at the outlet and at the measuring points below your hydrological unit that are checked for the reserve. On days it didn’t, the hydrological units upstream are asked to make it up, each in proportion to the water it used up or stored. Water that flows back to the river doesn’t count against you. On some days the river was low only because of low rain; those days ask nothing of anyone.

entries.title: Pump less (for the river)
entries.summary: How much less you would have pumped on the days the river needed water, so it kept its reserve.
entries.text: Your hydrological unit page gives this per day the river needed it, not averaged over the whole season: cutting a little every day does little on the days that matter. If your dam also held back water the river needed, the page says so separately. That part isn’t taken off your pumping; if your dam has an outlet or a bypass, letting that water through helps. This is the model’s estimate. Only a notice from your WUA or from DWS is a restriction.

entries.title: Modelled (worked out by the model)
entries.summary: Worked out by a computer model of the catchment from rain, river flow and crops, not read from a meter or gauge.
entries.text: Nobody measures your dam or your pump for this page. The model works out every day how much rain fell, how much water flowed down the river to your hydrological unit, what your crops needed and what your dam held. It can be wrong. If your meter or gauge plate reads very differently, tell your WUA: it helps them correct the model.

entries.title: Water you needed
entries.summary: What your hydrological unit would have to pump for its crops: what the crops use, allowing for the water lost on the way.
entries.text: Crops need a certain amount of water each day, less what the rain gives them. Not all the water you pump reaches the crop: some is lost to wind, evaporation and run-off. The model allows for that with your irrigation system’s efficiency (drip about 90 %, micro or centre pivot 85 %, sprinklers 75 %, flood 65 %). So "needed" is what you would have to pump, the quantity your meter shows. If the page names the wrong irrigation system for your hydrological unit, tell your WUA.

entries.title: Stop level
entries.summary: The dam level where irrigation stops: your pump intake, or water you keep back. The model won’t irrigate below it.
entries.text: "You can still use" is the water in your dam above this level. The days-left line divides it by what you used over the last 14 days, as a rough guide if nothing flows in. If the page says the model assumes your pump can empty the dam, no stop level is set for your hydrological unit yet: tell your WUA the level your pump stops at.

entries.title: Model: OK, watch or short
entries.summary: The model’s own rating of your season so far. Not a restriction: only a notice from your WUA or from DWS is one.
entries.text: OK: you would have had at least 90 % of the water you needed after pumping less for the river. Watch: 70 to 90 %, or your dam held back water the river needed. Short: under 70 %. These thresholds are a proposal the WUA may change.

entries.title: The copy kept on your phone
entries.summary: Your hydrological unit’s last figures, kept on this phone so they show at once and when there is no signal.
entries.text: It holds only your own hydrological unit’s figures, which you may see anyway. It is removed when you sign out, when someone else signs in on this phone, when you no longer have access to the hydrological unit, and when it hasn’t been opened for 30 days. On a phone you share, choose "Don’t keep a copy on this phone" in the Menu.

entries.title: WUA (Water User Association)
entries.summary: The body of water users that manages water use in your area. It publishes the figures on this page, and its own notices.
entries.text: A Water User Association (WUA) is a body of the water users in an area, set up under the National Water Act. It manages how water is shared among its members, and it issues the notices that tell farmers to use less water. Some areas still have an irrigation board instead, which does the same job until it becomes a WUA. The figures on your hydrological unit page are the ones your WUA published. Only a notice from your WUA or from the Department of Water and Sanitation (DWS) is a restriction. Ask your WUA if anything on the page is unclear.

entries.title: Season outlook (This season)
entries.summary: What the irrigation level your WUA set gave your hydrological unit in past years’ weather. Not a forecast, and not a promise.
entries.text: Before the season, the model runs the whole season from where the catchment’s dams stood on its first day, once with each past year’s rain and river flows. Your WUA looks at what several irrigation levels would give, decides on one and publishes it; the app never picks a level. The card gives what that level gave your own hydrological unit across those past years: about how much of the water you needed you got, the range in most of the years, and how full your dam ended the season. It never shows a neighbour’s figures. The weather this season will be its own, so your share can fall outside that range. Your WUA reviews the level on the date the card gives. Only a notice from your WUA or from DWS is a restriction.

entries.title: Forecast (Next 14 days)
entries.summary: What the model expects for your dam and your water in the next days, on the rain forecast. Not the season outlook, and not a promise.
entries.text: When your WUA publishes a forecast, the model runs the coming days on the rain forecast, starting from your hydrological unit’s latest figures. The card gives the lowest level it expects your dam to reach, and around which day, and on how many of those days you may be short of water. It is not the season outlook. The season outlook looks at the whole season in past years’ weather; the forecast looks only at the next few days, on the rain forecast for them. Rain forecasts change from day to day, so look at the date the card says the forecast was made: when it is more than a few days old, the card says so first. Only a notice from your WUA or from DWS is a restriction.

entries.title: Your registered water
entries.summary: The water use and dam storage registered for your hydrological unit with DWS. Not a right to that water, and not proof a use is lawful.
entries.text: Water users register their water use with the Department of Water and Sanitation (DWS). The card shows what is registered for your hydrological unit today: the surface water and groundwater a year, and the dam storage. It shows only your own totals, never a neighbour’s, and no names or registration numbers. Beside them it puts what the model supplied this season and what your dam holds in the model when full, so you can compare. The model works out your water from rain, river flow and your crops, not from what is registered, so the two can differ. A registered volume is not an entitlement: it doesn’t give you that water, and it doesn’t say whether a use is lawful. If the registered figures look wrong, ask your WUA.

entries.title: Percent, m³ and ML
entries.summary: A percent compares two amounts, such as the water you received with what you needed. m³ and ML are amounts of water: 1 ML is 1 000 m³.
entries.text: "83 % of what you needed" means you received 83 parts for every 100 parts of water your hydrological unit needed this season. "40 % full" means your dam holds 40 parts for every 100 it holds when full. A cubic metre (m³) is 1 000 litres. A megalitre (ML) is a million litres, which is 1 000 m³. The ML and m³ buttons under "Water you received this season" switch the volumes on your hydrological unit’s pages between the two: the water is the same, only the unit changes. Your choice is saved to your account and kept on this phone; you can also change it on your account page, under Language and units.

entries.title: Alert emails
entries.summary: Emails that tell you when the model puts your dam below the level your WUA set, or when your WUA publishes a restriction notice.
entries.text: Your WUA decides which alerts are switched on in the catchment, and for a dam alert the level it warns at. On the Alert emails page in your account you choose, for each one, whether you get it right away, in a summary once a day at 06:00, or not at all. On a day with many alerts, only the first few come right away; the rest wait for the next morning’s summary. A dam alert is the model’s estimate, from the latest figures or from the rain forecast. It is not a restriction: only a notice from your WUA or from DWS is one. Every alert email has a link to stop that kind of email, and one to say whether it was useful. If emails to your address bounce back, alert emails are paused; the Alert emails page says so and lets you turn them back on.

entries.title: Two-step sign-in
entries.summary: After your password, a 6-digit code from an app on your phone or from an email, so someone who learns your password still can’t get in.
entries.text: It is your choice: your hydrological unit’s pages don’t need it. Turn it on under Two-step sign-in on your Account page, in one way or both. An authenticator app on your phone makes a new code every 30 seconds. A code by email is sent each time you sign in and works for 10 minutes. The app is the safer of the two, since anyone who can read your email can also use a code sent there. The first time you turn it on, you get ten recovery codes, shown only once. Download or copy them, and keep them somewhere safe, away from your phone. Each one works once, in place of a code. Your Account page says how many are left, and makes a new set when you need one. If you lose your phone, sign in with a recovery code. If you have lost your recovery codes too, choose to use a recovery code on the step that asks for the code, then the link for lost recovery codes, and we email you a link. Once you open it, two-step sign-in is removed after 3 days, and you are signed out on every device; nothing else about your account changes. The wait keeps your account safe from someone who knows your password: we email you every day until then with a link to cancel, and signing in with a code cancels it too.

entries.title: An invitation to a catchment
entries.summary: An email asking you to join a catchment, usually from your WUA. Nothing changes until you accept, and you can decline.
entries.text: Your WUA, or whoever models the catchment for it, invites you by your email address. The invitation names the catchment, who sent it, what you join as, the hydrological units it links you to, and the date it is open until. After that date, ask whoever sent it for a new one. When you accept as a farmer, you see the pages of those hydrological units: the figures your WUA published for them, your dam and your water. You never see another hydrological unit’s name or figures. When you decline, whoever sent it sees only that you declined. Nobody can make you join. The people who run the catchment’s model see your name, your email address and which hydrological units you are linked to. Other farmers in the catchment never see your name, your email address or your figures. If the hydrological units named aren’t yours, decline and tell your WUA.
